, P:ittrg• SUNBEAM AND DEWDROP. Wawa on•-• 0, sunbeam! 0, sunbeam! I would be a sunbeam too. When the winter chill Hushes lark and nil; When the thunder showers Bow the weeping flowers; 1 , When the shadows creep, Cold, and dark, and deep, We would follow, swift, and bright, /777 r ' Blending all our love and light, • Chasing winter,trim and hoary, Shining all the tears away :1 Turning all the gloom to glory, • , , All the darkness into day. 0, dewdrop! 0, dewdrop I would be a dewdrop too. When the fatal glow— ? Sultry, still and slow— Makes the scentless flowers Droop in withering bowers: Leaf and shade and bloom Touched with early doom; We would follow, sweet and bright, Blending life and love and light; Making what was parched and dreary Glad and lovely, fresh and fair: Softly cheering what was weary, Sparkling, star-like, everywhere. FRANCES RIDLEY HAVERGAL.

THE TURNING-POINT. His wife besought him, with imploring words To spend the evening at home; for months He, with increasing frequency; had joined A group of friends who loved his Company. And beifig gifted with a splendid voice He sung, and drank too freely of the rich Red wine they pressed upon him; till at length His loving, tender-hearted wife was shocked To see the one for whom she would have dared All that a true, and faithful wife could dare, Rapidly losing all his choicest friends, Rapidly drifting to a drunkard's fate. His little daughter clung about his knees, And, in her pretty-, winning way, begged bard That her own darling Pa would'sing to her Some little bedtime song, but---all in vain. The evil habit was too strong. He rose, Made some convenient excuse, and went To join his friends at their convivial feast. Scarce had he left the house, and reached the gate, When he remembered he had left his purse; And, though hie knew his income scarce supplied His family requirements; and his wife With careful thought strove to economise, Be hurried back to fetch it, As he stole , Softly across the garden he could see, • By the soft glow of firelight, on her knees, His little daughter by her mother's side. Spellbound, he heard every word, as she Sang sweetly, "now flay me down to sleep." The very song which his own mother taught His infant lips to utter ere she kissed Her only boy, before she went to rest. Back, through the long forgotten years, it came As fresh, as of but yesterday. The tears Coursed slowly down his cheeks; his bearded lips Compresied with strong emotion, as again r His little daughter said, in silvery tones, "God bless Papa, and please to send him home' 1 Sober, and soon." Scarce had she said the words When, utterly regardless of his friends And:all the pleasure of their company, Be went into the room and closed the door, And put away his hat, took up the child, And, to her great surprise, kissed her, and sung The little hymns she loved, and when his wife, With anxious wonder, gazed as if she thought It was a dream, he kissed her many a time As fondly as of yore, and promised her ' That never, never more, would he forsake His God-sent household treasures for the sake Of his convivial friends.: but stay with them. When, tired and sleepy, little Mary went To bed, she whispered to her dear mamma, "I think that God did hear and answer me Almost as quick as that queer telephone Through which you talk to Pa when he's away." JOHN RYLEI ROBINSON

Tire Diersamemi.--Smitii keeps a savage dog on his premises, and near its kennel a board is displayed with the warning in large letters, "Beware of the dog." "I suppose," said Jones, pointing to the warning, "you have painted that sign in large letters so that he who runs may read." "No," said Smith, "but that he who reads may run." A FORTUNE IN A HAT.—There died in Germany not long since a wealthy old gentleman whose hat was' the beginning of his fortude. As a boy he had served an apprenticeship to a turner of wood. In Germany an apprentice having served his full time is supposed to travel a year or more, in order that he may see the world, and gain an extended idea of business before he begins to work for himself. Our boy set forth, with his scanty wardrobe upon his shoulder, and a daintily- turned staff of boxwood and ebony in his band. In th 6 oourse a his first year of travel, young Martin Muhl called at an extensive and thriving machine shop for work. The ragged boy, sore, weary, barefoot, and pale- faced, did not look promising, and the foreman told him they had no work to give. He was turning away sad- eyed and downcast when the proprietor of the shop chanced to enter. " Ah, my brave lad, tell me what sort of a hat is that you have upon your head ?" "A wooden hat, sir, made from fir, with a rind of fine white wood." "A wooden hat ? Whers did you find it ?" "1 made it, sir." "How ?" "I turned it upon my lathe. I had a long way to go, and no hat, and as I had no money, I made this, thinking it would answer every purpose for keeping off both beat and rain." " But,!rny dear boy, your hat is of a decided oval form, which cannot 'be turned upon a common lathe. How do you account for that?" "Nevertheless, sir, I made it, as I have said. I had but to find my central point, and from that I worked till the hat was finished." The far-sighted proprietor at mace engaged the lad, and the next day set him to work ea a last for the bootmaker, a piece of work which the boy turned off in perfect form, and in the highest style of finish. "Upon my life," cried the proprietor, holding up the Last, "here we have a genius we have long re- quired." And so it proved. The boy became a man beneath that rooftree, married the daughter of the wealthy proprietor, and himself died, in the fullness of his years, one of the wealthiest men in that part of the country. Lafleur SHOOTING STORIES.—When holding office in eamp on one occasion, an iguana, a lizard between three and tour feet long, suddenly appeared, probably from a hole within the tent, and, dashing about in a state of great alarm, put to flight the Brahmin scribes. The in- cident stimulated the author's moonshi to recount some Munchausen-like stories. He declared solemnly that in ancient days iguanas were employed in gaining access to fortified places. "A large iguana, sahib," he said, "is so strong that if three or four men laid hold:of its tail, he could drag them up a wall or a tree." He told of a courageous postal runner, who, meeting a bear which tried to seize him, slipped behind a tree. The bear at once hugged the tree; the runner pulling at the bear's forelegs caused Bruin to hug the fiercer, until his:violent exertions caused his death! This is as good as the Baron's wild-boar adventure. In Mr. Forbes's opinion, the point to hit in shooting big game is high up behind the shoulder, just beneath the spine. A bullet;there is more deadly than lower down. The author is surprised at finding in a puddle left by a shower of rain a lively fish, about an inch in length. No river or pond was near, and Mr. Forbes concludes that the fish had descended in a shower. He seems to be unaware that in India fish of the carp species (as this one appeared.to be) hide in the mud of a drying up pond, to reappear in the rainy season. He gives the following account of a courageous act on the part of a native, who, we may observe, was a brave Mahratta, and not a" mild Hin- doo :"—Another leopard was killed duringtherlins, near Sedasheghur, seventeeri miles north of Belikeri, in a very gallant manner by a fine young fellow of the same race as my friends the spearmen. Wild animals find .the deeper forests unpleasant quarters in the monsoon rains; eloudy skies, frequent showers, the' perpetual drip from the trees, and above all the persecution of the tiny jungle leeches, drive them to the more open glades, where they have the benefit of occasional sunshine; and at such seasons they are at no great distance from human habitations. Thus it happened that the leopard in question was found at daylight in the middle of a small hamlet, trying to conceal itself under the low, projecting eaves of one of the huts. There were no fire- arms at hand,so the young fellow who discovered the leopard, folding his goat's-hair blanket over his left arm, toad armed with his sheep sickle-shaped wood-knife, made at the brute/ and receiving its spring on his left arm and shoulder, gashed it so terribly about the vitals that he killed it without sustaining any very serious yunes to himself. His shoulder was a little torn by the leopard's claws, and he was slightly bitten on the arm where the leopard had got its teeth through the folds of the blanket, but that was all. The skin was brought in to me for the usual reward, and I saw that the leopard was of ne.ereat size, but still a very formidable antago- nist. its conqueror as a remarkably handsome young saan, and looked like a bronze cast of the Apollo." It is commonly believed that tiger shooting from a tree is safest for the sportsman. No doubt it is So as a rule, which has Unfortunate exceptions. Near Hyderabad an officer and a shikari were dragged from a tree by an in- furiated tigress, and so dreadfully mauled that they both died not long afterwards.—Gorden 8. Forbes, Madras (7.8. Fenn, who has recently become totally blind, writes :—" The difference between the sleep- ing and waking state is not so marked as might at first be expected, for, unless by an effort I remind myself that lalalkbelianndd tlairi3ngllltyo firiimendn,eaatrter as ashi nearly vif 'Aridl'aws I. shloUla do at times in a dream, the fact that in reality I cannot see him in either state being scarcely more present to me in one than in the other." PREPARED FOR MARRIAGE.—" Yes, stranger," said a passenger from Texas, "I'm goin' down East on an im- portant errand. -Don't mind telling you that I'm going to be married. You can imagine how good-natared and jolly I feel." "Yee, but don't you feel a little anxiety,a i little trepidation about taking such an important step n life ?" "Nary a trep, stranger." "Have you ever been married before ?" "No, but I've been in one fight with Injuns, two scrimmages with cowboys, an' went through four cyclones. I'm no chicken." . Music a. OATS.—A report says that a horse in Brooklyn would rather listen to music than eat. The report is founded on the fact that whenever a street band is play- ing in front of the stable where the horse is kept, the horse will not touch the oats in his trough. The inference may not be accurate. It does not follow necessarily that a horse likes music because he does not eat his oats while the music is playing. It may be that he wishes the music would go along so that he will be able to at. It is well known that there are certain kinds of music which will destroy the appetite of a horse or anything else. . RECKLESSNESS or Men us THE Russtax Atom—Some Russian troops were being transported on a steamer in the Black Sea. The waves rolled heavily, and the soldiers were in great daqer of falling into the water. A surgeon, Dr. Skariatim, suggested that means be taken to prevent that calamity. "What matters it ?" replied an officer; "we have enough of that sort of mer- chandise. A soldier is not like a horse, for the loss of which we are held responsible." Not long ago a young Commissariat officer named Dantchenko committed suicide, because, as he wrote to his wife, "The soldiers and waggoners of my brigade are in rags; they freeze as they sleep on the bare ground, and I can do nothing to help them." A PUNSTER'S ETYMOLOGT.—Swift, in his "Art of Pun- ning," gave the etymological rule, where a man hunts a pun through every, letter and syllable of a word. For example :—Achilles, being a hero of a restless nature, never gave himself any repose, either in peace or war; and, therefore, as Guy, Earl of Warwick, was called a kill-cow, and another terrible fellow a kill-devil, so this general was dubbed a kilt ease, or destroyer of ease, and at length, by, corruption, Achilles! Mark you the brevity? Andromache, the wife of Hector, he traces thus :—Her father was a Scotch gentleman of a noble family, but, being a foreigner in Troy, to which city he led some of his countrymen in the defence of Priam, as Dictys Cretensis learnedly observes, Hector fell in love with his daughter, the father's name being Andrew Mac- kay. The young lady was called by the same name only a little softened by the Grecian accent! Scotch historians will no doubt be greatly interested in this in- formation, as probably hitherto it has escaped their notice. - Wm) Does Ist IN-DlA.—Wild dogs hunt their quarry in packs. They are so pertinacious and staunch that they seldom fail to run down the swiftest deer. They possess many of the qualities of the domestic dog. They seldom molest man, but no other animal is safe from their attacks. I once fell in with a pack of wild dogs not far from Pvjaroo, as I was riding to Sispara. Ap- parently they had just concluded a run, as they were lying at ease on the sward outside a wood. I cantered up to the pack in order that I might see the wild dogs more closely. They did not run off as I expected, but rose lazily and moved but a short distance.,2When I re- turned to the bridle road, four of the dogs rose and trotted after me sniffing at my horse's heels. On one side of the scarped path the hill rose steeply, and when one of the dogs leaped up the bank, and trotted along- side-me, he was on a level with my saddle, and not three paces off. I thought it necessary to draw my:hunting knife, and held it between me and this inquisitive dog, as I did not half like these attentions. I kept the horse at a walk, lest they should fancy he was a beast of the chase, and so we went on for about a hundred yards, to a point where a small stream crossed the track. Here the clogs began lapping the water, and lay down in it, nor did they follow me any further; probably they never meant to do so, but their familiarity, so different from the habits of wolf or jackal, struck me as very strange.— Wild Life in Canary and Ganjam, by Gordonl S. Farbei, Madras C.S. THE WOMEN OF AUSTRIA'S CAPITAL.—The education of girls in Vienna is somewhat peculiar, and perhaps worthy of note. Up to fifteen years of age they are kept ats their studies, but are not deprived of society. They dress very simply, rarely wearing a silk gown till the day they leave the schoolroom for the ballroom. After they leave school they go through a year's, or even two years', teaching in the pantry and in the kitchen, under some member of the family, or even in some cases in another family, under trained cooks. They may never be required to cook a dinner, but they are thus rendered independent of cooks and servants, as they learn to do everything themselves long before theybegin housekeeping on their own account. When married they are most affectionate wives.and mothers. An Austrian lady, in fact, is as accomplished and learned as an Eng- lish governess, as good a housekeeper and cook as a Ger- man, as witty in society as a Parisian, as passionate as an Italian and as handsome as an American—some of the most. Italian, women in Europe being in Vienea. Germans, and also Austrians, are celebrated for their stocks of linen. Here, as soon as a girl is born, the weaving of her linen is begun, and every year a piece or a number of yards is set aside for her trousseau, ready for her marriage. Grandmammas on their side are not idle. They pass their time in knitting for their grand- children, supplying not only present needs, but also lay- ing aside for the future, a dozen dozens of stockings of every kind being the usual number for any bride's trous- seau, and some of these knitted stockings are as fine as the finest woven ones. An Austrian girl or lady is never, I may say, seen without some kind of work in her hand. Ladies work even in society. They do nothing at balls, of course, but I think that is the only exception to the rule. When several labour thus together in a family, one reads aloud while the others work, and thus they keep abreast of all the newest literature of the day. Not a minute of their day is lost, and, in Solomon's words, they find a time for everything—for work, housekeep- ing, visiting, learning, balls, amusement, and even for love.

THE WOOING OF WiLLIAM AND MART HOWFFT.— Again it was autumn, twelve moiihs after our Leicester visits, when William Howitt, having been to Lichfield Cathedral to see the monument, finished the previous year by Chantrey, of the sleeping children, the daugh- ters of the Rev. W. Robinson, came round by Uttoxeter ostensibly to visit his cousin, Susanna Firth. We were delighted to accept her invitation to meet him. He ad- dressed us with great cordiality and spoke in gratifying terms of his desire to make our acquaintance, having heard much of our tastes and pursuits from his cousin. He described with feeling the exquisitely tender group in marble, which he had just seen at Lichfield. Our father's religious scruples had debarred us from ever entering the Cathedral, and of this new monument by Chantrey, then creating a well-deserved sensation, we were equally ignorant. He spoke of the nature and im- portance of sculpture; it was again an entirely new sub- ject to us. We had already sought to understand pic- torial, we were henceforth to learn the value of plastic art. Botany was the first intellectual topic on which Anna and I ventured to open the treasures of our know- ledge to our new acquaintance. It was in a walk which he took with his cousin and us that same afternoon. Crossing pleasant pastures, where we had gathered in the spring the meadow fritillary, a peculiar and beauti- ful flower, which this accomplished botanist told us he himself had never found, we went by the banks of the sweet placid Dove to the old mill, where all around was peaceful and picturesque. It is nearly sixty-seven years since that walk, which comes back to me with such fresh fragrant memories as I write. Thanks be to the blessed Lord, the great Botanist, for the simple, natural tastes which he had given me! It was the first link in the golden chain of His providence which united my life drith that of one of the best and purest of men. Be- fore the close of the year I became the affianced bride of William Howitt. He was six-and-twenty and I was nineteen. The tastes of my future husband and my own were strongly similar, so also our mental culture; but he was in every direction so far in advance of me as to become my teacher • and guide. Knowledge in the broadest sense was the aim of our intellectual efforts; poetry and nature were the paths that led to it. Of ballad poetry I was already enamoured. William made us acquainted with the realistic life pictures of Crabbe; the bits of nature, life, and poetry in the vignettes of Bewick ; with the earliest works of Wordsworth, Cole- ridge, and Shelley; the first marvellous prose produc- tions of the author of " Waverle7 ;" the Edinburgh Review, and other works of power and influence. I say us, be- cause Anna was as it were, the very double of thyself, and shared in every advantage that came to me. We had always been great walkers, but girls alone cannot tramp the country as men and boys do. With William as a most delightful and efficient companien, we could enjoy to the full the Arcadian scenery that surrounded us. We:took him to our frivourite Altoni Towers, that wonderful region of beauty and romance, which was growing up year after year under the Earl of Shrews- bury', taste and religious ardour; to the secluded ruins of Q•oxden Abbey; to the airy heights of the Weaver Hills; to the ancient lordly oaks and birches of Begot Woods; to the still more hoary fragment of nature's antiquity, Chartley Moss; to Tutbury and S,udbury.• It was a' happy time, yet accompanied by some little clouds and rufftings of the smooth current of daily life, which must always be the case when strong characters are brought into juxtaposition. On the 16th of fourth mOnth, 1822, we were married, I wearing my first silk gown—a very pretty dove colour—with bonnet of the same material, and a soft white silk shawl. Shawls were greatly in vogue, especially amongst Friends, and my attire was thought very appropriate and becoming. For a wedding tour my husband took me to every spot of beauty or old tradition in his native county—roman- tic, picturesque Derbyshire.—Good Words.

Herr 'Oppenheimer, of Hanover, is said to be the greatest breeder of horses in Europe. He generally has on an average 600 horses in his stables, and the colours are invariably chestnut or bay. ' Advices from the Canadian North-West announce that nothing has arisen to interfere with the satisfactory har- vesting of the crops, and that they are now nearly secured in, all parts in excellent condition. . The harvest has proceeded with much interruption in Yorkshire. Barley is turning out the heaviest crop. The first delivery of new wheat is three weeks later than in 1884, which was an e2cpeptienally early year, and is sell- ing at 295. to 325. per duarter. The price of best bread has been reduced in East Yorkshire to 21(1. the 21b. loaf. The sale of Shropshire rams and ewes from Mr. J. Darling's flock took place at Beaudesart recently. Some rams fetched up to 14, 15, 17, and 20 guineas. Five splendid show shearling ewes brought £78.155. ; five by Royal Hero" brought £2B 15s. ; and four lots of fine shearling ewes brought £2O each. The :others ranged from £l5 12s. 6d. to £l9 7s. 6d.

INJUDICIOUS Fele:amt.—Alluding to this subject, ones writes :—At this season of the year horses are frequently injured by being over-fed, and this is often brought about by farmers labouring under the impression that because a horse is hard worked he must therefore have a large amount of grain food. This is a mistake; for if grain is given in too large quantities its tendency is to destroy the appetite of the animal, besides souring its stomach, which is still worse than feeding insufficiently. THE STORM AND THE HARVEST.—SIOTIIIy weather has characterised the past week, the gales of the nights of Thursday and Saturday having done considerable damage to odtstanding crops and to unthatched ricks. The rainfall has been very heavy, and reports of sprouted grain have come from the later districts, where a considerable bulk of the harvest remains in the fields. The deliveries of native wheat have been consequently restricted, and complaints as to the condition of the samples offered have been very general. In London the trade has been slow at unaltered values. VALUE OF SALT AS MANURE.—" J. W." asks if some reader will give him the manure value of salt Some years ago he sowed 8 to lOcwt. of land salt per acre on poor sandy soil, and then fold et sheep all over the land and Moved them every day. He thinks the! salt made the land more solid, but cannot tell the manure value. He has now received, by mistake, a quantity of ground rock salt instead of land salt. Can he apply it the same as land salt, viz., scwt. to the acre, or will it be danger- ous to the crop, as he has had no experience in rock salt?—Ground rock salt may be applied lathe same way as you would apply land salt. THE Filexcaz HARVEST.—Messrs. Barthelemy Estienne, of Marseilles, have published their annual estimate of the French harvest, according to which wheat is very good in three departments, good in forty-three, pretty good in twenty-six, and poor in four. Oats are very good in five departments, good in forty-six, pretty good in twenty, and poor in fiftern. Barley is very good in eight departments, good in forty-two, pretty good in seventeen, poor in eight, and bad in one. Rye is very good in three departments, good in thirty-three, pretty good in twenty, poor in seventeen, and bad in ,two. In- dian corn is very good in one department (the Yers), geod in twenty-five, pretty good in seven, and poor in five departments. WOODEN-LEGGED Cows.—Mr. W. E. Litt, M.R.C.V.S., Shrewsbury, writes to the Standard with reference to the report of 'A novel feat in surgery",—namely, the ampu- tation of a cow's leg by Mr. Suarry, V.S. :—" This is by no means so novel a feat as may be supposed. I myself performed the operation, close under the knee-joint, in a badly comminuted case of. fracture, so 'long ago as August,. 1878. The animal was a pedigree shorthorn heifer, in calf, and of considerable value for breeding purposes. There was no difficulty at all in fitting her with a wooden substitute, and this she wore for some three years, rearing in the meantime three very valuable calves. I believe this was the first recorded case of the kind in Europe. There is no reason why amputation should not be resorted to in breeding animals when ne- cessary, and in pedigree stock there should be no hesita- tion whatever. I have repeatedly performed the opera- tion on pet dogs." THE ENCLOSURE OF COMMONS.—The Mark Lane El.- press says :—Mr. H. R. Grenfell, in the Nineteenth Cen- tury, defends the enclosure of commons, and advocates the enclosure of those remaining open. He declares that all commons which do not belong to the Crown are private property, but does not bring forward a tittle of evidence to support that statement. If they were pri- vate property they would not be unenclosed to this day. Mr. Grenfell is of opinion that the immense open spaces such as the New Forest and Dartmoor are not needed as playgrounds for the people in the districts; therefore, he argues, they had better be enclosed, except a portion in each case as a recreation ground. He quite ignores the real objection to the enclosure of commons, which is to their enclosure by private persons, instead of by the public and for the public benefit. Apparently he would let every lord of a manor having some rights over a com- mon take the whole after paying some kind of c9mpen- sation to the commoners. But the commoners have no right to sell the birthright of their successors for all future generations, and in so doing they are conniving at the theft of public property. Mr. Grenfell's article is as weak as an article well could be. Issscr Pssrs.—ln a letter to Mr. Benjamin Walker, Hay-a-Park, Knaresborough, on the 24th August last, Miss Eleanor A. Ormerod, Consulting Entomoligist to the Royal Agricultural Society, writes as follows as to some black insects found on corn forwarded to her by Mr. Walker:—" Your insects are the corn aphides which are doing so much harm in various places in the north of England and south of Scotland. They are like the aphis (green fly) of the rose, or hop or turnip aphis, in their habits, and the hot dry weather we had for so long has been exceedingly favourable to their multiplication. The injury they cause is by driving their suckers into the tender part of the stem or base of the Haunches of grain in the ear, and by this means not only drawing away the juices, but likewise pricking, as it were, the tissues full of little holes, which are very bad for healthy growth. It does not seem possible to do anthing to check attack when it is established, for no washes:such as are of service with hop aphis can be applied to the wheat ears—neither would dressings be of use. The only remedy that appears to me to he in our power ieto pre- vent small—really insectivorous—birds being tdriven away. Some birds (especially tit mice) would be likely to do good now, and also on the stubbles, by clearing the insect pests that would be in due course establishing themselves to start another season's mischief. To this end I would advise giving an eye to that worst driver away of small birds, the sparrow. This bird does not, as far as we know, when in the fields at this time of the year, clear either corn aphis, cora thrips, corn !red mag- got. or other corn insect; and if to its other habits it adds driving away the insectivorous birds that help, it would be highly desirable the matter should be looked to." TEST THE Cows.—Every owner should know what cows are individually worth to him. Very few herds can be found in the country but will contain cows that not only do not ,yield any profit to their owners, but are even kept at a loss, which loss must be made up by the profitable cows. Many cows will give a good quantity of milk while fresh, but will hold out so poorly as to be unprofitable in the end. A cow giving a smaller quan- tity per day but holding out nine months in the year, will often prove to be the more profitable cow. Again, a cow giving a large mess of milk, but of poor quality,

may not be worth her keep, especially if butter-making I is the object. There are many points to consider in de- ' termining the value of a cow; the quantity of milk given• in a year, its value for the purpose for which the. cow is kept, the amount of food required to keep her, her disposition, ease of milking, &c. It is: attention to such points that will often turn a losing business into a Ipaying one. \ln these times of low prices and small pro- fits, business men of all classes expect to watch all corners stop all leaks, and use less expense, and utilise everything. Manufacturing interests which a few years ago yielded a large profit now often depend for profit on utilising what then was wasted. The agriculturists in the various departments must not expect to succeed unless they pursue a similar policy. The: dairyman then should have his scales and record book,and should weigh and record *hat he gives his cows, and what they give him in return, .until he knows what each cow is capable of doing: then, knowing the unprofitable ones, he can weed them out. Farmers do too much guessing in their business, and truse too much to chance, luck, and the moon, and de too little close figuring. Figures are wonderful eye-openers, and form mighty interesting reading sometimes.—Colmaal Rural World. PONY BREWING IN Scarimen.—Lords A. and L. Cecil, who have attained much distinction in Clydesdale . horse breeding, are now turning attention to the improvement of Highland ponies on the farm of Orchardmains, and their efforts so far have been attended with gratifying suecess. Two years ago they established epony breed- ing stud by the purchase of seven mares of the pure Ice- land breed. These ponies stand 12 hands highZare ex- ceedingly . hardy, have strong legs and backs,:and are noted for their endurance and sure-footedness. They have somewhat large, heavy heads, and, though very fast, are deficient in style and action.' They stand about two hands higher than the Shetland pony. For crossing these Iceland mares, and breeding large ponies, no class of stallions could equal Arabrt ns, and their lordships are the fortunate possessors of wo Arabian Ilona nf the right type. One of these, The Pasha, is a Turkish Arab, bought from a Jew hi Odessa. The Pasha is 15 years old, and was originally steel grey in colour, but is now quite white. He stands 14 hands high, and has great speed and action, with immense mettle and hardiness. Lord Arthur Cecil, who rides 15 stones, has ridden The Pasha at the canter for 16 hours at a stretch, and often galloped him for hours. together, but never saw him tired. It is not intended to stop at the first cross' be- tween Iceland and Arab. By judicious mating of the first cross with a pure Arab sire, it is hoped to 'breed a race of ponies with greatly improved style, and action, and speed, and which shall be far hardier than the so- called pure bred pony. Hadeed, their lordships' second Arab:stallion, is a singularly fit horse to use to the cross between the Icelanders and The Pasha, and for that pur- pose Hadeed was putchased from his breeder, Mr. Baird, ef Urie. He is a fur-year-old, bay in colour, got by 4' osta, out of a pure bred Arab mare, and is onepf the very few pure bred Arab horses that have been bred and reared in this country. He stands 15-1 i hands, and is very compact, with great bone and constitution, and good style and action. Their lordships have:also four Highland mares of a larger stamp than the Icelands, 14-2 ' hands or thereabouts, covered by Hadeed, from;which they hope to produce ponies something the same ithityle as the Iceland cross, only bigger. This year six Of the Iceland mares have foals running at '', foot, and the off- spring proixdsetto excel the original stock in all the best points of the sire. In action, Reed, oourage,leroper, firmness of bone and muscle, and in general appearance, they seem.to have strongly inherited the good qualities of the Arabian. In point of size, too, they will be bigger than the Icelanders. .

Mr. EnlroB.—While spending a few days at the pleasant seaside town of Aberystaltb, Osralganskire, 'ales. I heard related what seethed to me either a fabulous story or a mar- vellous cure.

The story was that a poor sufferer who had not been able to lie down in bed for six long tears given up to die by all the Doctors. had been seedily cured bygome Patent Medicine, It was related with the more implicit confidence from the circum- stance, as was said. that the Vicar of Lianrystyd was familiar with the facts, and c uld vouch for the truth of the report.

Raving a little euricalty to knew how such stories grow in travelling. I took the liberty while at the village of Llanrystyd to call upon the Vicar, the Rev. T Evans, and to inoulre abou this wonderful cure. Though a total stranger to him, both he and his wife most graciously entertained me in a half hour's con- versation. principally touching the case of Mr. Push, in which they seemed to take a deep and svmpatheic interest having been familiar with his sufferings, and now rejoioe I In what seernel to them a most remarkable cure.

• The vicar remarked that he presumed his name had. been connected with the report from his having mentioned the cams ,to Mr. John Thomas, a chemist, of Llanon. He said Mr. Pugh was formerly a re‘ident of their parish, but was now living in the parlsh•of Llanddelnol. He strongly vouched for Mr. William Vu ;h's character as a , respectable farmer and worthy of credit. I left the venerable Vicar with a livelier aware of the happy reialon of a pastor and people, feeling that be was sue who truly sympathiseel , with who are afflicted in mind, body, or estate. On-env return to aberystwith, I was impressed with a desire to see Mr. Pugh, whose reputation stood so high. His farm I. called Panemi-Mawr, signifying " above the dingle," situ• ated near ths summit, of a smooth round hill, overt-silting a beautiful valley in which, is situated the lovely Ivy mantled °burets of Lianddeinol. I found Mr. Pugh, apparently about 40 years old, of medium height, rather slight, with a pleasant and intelligent face. I told him I had heard of his great afflic- tion and of his remarkable and almost miraculous relief, and that I had come to learn from his own lips what there was of truth in the reports.

Mr. Pugh remarked that hi; neighbours had taken a kindly and sympathetic interest in his case for many years, but of late their interest had been greatly awakened by a happy change in his condition. What you report aa having hetird abroad, said he. is substantially true with one exception. I never under- stood that my case was ever given up as hopeless by any phy- sician. I have been treated by several ssiccters hereabouts, as good as any in Wales, but unfortunately no prescription uf theirs ever brought the desired relief. Fifteen years ago, he said, I first became conscious of a sour and deranged stomach and loss of appetite, which the doctors told me was dyspepsia. What food I could hold in my ate.msett seemed to ao me no good, and was often thrown up with painful retching.. This was followed after a time with hoarse- ness, and • raw soreness of the throat which the doctors called bronchitis, and I was treated for that, but with little,succees. Then came shortness a breath and a sense of suffocation, es- pecially nigh s, with clammy sweat, and I would have to get out of bed and sometimes open a door or window la winter weather to fill my lungs with the coldish-. About six years ago I became so bad that I could not sleep In bed, but bad to take my unquiet rest and dreamy sleep sitting loan armchair. My aftbctio,, seemed to be working downward into my bovnis as well as upwards into my lunws and throat. In the violent roughing spasms which grew more frequent, my abdomen would expand and eolla.se and at times it would seem that I should suffocate. All this time I was reduced :in strength so that I could perform no hard la- bour and my spirits were oon•equently much depressed. Early in this last spring I had a still more severe spasmodic attack, and my family and neighbours became alarmed, be- lieving that certainly I wouid not survive, when a neighbour, who had some knowledgs, or had heard of the medicine sent to Abervstwith by the driver of .he Omnibus Post, corn seven mile; distant, and fetched a bottle of Mother Biegers Curative Syrup.

This medicine they administered to me according to the directions, when to their surprise and delight no less than my Own, the spurn ceased. I became at ease, and my sto- mach was calmed. My bowels were moved a. by a gentle cathartic, and I felt a sense of quiet comfort all through such as I had not before realised in many years. I could walk around the house and breathe comfortably in a few hours after I had taken the medicine. I have continhed to take the medi- cine daily now for something over two mcnths, and I can lay down and sleep sweetly at nights and have not sInC9 had a recurrence of those terrible spasms and sweatings. I have been so long broken down and reduced in my whole system the I have not tried to perform any very herd out-door labour, deeming it best to be prudent lest by over exertion I may do myself Injury before my strength is fully mitered. I feel that my stomach Is d bowels have been and are being thoroughly renovated and renewed by the medicine. In fact I feel like a new min. - -

I have been much congratulated by my neighbours. especi- ally by the good Vicar of Llacnrystyd, who with his sympa- Untie wife have come three miles to shed tears 0; joy en my recovery. bade Mr. Pugh goodbye, happy that even one at haat among thousands had found a remedy for an aggravating dig. ease
Believing this remarkable ease of Dyspeptic Asthma sh-uld be known to the public, I beg to submit the above facts al they are related to me.

Moro FOR GREENIFICH.—" The early Boord picks up De W orms." —Punch. A half-famished fellow tells of a baker whose loaves had been growing'smaller by degrees and beautifully less, who, when going on his round to serve his customers, stopped at the door of one of them and knocked. The lady within exclaimed, "Who's there ?" and was answered, "The baker." "What do you want ?" "To leave your bread." "Well, you needn't make such a ' fuss about it; put it through the keyhole." How innocently unfortunate is the utter frankness of childhood. Young Orotund Delsarte, the dramatic reader, was taking tea, on invitation, with the family, and in the evening favoured the guests with a few of his most startling recitations. He was approached by the midget of the family, a fairy in looks, but with an early development of speech. "Now, I know why you talk so loud when you speak pieces," she said to him. "And why, my dear?" with a little patronising stroke of the golden hair. "'Cause you're a Bellowcutionist'; ma said so." That child will be put to bed early after this.

SOIENCE, ART, &o Lord Wolseley has just finished a complete revision of his well-known Soldier's Pocket Book." I According to • the Voltaire, one of the largest picture dealers of:Berlin has committed suicide after losing up- wards of 2,000,000 f. in the gambling hells of Paris. Lady Bmssey is about to publish an account of the recentjourney made in search of health in the Sunbeam to Norway. In order to lend a pictureSqueness to the facts, the little volume will be illustrated by photographs taken at various points by Mr. Harcourt. The State Library at Monacco is being catalogued. Among its contents have been found about twenty thousand leads from persons who have filled most im- portant positions in French political or literary history, such as Catherine de Medicis, Richelieu, Mazarin, Louvois, Colbert, and Montaigne. . . . . .

We regret to hear-that the committee formed for re- newing the excavations on the site of the great temple of Ephesus have been unable to obtain by subscription the minimum amount needed for the work Mr. Wood will next week leave for Rome, but it is hoped suffici- ent money may yet be raised to enable him to begin work at Ephesus.—Athewrum. Mr. Juason (Ned Buntline), a ready writer‘of cheap fiction, has recently been making some confessions as to his authorship. He admits the authorship oftbetween 300 and 400 sensational novels, and claims to have made from 20,000 dols. to 60,000 dols. a year. Besides " Ned Buntline," Mr. Judson has five other pen names—" Ed- ward Minturn," " Clad Garnet," "Reckless, Ralph," "Sherwood Stanley," and Julia Edwards." Mr. H. K. Lewis has in the press a new:practical work on micrb-erganisms by Dr. Edgar M. Crookshank. The volume will bear the title " • logy," and it will aim at being a practical, systematic, and descriptive hand-book on the subjects of which it treats. It will contain an introduction to the study of bacteria, based upon the most recent methods employed by the school of Koch. An appendix will be given, including a de- scription of yeast and mould fungi, and the methods of examinations of air, soil, and water. Prof. Vambery has published "An Uzbeg (Tartar) Epic," which treats the career of the famous Urbeg war- rior and conqueror of Central Asia in the beginning of the sixteenth century, who drove Baber out of the coun- try north of the Oxus, and was the chief cause:of the foundation of the Mogul empire of India. The epic consists of 4,900 double verses, which the Professor copied from the only existing MS., which is in the pos- session of the Emperor of Austria. The text is accom- panied by a translation and annotations, and is brought out at the Professor's expense.—Atheneum. Professor Thorold Rogers, M.P., has made, says the At/tour:on, a very important discovery while pursuing his investigations at Cambridge for additional volumes of his work on the " History of Prices." This is a set of accounts kept at King's College during 120 years, with the exception of one year, beginning with the year 1583. There is information accessible with regard to the mis- sing year, so that the series of accbunts is practically complete for the entire period. In addition to the facts furnished as to prices, these accounts contain many curious details illustrative of social life in olden doys. A remarkable circumstance is reported from' Whit- stable by a local naturalist. A few evenings sine two or three oysters were put away in an earthen pan, and during the night a couple of young mice found out the dainty dish and inserted their hungry mouths within the open shelves of one of the bivalves. In the morn- ing they were found fast held by the closed shells of the oysters, and, of course, quite dead. The oyster con- tinued its firm hold on the intruders, and the trio having been handed to Mr. Sibert Sanders, a member of the East Kent Natural Histo7 Society, were at once im- mersed in spirits, and will in due course be placed in the local museum. Tag FirzALAN CHAPEL—The Duke of Norfolk is be- ginning the "restoration" of the ancient choir at Arun- del generally called the Fitz Alan Chapel. The part now undertaken is the wood vaulted ceiling, most of which fell in the eighteenth century. The building is private property, and the duke may do what he will with it; but we hope he will strive rather to preserve it as a precious vrorklof his ancestors: than to make it new as his own work. The building needs some repair, but any "re- I storation" in the ordinary sense of the word could, in this case, be nothing else than destruction, and as the place is not used there is not the common excuse for it. Mr. Buckler is the architect.—Atheneum. A Nzw Muni/ma InsrEtrinnir.—Experiments have been conducted on the Thames Embankment, close to Blackfriars Bridge, with the patent teletopometer of Pro- fessor Dr. Luigi Cerebotani, of the University at Verona. The surveying instrument of the Italian Professor con- sists of a telemeter, which, according to the description given, dispenses with the resources and trigonometrical calculations hitherto required. It is stated that in using this apparatus it is merely necessary to observe a certain point in order to ascertain its distance from the station of the observer by reading off the numbers on the ap- paratus, and by the aid of it there can easily be deter- mined the distance between the two banks of a river, between mountain tops or steeples, or the remoteness of any moving point or vessel. Further, the telemeter is employed in topography and curvography to ascertain measurements in inaccessible and remote ground. It is mentioned that the apparatus is so arranged that during the operation of measuring a sketch of the ground already measured can be pricked off, by which means a complete plan of the whole country under measurement can be drawn. This ingenious, instrument has been specially brought forward for war and civil engineering purposes.

NEW (SPANISH) VERS/ON OF AN OLD PROVERTL—" Yap may be a good dog, but Hold-fast is a better."—Punch. When a man is dismissed from employment, he always has a good deal to say against his late employers. A man, in fact, is like a gun. He makes a great noise when he is discharged. A gentleman lately, it is said, confused George Eliot with her namesake, the Conservative member. "Bet, my dear sir," reasonei a friend to whom he confided this astounding error. "you do not surely suppose that Sir George Elliott wrote the 'Mill on the Floss?" "Why not?" was ihe unabashed rejoinder. "He is just the man, knowing as he does so much about machinery." 4 VESTMENTS.—(Our new incumbent was disposed to be "high.")—Younger Countryman: I zap, Gearge, what wur that parsoh had acrost his shoulders 'Sunday? More like some o' these ere new 'armst dick'mtions I—Punch.

IyARRINGTON MUSICAL SOCIETY. I Qu Monday evening the annual general meeting of the Warringtoe Musical Society was held in the Cairo-street Schoolroom. The chair was occupied by the president, Mr. John Rylands. There was a moderate attendance. The Hon. Sec. (Mr. L. W. Reynolds) read the annual report, which stated that the society had fairly maintained its position during the past year, and had received an amount of support which could not fail to encourage those con- cerned in its management, and all interested in ite success. The total receipts from the two concerts of 1884-5 amounted to•A183 17s Bd, which was, by £25 6s 4d, more than the average receipts from the concerts of the previous seven years. (Applause.) On the other hand the expendi- ture was unusually heavy, and had exceeded the income by £29 53 3d, which result was largely due to an effort (un- hnppily not attended with success) made by the committee to establish in connection with the society a more satisfac- tory orchestral band of local instrumentalists. With this object in view, all likely to be interested its such a move- ment were invited to attend a meeting on September 25th, 1884, when it was arranged that the band should be under the,direction of the society's conductor on the same terms as the choir, as regarded subscriptions, and meeting weekly on choir rehearsal nights, Dr Hiles, who was present, hay- ing expressed his willingness to stay an hour later to give the band independent practice. There was a very good muster of instrumentalists at the first practice, and there seemed to be every prospect ef the formation of a really good amateur band, but instead of increasing, the attend- ance gradually fell off, so that in the end the concerts of 1884-5 were less assisted by local talent than those of pre- vious seasons. The cost to the society of that experi- ment wati over £2O, while more money than ever had to be expended on professional instrumentalists. Music also was a heavy item, the hire of orchestral parts of the works per- formed being unusually costly. At the first concert. on Dec. 4th, was performed Rossini's oratorio `• Moses in Egypt ;" the second, on March 26th, was a miscellaneous one. Both concerts proved mere than usually attractive, as evidenced by the sale of tickets, and were else decided musical suc- cesses, which must have tended to enhance the reputation of the society. Vocalists, band and chorus alike, gave complete satisfaction ' • but to Dr. Hiles belonged the prin- cipal share of credit for the able manner in which he con- ducted the performances. (Applause.) Mr. Pattison also rendered invaluable service—(hear, hear)—not only as or- ganist at the concerts, but as accompanist at the rehearsals ; and the committee regretted haying to add that the society would not in the coming season enjoy the benefit of Mr. Pattison' a able assistance, he having, on the 24th of August, tendered his resignation in consequence of his arrangements necessitating his future residence in Lon- don, though his connection with Warrington would not cease. The elementary singing class, under Mr. W. S Woods, was continued with success, 107 being enrolled, and there being an average attendance of 50 at 20 lessons, which were given on Monday evenings at St. Paul's Girls' School. The society was indebted to Mr. Matson for a timely dona- tion of £6 10s, being the amount realised by the sale of the double bass, the property of the late Orchestral Society, the liabilities of which Mr. Marson, the president, discharged , when the society was dissolved, and the music had been , handed over to the Musical Society to be deposited, with other music belonging to the society, in the library of the ; Warrington Museum, under an agreement with the Museum Committee, so that it might be available for public use. The abstract of the accounts showed that the receipts from , subscriptions had been £143 17s 6d ; sale of tickets for con- . certe' £32 4s; programmes, £7 18s 2; Mr. Mareon's done- tion,ZB 10s; balance from last year, £4 Hs fid, leaving a balance due to the treasurer of £7 18s 7d. The principal items of expenditure were £6O 18s paid to Dr Hiles as con- . doctor and on account of band; £44 16a to Mr. Petition as , organist and for professional vocalists !at the concerts, and £35 43 for instrumentalists, these items, with minor expenses, making a total of £213 Se 11d. The CHAIRMAN, in moving the confirmation of the report, said that it was a matter of regret that they should have a deficiency at all, but, everything considered, be thought they need not trouble their minds much about it. (Hear, , bear.) They had, unfortunately been spending money ,without the results they anticipated being fulfilled, and SO far it was a matter of regret: but they had done their duty. Under the circumetances they were bound to try the experi- . ment, and some of them were sanguine that it would result , differently to what it had done. (Hear, hear.) He very much regretted that they had not succeeded, and he could not account for it, for he remembered in the earlier days of , that society they never had any trouble at all, for people took a great interest in it, and they had not to engage pro• fessional assistance with the exception of the conductor, and his was, in fact, an honoraly position. They were in a very much happier position in those days. If the young men of Warrington, who played various instruments, had , not sufficient interest in the society to take advantage of the faeilities offered them, he did not see what the society could do. Of course, the best thing he thought for the young men was to get up an orchestral society, and obtain . someone to lead and conduct them, and fit themselves to take part in the society's concerts by coming to two or , three rehearsals before the concerts. (Applause.)— Mr. D. GARNETT secondecithe adoption of the report, which ; was agreed to.—On the motion of Mr. R. FAIRCLOVGH, Mr. John Rylands was re-elected as president, and the . following gentlemen were elected vice-presidents :—Messrs. Jamee Maroon, William Beamont, J. White, C. White, C. Broadbent, F. Monks, and P. Pearee.—Mr. WALLINcrrom moved that the foil ming geutlemen form the crimrhittAP • , —Messrs. R. Fairclorigh, T. Dinwlddie, D. Garnett, J. New- combe, P. C. Price, and J. P. Reynolds. He (Mr. Walling- . ton) suggested that greater care might be exercised with ' regard to the expense of the orchestra. He thought £52 was a large amount to pay for the services of the orchestra, especially when they had a number of instrumentalists in • Warrington. (Hear. hear.)—The committee was unani- mously elected.—On the motion of Mr. DINWIDDIE, Mr. Reynolds was unanimously re-elected hon. secretary and treasurer, and Mr. W. Scot-son assistant-secretary.—he CHAIRMAN read a letter which the secretary had recerved from Mr. Pattison, organist to the society, in which he re- signed his position, as his residence would in future be in London. During his term of office, be wrote, there had never been the slightest objectionable incident, either with the conductor or any member of the committee. The Chair- man moved a resolution expressing the sincere regret of the members of the society that Mr. Pattison had found it necessary to resign the post of organist, and according him a hearty vote of thanks for the valuable services he had ren- dered during a long series of years, for the most part with- out remuneration, and wishing him all possible success in his new business arrangements. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. WAL- LING-roN seconded the proposal, which was carried by ac- clamation.—The CHAIRMAN read a letter he had received from Mr. Johoson. offering his services as hon. organist to the society.—Mr. NEWCOMBE! moved, and Mr. FAIRRHRST seconded a proposal, that Mr. Johnson be appointed as organist, and this was agreed to.—The CHAIRMAN expressed a hope that the oratorio "Elijah " would be performed during the coming winter. (Applause.)—A vote of thanks to the chairman brought the proceedings to a close.

ALLEGED; ILLEGAL ACTION OF A RESOIDI SOCIETT.—The Commissioners of Police for the Metropolis have ordered a special inquiry into the statement made by Mrs. Norton before Mr. Hannay at the Worship-street Police Court that her daughter, 16 years of age, had been detained by a a rescue society," which had got hold of her and incarcer- ated her in a " home " without the knowledge or consent of her parents. MURDER AT BOOTLE- A terrible tragedy was enacted in Bootle on Saturday night. About eleven o'clock four young men and some women quitted a dancing class in Brasenose-road, when one of them, named Edward Pear- son, was told that a man wanted to speak to him. He went across the street and found a matt named Flynn, who wanted to fight with him. Pearson however, declined, and joined his friends, but the party 11;(1 not gone far when Flynn, with an open knife in his hand, rushed upon them. Flynn aimed a blow at one of the young men, named Lock- wood, but missed him. He them stabbed Pearson's brother, Thomas, after which be turned upon a third man, James Savage, and after cutting him, attacked Edward Pearson, and stabbed him near the heart so that he died on Monday. Flynn then fled, but was subsequently captured, and is now in custody charged with wilful murder. He was brought before the magistrates on Monday, and remanded. Witnesses were called who deposed to seeing the accused attack the deceased and a number of others with a clasp knife. ESTABLISHED NEARLY 50 YEARS. White's Celebrated Moe-Main Trusses. COPENHAGEN, SATURDAI.—The ceremony of laying the foundation stone of the new English church .took place to- day. The proceedings commenced with the singing of a hymn, after which the Prince and Princess of Wales, RC- companied by their three daughters, advanced to the founda- tion atone, which was suspended over the spot where it was to be placed. The Prince of Wales delivered an address, in the courstrof which he thanked those wise had contributed towards the cost of the church, especially the countrymen of the Princess of Wales, and also the Danish authorities for their cordial assistance. THE AFGHAN FRONTIER.

- ST. PETERSBURG, SMIDAY.—The Novoe Vreraya to-day states that M. Lesser, accompanied by Colonel Kohlberg will leave this week for the Afghan frontier in order to meet the British Commissioners. The work of the delimitation of the frontier will, it is stated., occupy at least eight months. SIMLA, THURSDAY.— It is expected that the Afthan Boundary Commission will complete the delimitation of the frontier between the Heri Rad and the Morghab before winter sets in. They will remain encamped during the cold seaserrnear Herat and resume work in the spring, proceeding, then With the settlement of the frontier betweem the Murg-, hab and the Oxus. OSMAN DIGMA'S DEATH.

CAIRO, SIINDAY.--Intelligence confirming the reports of Osman Dignia's death continues to be received by the, authorities here. The rebel leader, it appears, was killed, after a crushing defeat of his force of 3000 Hadrndowas by the Kassala garrison and friendly tribes. The latter, immediately after, despatched ample supplies and cattle into Kassala. SIR H. D. WOLFF'S MISSION. 'CONSTANTINOPLE, SATURDAY.—The report that the nego- tiations between Sir'''. D. Wolff and the Turkish Commis- shmers encountered some difficulties, and that Sir Henry was thinking of leaving Constantinople shortly was devoid -of foundation. Tne negotiations are progressinz, and ter- 'lain general principles have already been agreed upon as a' basis for an eventual arrangement. THE CAROLINE ISLANDS QUESDION. MADRID, SZVIDAY.—The ironclad Arragon has returned to Manila _from the Carolines, after having occupied and gar- risoned all the more important islands of the Pelew groups. The Spanish,commander states that no signs of any Ger- mane were to he seen on any of the Wands. MADRID, WEDNESDAY EVENING.—A rumour that G-er: many has suggested the Pope as arbitrator in the Caroline Islands question is believed here to be correct, and although the Spaniatt Government appears at present unwilling to admit arbitration, it is regarded as not improbable that in case Germany and Spain should in the end be unable to agree the flatter country would accept the'friendly mediation of His Holiness. LADIES CAPTURED BY BRIGANDS.

&swim— MOND4Y.—Two Grath ladies, one of them a, niece of the Archbishop of Verria, have been captured near that town by brigands, who demand a ransom of L 3,000. Hassan Pasha has gone to the spotin order to try to rescue the ladies.

div.head: CHOLERA.
div.p: THE CHOLERA.

- GIBRALTAR, MONDAY.—Official reports shOW37 cases and 14 deaths from cholera on Sunday in the Spanisti lines. Gibraltar is free from the infection. Thousands of fugi- tives enter daily from the Spanish lines, and no restrictions are imposed. There is a great outcry against the Governor, who refuses to close the communication. The Lord Mayor of London has sent £lOO for the relief of people suffering from cholera. MADRID, MONDAY.—There were £Bl cases and 334 deaths in Spain on Friday. 998 cases 337 deaths on Saturday, and 311 cases 313 deaths on Sunday in Spain. ROME, MONDAY.—TO-day's bulletin reports 182 cases and 128 deaths in the province of Palermo, six cases and three deaths in Parma, and two cases and one death in Rorigo. At the last meeting of the Mansion House Committee for the relief of the sufferers by the cholera in Spain it was announced that the fund amounted to T 2,430. A further sum of £750 was sent to the Madrid Committee, and also £lOO to the Governor of Gibraltar, for distribution amongst the Spanish community of Cenia. MADRID, TUESDAY.—The official cholera bulletin issued this morning reports 759 oases of cholera and 270 deaths in Spain yesterday. In Madrid capital there was only one ease and ne deaths, while in the province nine cases and two deaths occurred. Rome, TUESDAY.—To-day's official bulletin reports 216 cases and 117 deaths in the province of Palermo, in- cluding 214 in the town; 16 cases andl deaths in ether provinces. The steamer Cartagena, which has been detained in quar- antine in the Mersey since Friday, was on Tuesday released by the officers of the Health Committee, who certified she is now clear or sickness. SIR CHARLES WARREN. DURBAN*, SATURDAY. Sir C. Warren's reception at Grahamstown, Port Elizabeth, and other places in the Eastern province has been marked by effusive tokens of support. sympathy, and admiration. His addresses express unqualified confidence in the ability of South -Africa and its people to work out their own destinies if peace pre. veils.
• --- CAPBTOWN, MONDAY.-Sir Charlea Warren, after a trium- phal progress through the colony, has arrived here, and has received an enthusiastic welcome. THE DISTURBANCES IN SICILY.

ROME, TUESDAX.—The energetic measures adopted by the Government for the restoration of order in-Sicily are producing a good effect in the island, where railway com- munication has been re-established by the troops recently landed at Mesina. The excitement has almost ,calmed down, and at Palermo the people are regaining confi- dence. The railway stations at small country places will be occupied by troops. INDIA AND BURMAH. NINLA, WEDNRSDAY.—It is underetood that the Indian Government, having had its attention directed to the dis- pute between the Burmese Government and tbetombay and Burmah Trading Association, proposes to take steps to pro- tect the interests of British subieets. Colonel !Lockhart is reported to have arrived at Chitral. THE EASTERN SOUDAN. SUAKIN% WEDNESDAY.—News continues to arrive here confirming the previous reports that the Kassala garrison have made terms with certain Arab tribes, and have at- tacked the rebels with success. No official confirmation has been received as yet of the rumour that Osman Digma was amongst the slain. GERMAN ACQUISITIONS IN EAST AFRICA. BERLIN, WEDNESDAY.—The German East African Society announces that Herr Hoernecker, one of its agents in East Africa, has acquired by means a a series of treaties with native chiefs the territories north of Kilitnandjaro as far as the Dana river on behalf of the sosiety, and has incorpor- ated these territories with Vitu, which is also a German Settlement. It is added that the possessions of the Bests African society are by this acquisition extended to 2 degrees north latitude, and that the society's programme for ac- quiring territory in a northern direction is thereby com- pleted.

ARREST OF A GANG OF FORGERS, PARIS, THIIRSDAY.—A telegram has' been received here this morning announcing the arrest of a gang of forgers, eleven in number, add the seizure not only of the whole of their apparatus, but of notes and gold amounting (0 7,000 francs, showing that they had been carrying on their busi- ness to a very large extent. ELECTORAL MANIFESTO BY PRINCE NAPOLEON.

PASTS, TITURSDAY.—Prince Napoleon bas Issued his elec- toral manifesto, in which he says that France neither wishes a monarchial restoration nor Utopian reforms. He accuses the Imperialists of having placed themselves at the service of the Bourbons, and of having stirred up a revolt in his family. The Prince,concladeS by declaring that he will hold aloof from the electoral movement until the day ar- rives when the necessity is felt of summoning a constituent assembly which will assign to the people the task of nomi- nating the head of the Cate.

The Duke and Docile.% of Connaught arrived in London i on Tuesday evening from Calais. The Duke of Cambridge on Thursday reviewed in Hyde Park the brigade of Guards which took part in the Soudan Operations. There were 65 officers and upwards of 1500 men on the ground. His i-toyal Highness congratulated them on their fine appearance. 431RETIIITIES TO SOUDAN TAOOPS. --' The gratuities to the troops which took part in the Nile and Soudan campaign were handed to the men of the Grenadier and Scots Guards on Monday afternoon' at Wellington Barracks, London. The Coldstream Guards having been on duty th,e whole of Mondaycreceived their share of the ' awards on Tues- day afternoon. The privates who took part in the Soudan. campaign received £2, whilst those who belonged to the Camel Corps and went through both campaigns have £5. Axe EXTRAORDINARY CASE. —The .ease in which four persons—named Genese, Mordaunt, Boyfus, and Bass—are charged with conspiring to defraud a Mr. Painter of a re- versionary interest in land in New. South Wales came on again at the Marlborough-Street Police Court, London, on Wednesday, before Mr. Newton. Counsel for the prosecu- tion, however, now stated as a reason for not going on with the matter that Mr. Palmer had found himself in a dificulty as to proving the value of the reversion. Mr. Newton said the case must proceed, whereupon counsel said that since the adjournment it had been arranged that the prosecutor should have hi a property back at the price he received for it. Mr. Newton said this made him more deter- mined to pat the case in the hands of, the pub. lic Prosecutor, and he remanded the defendants on bail with that intention. MR- GLADSTONE'S MANIFESTO. • In our last issue we gave a summary of Mr. Glad- stone's address to his constituents, and, through them, to the electors of the United Kingdom.— Be- low we give the full text of the manifesto as it re- lates to the future programme of the Liberal party. The first portion of the address is an explanation and justification of the course taken by the Liberal Government whilst in office t‘ it then proceeds as follows

the four great subjects which.' have mentioned as going far to supply a scheme of present action for the party, I could not but anticipate such co-operation with con- fidence. , SIIBIECTS OF LEGISLATION OR DISCUSSION, I Thus far I have only mentioned political matters which have been for a sufficient time before the public mind, which have undergone much discussion, and on which it may be reasonably hoped that the Liberal party is ripe for united action. Generally they may be said to stand among the. unrecovered arrears of public business. But they constitute only the vanguard of the hosts of sub- jects with which the coming Parliament and its succes- sors will or May have to deal. Many of them ought already to have been overtaken and disposed of had the^ obstacles to the efficiency of the House of Commons been effectually overcome. But, apart from this unsatisfac- tory reminiscence, it appeafs probable even after all *which the last half century has achieved that the growth ^of population, the expansion of our relations throughout the world, the rapid development of social interests, and the extension of popular power will, at least for a con- siderable time, be aniply represented in new legislative wants. From any full attemrt to set them forth the law of nature at my time of life eispenses me. But there are some among them as to which the foundations of dis- cussion have already been lid, and which may there- fore demand from me a few words, such as the reform or the reconstruction of the Louse of Lords, the aboli- tion of all payment for primary education, and the severance of the Church front the State. I place these subjects together without intending to imply that I take personally the same view of tie whole of them. 15. CHANGES DI THE 11017 SE OF imps. As respects changes in the rouse of Lords, by far the best guarantee for the safe thatment of this important subject is one that can only bt supplied by that House itself, in the moderation and wisdom of its future con- duct. Since 1832 it has bon continuously identified with the Tory party in the Sate, which has obtained the suffrage of the nation in only two out of twelve Parliaments, and few outside that party will maintain that the legislative action of tie House of Lords has on the whole been satisfactory. It is likely that if its con- stitution remains unalterea :he ties of its present party connection will progressivel;? be tightened rather than relaxed. I certainly canna deny that there is a case sufficient to justify importmt change. Those who hold with Mr. Burke, as 1 do, hat knowledge and virtue alone have an intrinsic righl to govern, might desire to constitute a second chambei strictly on this basis. But we cannot in the nature of hings exclude the action of other influences,'especially he permanent, growing, and highly aggressive power of wealth. Among these se- condary influences, as a linl with the past, as a force congenial to the character aid habits of the people, and as a check on other and yet nore mixed agencies, Ihope that in the reconstruction dthe House 04 Peers,.when it arrives, a reasonable shareof power may be allowed under wise conditions to Gm principle of birth. 18.—ESTABLISIED CHURCH. .

• 9.—rsocuntans. I will now approach the consideration of domestic affairs in a prospective light, and at the threshold I place the question of Parliamentary procedure. It has gratified me to find abundant proof that the country was and is fully alive to the vital im- portance of devolution and generally of procedure in the House of Commons. lb insist upon these weighty mat- ters implies nothingderogatory to the wisdom of the old rules of Parliament. They were well adapted to the. work which Parliament had formerly to do. Nothing is now required but to bring about in a like spirit a similes. adoption. The task of the House of Commons in our time has habitually exceeded what had over been im- posed upon a legislative body in the whole history of the world. Those who are reasonably so keen 'for legislation on one subject or another should recollect that with re- gard to each and all of them the primary question is as ' to the sound working condition of the great instrument by which all legislation is accomplished. If the instrument is properly adjusted I believe the House can do i s work; itthat operation is defeated or evaded I am certain it cannot. The constiuencies have now to choose a new House, and it depends entirely on the selection among candidates and on the treatment of candidates with reference to these questions whether the work shall be done or not. Meantime I desire clearly to point out the three cardinal points of the question. First, the con- gestion of business, now notorious and inveterate, de- grades the House of Commons byplacing it at the mercy of those among its members who seek for notoriety by ,obstructing business instead of 'pursuing the more hon- ourable Toad to reputation by useful service, or of those who will with more senlblance of warrant seek to cripple the action of the House of Commons in order to force the acceptance of their own political projects. Secondly, it disappoints, irritates, and injures the country by the suspension of useful legislation; and, lastly and perhaps worseof all, it defeats the fundamental rule of our ;Par- liamentary system that the majority shall prevail and puts it in the power of the minority to prevent by un- dulyaonsuming the time of the House, the pawing of measures which it dislikes but of which it is- afraid openly to declare its disapproval. This country will not in the full sense be a i self-governing country until the machinery of the House of Commons s amended and its procedure reformed. 10.--TOCAL GOVERNMENT.

'I am not sure that the views of the country are so clear and its mind so fully ripened on the next great subject which I have to mention—that of local govern- ment. First, it is involved in great intricacy of financial and administrative detail. We are proverbially apt to become careless and 'remiss about what we have long securely and familiarly held in possession. And, more- over, the position Of the question has been seriously damaged by the profuseness of the Tory party in charging local burdens on the Consolidated Fund 'with- out making due attempt to improve the organisation of local authority and centralising measures of which when in power they have procured the adoption. lam glad to see that Lord Salisbury has recently spoken in strong terms of the advantages of local government But the opinions of Lord Salisbury have already been in strong contrast on the great subject of Irish administra- tion with more influential opinions of his colleagues in the House of COmnions. Even the limits of.this address do not pirmit me to set out in detail what Athink of the weight and moment of t,his thoroughly unexciting but as thoroughly vital subject. ,I believe it to he at the root of all our liberties and of all our aptitudes. It is the instrument of our public education, and it is the guar- antee of our political stability. Even in its imperfect development it has been of inestimable value, and it may and should be made to do yet more for us in the future even than what ,it has done for us'Zn' the past. In the reform of local government the first objects to be aimed at, in my judgment, are to rectify the balance of taxation as between real and personal property, to put an end to the gross,injustice of charging upon labour, through the medium of the Consolidated Fund, local burdens which our laws have always wisgly: treated as incident to property; to relieve the ratepayer, not at the charge of the -working population, but wholly(or mainly by making over for local purposes carefully chosen items of taxation; to supply local management with induce- ments to economy, instead of tempting and almost forc- ing it into waste; finally, and most of all, to render the system thoroughly representative and free. The gentry of this country have, especially in the counties, long, and with justice, been commended for the upright and intelligent discharge of local duty. lain confident that they will continue to enjoy this honourable distinction none the less when our system shall have been placed throughout under effective popular control. 'Other ques- tions go to the modes in which local government may prudently be applied, and the extent of its attributions will doubtless arise for consideration when the primary work shall have been accomplished, but I will not omit to observe that this subject furnishes the medium through which we may reasonably look for an effectual adjustment of the laws relating to the sale,of alcoholic liquors.

When the subject of Statereligion comes into discus- sion. although it has been more fully probed and un- folded in Scotland than elseveure, and although a lively feeling, as was naturally to le expected, exists with re- gard to it in Wales, yet it is tie larger case of 'England which principally arrests attereion. Bearing in mind the circumstances of the quelim in connection with the length of my own past caree; 'might perhaps plead for an exemption from all share in this controversy. But having regard, on the other land, to the deep interest felt in it, with strong conviction, on the part of so many whose confidence I have enjtyecl, I think it right to say a few words, if they only tad to qualify over-sanguine expectations and to mitigate alarms which appear to me exaggerated, - though they ere entertained by many whom both officially and personally I revere. With re- spect to the severance of the Church of England from the State, I think it obvious that so vast a question cannot become practical until it shall have grown familiar to the public mind by thorough discussion, with the further condition that the proposal, when thoroughly discussed, shall be approved. Neither, I think, can such : a change arise in a country such Si ours except with a large observance of the principles d equity and liberality, as well as with the general comet of the nation. We can hardly, however, be surprise3if those who observe that a current almost throughat the civilised world slowly sets in this direction shoul desire or fear that among ourselves, too, it may be found to operate. I • cannot forecast the dim and &stem courses of the future, but like all others I have observd the vast and eeer- increasing development for the Ist fifty years both at , home and abroad, in the Churcloo which I belong, of the powers of voluntary support Those abridgements , Of her prerogatives eta an establisluent, which have been frequent of late years have not brught about a decrease, and have at least been contemporneous with an increase of her spiritual and social strengd. By devotedness of life and by solidity of labour, to clergy are laying a good foundation for the time to erne. The attachment of the laity improves, if I mad' scspeak, both in quantity and quality. The .English Chuch also appears to be eminently suited in many ans weighty points to the needs of the coming time, and I lave a strong conviction that if this great modification al our inherited institu- tions shall hereafter be accoingssaed, the vitality of the Church of England will be fouls] equal to all the needs of the occasion. N. 17.—GRATIIITOUS 1:11JCATION. The subject of a gratuitois pr mary education, to be paid for from sources wholy pion; is one on which I desire to reserve a final julgmeat. There are obvious arguments in favour of the ilan,which'because they are 11.—LAND. obvious it is unnecessary torepeat, but it appears to me to suggest some difficulties which demand at any rate a The next of the important subjects Which I have pre- sumed to name is the reform of the laws relating to land, grave consideration. Accerding to the habits of this j country a contribution tossrds the cost of the article I shall treat it as I have treated local government, with- country its being more deroughly valued by the re- out any attempt to embrace all the topics which maybe ceiver. It seems necessary to consider with'care what will be the effect of the comp on primary education usefully or legitimately raised in regard to it. I shall 1 other than that which is supplied by public authority. only touch oil those parts of the question which I hope The rule of our policy is tht nothing should be done fiy may be found mature for very early handling by the Liberal party. Belonging to a school which has much faith in economic laws, I disapprove of interference withthe -State which can be bettr or as well done by volun- tary effort, and I am not asare that either in its moral them by entails, to which I am still more opposed on iteral aspects the work of the State for education has as yet proved its superiority to the work social and moral grounds.
