Idelivered, the limit is clear within which any desires of Irsiand constitutionally ascertained, may and beyond which they cannot, receive the assent of Parliament. To maintain the supremacy of the Crown, the unity of the Empire, and all the authority of Parliament necessary for the conservation of that unity is the first duty of every representative of the people. Subject to this governing principle every grant to portions of the country of enlarged powers for the management of their own affairs is, in my view, not a source of danger bat a means of averting it, and is in the nature of a new guarantee for increased cohesion, happiness, and strength. We have no right to expect that the remedial process in human affairs shall always be greatly shorter than the period of mistakes and misgovernment, and if in the case of Ireland half a century of efforts at redress, not always consistent or sustained, and following upon long ages for which as a whole we blush, have still left , something to be attempted, we ought not to wax weary in welldoing nor rest until every claim which justice may be found to urge shall have been satisfied. The main question is whether it is for the interests of all the three countries that the thorough and enduring harmony which has now been long established, but only after centuries of manful strife between England and Scotland, should include Ireland also. My personal answer to the question is this. I believe history and posterity will consign to disgrace the name and memory of every man, be he who he may, and on whichever side of the Channel he may dwell, that having the power to aid in an equit- able settlement between Ireland and Great Britain shall use that power not to aid but to prevent or to retard it. If the duty of working for this end cannot be doubted, then I trust that on the one hand Ireland will remember that she too is subject to the authority of reason and justice, and cannot always plead the warnings of other days in bar of submission to them, and that the two sister kingdoms, aware of their overwhelming strength, will dismise every fear except that of doing wrong, and will make yet another effort to complete a reconciling Work which has already done so much to redeem the past, and which, when completed, will yet more redound to the honour of our legislation and our race.

19.—TH; PRESENT GOVERNMENT. In this lengthened address, which from its very length has enabled me to write with much of individual free- dom, I have avoided criticism upon the proceedings of the Government now in office, for the most important part of them, so far as they are known to me, relate to the government of Ireland, and I am desirous to hold that subject altogether separate from retrospective con- troversy. I also refrain from all comment in detail upon the conduct of the party as an Opposition:in the House of Commons, but it was so novel and so ominous by way of precedent as to oblige me briefly to observe that on many matters, and especially on many matters relating to foreign affairs, it supplied an example of everything which a high-minded Opposition should avoid. I may, however, say that we have given, as was our duty, a cor- dial support to the new Administration in its endeavours to conclude an arrangement of the Afghan frontier with Russia on the basis which had been laid down by Lord Granville. And I have observed with satisfaction that the Secretary of State for the Colonies appears, so far as we are informed, to exercise a wise caution in South I Africa with reference to any further extension of our territorial responsibilities, which I hold it most unwise.to enlarge without an overruling necessity. _

div.head: 20.—CoNausioN.
div.p: 20.—CoNausioN.

In conclusion it may be observed that much of what I have written refers to a future which, according to all expectation, lies beyond my reach. Nevertheless, as.it appears to me, the great occasion of choosing a Parlia- ment entails the duty of preparation for contingencies which it may take long to develop, and it is to aid, so far as I may, in the fulfilment of this duty, that I have thus submitted my views to your consideration. Trusting that the constituencies of the country may, by their devotion to the public good, prove themselves worthy of the great and noble stewardship committed to them, and, confident that you will continue to hold your high place among those constituencies, I remain, gentlemen, your obliged and obedient servant, W. E.GLADSTONE. Hawarden Castle, Sept. 17, 1885.

LIBERAL MEETING AT FRODSITAM. Mr. Lawrence Irwell, of Bicester, Oxfordshire, the Liberal candidate for the Eddisbnry division, opened his campaign 'on Monday evening, when a public meeting was held in the Frodsham Town Hall. The room was crowded with an enthusiastic audience, who appeared quite in touch with the speakers, and the applauss was frequent and hearty. There were several Tories present, but only one made him- self noticeable by frequent and ill-timed interruptions. This was Mr. John Hargreaves, who drew upon himself the amused banter of the audience, and amid loud laughter was invited to take a seat on the platform. He did not accept the invitation. The chair was oc- cupied by Mr. F. Rigby, J.P , of Warrendale, Frodsham, and he was supported on the platform by the candidate; Dr. Forster, candidate for Chester; Messrs. Seger, barrister-at- law; E. Brassey, election agent; and F. Thornton, Helsby. Amongst the audience were the ROTS. R. B. Borwick and J. Lewis; Messrs. J. S. Rimmer, Nicholas, P. Harrop, W. H. Pickering, John Challoner, A. Linaker, F. Spencer, H. G. blinker, J. Rothwell, and W. Rhodes, all of Frodsham ; T. Rigby, Sutton; Harvey, S. Lewis, Thomas, and Nixon, of Kingsley; W. Collier, of Helsby ; T. Handley and B. Knive- ton,of Runcorn. The Chairman referred with regret to the abeence of Mr. Charles Reynolds, J.P., from his usual position as presi- dent, and added that though thousands of 'mks separated him from them, his heart was in full nnision with them and their candidate that evening. (Hear, hear.) Alluding to the Franchise Bill, the chairman said things were entirely changed. Formerly, the workingmen had been mere listeners and spectators in the political struggles, but now they were the backbone of the elections. (Applause.) To the workingman they looked, in him they had confidence, and they felt perfectly certain that the rest.lt of his vote would proclaim the return of Mr. Irwell, b cause he was assured from his knowledge of the ordinary British work- man that he would record his vote for the champion of liberty. (Applause.) Personally, he had not a word to say against Mr. Henry Tollemache, the Con- servative candidate, and of his father, Mr. Wilbraham they had every reason to speak in the highest terms of encomium. He was, he believed, a most excellent landlord; as a member of society he was justly praised by both sides, and if Mr. Henry Tollemache had only had the good for- tune to follow the convictions of his father, who is a Liberal, they would not have had one word to say against him. Mr. Tollemache appealed to them because he had been a mem- ber for the county for four years. Daring the last session there were 266 divisions in the House of Commons, and a man who had voted on all those occasions would deserve not only well of his constituency, but of his country. It would be unreasonable to suppose he voted in 266 divisions, but did he vote in the odd 613? No; he voted in 31 divi- sions, and that was the reason be commended himself to them as a hard-working member of Parliament with the addition of "my family and my connections." In answer to his family and connections, they would repeat the tails. manic words " 266 " and "31." (Cheers.) It had been urged by some that Mr. Irwell was a stranger, but he ven- tured to say that he was no more a stranger than 'dr. Tolle- mache, who never came amongst them, and lhat he was as fit and proper a person to represent them as Mr. Tolle- mache, or Mr. Egerton, or any other great landowner of Cheshire. (Laud applause.) Mr. Irwell, who had an euthusiastic welcome, referred to the statement made by Mr. Tollemache that he was opposed by a gentleman who was a perfect stranger, and said they seat gentlemen to the House of Commons not to represent . . . .

' John Kennedy was sent to gaol on Saturday, at Liver. pool, for a month, for horsewhipping his son, aged siz years. A wall in course of erection in Glasgow fell on Monday afternoon. Michael Duffy, a reason's labourer, was killed, and two masons were injured. Saturday was observed as the Great Hebrew Feast of the Atonement—the most solemn of the year—known as Chi. pur " or," The Whit Fast." Lord Teignntouth dftei at his residence at Edinburgh on Saturday. His lordship was born in 1798, and represented Marylehone from 1838 to 1841.

At Croydon, on Sunday morning, the body of a child was found in brown paper on a doorstep. A surgical exam ma. tion showed that it had been strangled. Sir Charles Bilk° will, it is understood, be married, pro. loably in Paris, in the latter part of next month, to Mrs. Mark Pattison, who is on her way home from India. The Bolton County Magistrates on Monday committed for trial a collier named Mann, who had beaten his wife about the bead with a poker, and caused severe injuries. A shunter named James Lowe, of Moston, near Sand- bach, was killed instantaneously on Monday whilst en. gaged in shunting operations at Malking Bank railway . _
- Fears are entertained that the barque Blanche Maud, of Leith, which is thief months overdue, has been wrea- ked in the Atlantic, with the whole of her crew, 17 ist number.
A 20.Acna PARK was opened on Saturday at Low Moor by Viscount Cranbrook. The park has been formed out of waste common lands, until recently covered with slag and refuse.

At the Old Bailey, an Saturday, William John Smith was sentenced to one month's imprisonment, for having falsely pretended to be a clergyman and performed a mar- riage ceremopy. At an inquest held in York, on Saturday. two women ap- peared to claim the body of a man, John Fields, a draper, as that of their husband. Both women produced evidence of marriage.
The Buxton Market Hall was on Saturday night com- pletely destroyed by fire, which originated in one of the shops into which the building is divided. The damage is estimated at £5 000.

At Stansty Farm, on the estate of Lady Ffrench, Wrex. ham, on Saturday night, the whole of the farm baildings were gutted and the contents destroyed, as were also eight new stacks of wheat, barley, and hay. Two lads, under ten years of age, were ordered to be flogged by the Barnsley magistrates on Monday for stealing a horse worth .£4O. They rode to Doncaster on the St. Leger Day, and tried to sell the animal for 10s. While some workmen were engaged in laying the founda- tions of a new bridge over the Tiber at Rome, they came upon a magnificent statute in bronze, sft. sin, in height, representing a slave in the attitude of striking. Monsignor Smith, of the Roman Catholic Pro-Cathe- dral, Edinburgh, has been appointed Archbishop of St. Andrews and Edinburgh. The affairs of the archdiocese have been under his charge since the death of Dr. Strain in 1883.

THE CANADIAN REBELLION.—RESPITE OF RIEL.—Riel, who was sentenced to death for leading the rebellion in the north-west provinces of C4nada, has been respited to the 16th of October, pending the hearing of the appeal against the sentence.

On Saturday night last Mr. Morris Jones, a coach pro- prietor, was assailed by three men on the highway at Bettws- y-Coed. He was knocked dewn and kicked in the most savage manner, receiving such injuries to the head that he died on Wednesday. Two men are in custody. MINERS' WAGES. The Derbyshire miners at a con- ference held at Chesterfield, on Saturday, resolved to aunpert a general movement of the mining centres in fa- vour of securing an advance in wages. The Derbyshire men, it was stated, were agreeable to a reduction of the out- put. A POLICEMAN SHOT.—While endeavouring to arrest a man at Leek, on Saturday afternoon, who had offered in pledge a ring which was alleged to be a portion of the pro- ceeds of the recent Dublin jewellery robbery, P.C. Bryan was shot in the knee and disabled, the man making good his escape. •

Immarrsn FIND or COAL IN WALES.—Fourteen months ago Messrs. Davies, Scott, and Co., commenced sinking for coal three miles from Pontypridd. O Monday it was announced that their efforts have been successfal. A seam of coal six feet thick has been struck at a depth of 44i yards. Three hundred cAtages will be at once erected.

Trutormt EUROPE AND ASIA ON A BICICLE.—A telegram from Tabreez, North Persia, on Saturday, says :—Thomaa Stevens, who left England in May last, travelled on a bicycle through the Continent to Constantinople. He thence made his way to Angora, Yozgate, and Erzeronm, finally arriving here. He intends proceeding to India, via Teheran, Meshed and Herat.

SERrOIIS CHARGE AGAINST A SIIRGEON.—Dr. G. IT. Heald, police surgeon at Leeds, was on Saturday charged, on remand, with having criminally assaulted a pupil teacher, aged 15, in his surgery a sve,,le ago, when the girl attended as a patient. After a long hewing, the prisonaL was committed for trial at the assizes, bail being ac- cepted, Dr. Heald himself in £5OO, and two sureties in £5OO eac'4.

MURDER AND SITICIDE.—EarIy on Monday morning a railway servant named George Powcock was found to have hanged himself in the kitchen of his house at Derby. In a bedroom was the dead body of Mrs. Powcock, with two dreadful wounds in the throat, and it is supposed that after murdering his wife the man went downstairs and committed suicide. He had been suffering from mental aberration for some months.

A Meow OCCURRRNCR is reported from Shallee, in county Tipperary, where, it appears, a young farmer named. Ryan was shot on Saturday night by his cousin, Morgan O'Brien. Ryan, while returning from Nenagh market with a man named Lynch, met O'Brien, and, some hasty expres- sions having passed, Ryan called O'Brien a Government man. The latter, it is alleged, ran home and secured a fowling-piece. and shot Ryan in the side, causing his death. O'Brien was placed under arrest. FORGING & HALL Manx.—A young man named Robert Willis was convicted in London en Saturday of forging the mark of the Goldsmiths' Company on two watches. The prisoner had pawned for £9 a watch which was re- presented to be a gold one, and which bore the stamp of the Goldsmiths' Company. The watch was afterwards found to be silver, gold gilt. The priionec offered a second watch of the same kind in pawn, but was given into custody.—The Recorder deferred passing stntence till Monday. when he sentenced Willis to six years penal servitude.

" SMASHING MR. PARNELL."—EXTRAORDINARY BOYCOT- TING.—An extraordinary occurrence was witnessed in Mid- dleton, Cork, on Friday. Captain Foster, who is on a visit with Captain Smith Barry, a popular local landlord, during a stroll through the town, was attracted by a picture of Mr. Parnell exhibited in a shop window. This he purchased. and smashed with his stick in the street. A large crowd collected, and would have given him a drubbing but for the timely intervention of the police. Such is the state of feeling aroused, that subsequently the bakers and other shop- keepers were warned to dir.continue supplying Captain Smith Barry with food as long as Captain Poster remained his guest. BOYCOTTItsm—A herd in the employment of Mr. Crowe, residing near Ennis, was met on Saturday by men in dis- guise, and threatened if he continued in the employ that he would be shot. He disclosed the facts to his master, and the same night the gates and the gate piers on Mr. Crowe's farm were destroyed. • Mr. Crowe had recently taken some action with regard to the recovery of rents.—Major Turner, agent to Lieutenant Bagwell. Idndlord in Tipperary, sent in butter to Tipperary market on Monday, but no buyer could he found for it.—The fair of Rosscartiery has been boycotted by the Cork Cattle Dealers' Association, because the people of the district had refused to establish a branch of the National League.

WRECK OFF WORKINGTON.—GALIANT ATTEMPT AT RES. —The vessel Margaret, of Ramsey, was seen to be on cg.—The off Workington at an early hour en Saturday morning, and in the face of a strong south-westerly gale a tug towing a boat put off to the rescue. Long before the wreck was reached the beat capsized and one of its have occupants, Alexander Bowrirg, of Workington was drowned. Another tug boat put off from Harrington. and every effort was made to save the crew of the Margaret, the exertions of those who went to the rescue being stimulated by the sight of a man clinging to the mainmast. Soon, however, the mast was swept away, ad all the crew perisned. The bodies of K. Christian, the master, and William Keunish and William Cowie, of the Margaret, have since been recovered at Workington.

THE METROPOLITAN POLICE AND SOCIALISTS.—A large but orderly meeting was held in Dod-street, Mile-end, on Sunday morning, to protest against the recent action of the police in regard to the open-air meetings of socialists. , Several working men's clubs were represented by delegates. The police arrested some of the speakers, but us soon as one was arrested enother took his place. Five wearers of badges were alert arrested, and the banner of the Social Democratic Federation was seized. On the motion of Dr. Avelitag, a resolution was passed protesting "against the attempty of the police, at the bidding of the privileged classes, to inter- fere with the freedom of speech." On Monday, those arrested were prosecuted at the Thames Police Court for re- sisting the police in the execution of their duty, one of the defendants was committed to prison, and otlit,irs were fined. The case was heard in an excited court, many , Socialists being present—among them Mr. William Morris, I Dr. and Mm. Aveling, and Mr. llyndman. Dr. and Mrs. Axteling were examined as witnesses, and both declared their intention to take part in similar demonstrations next Sunday, which led the magistrate (Mr. Saunders) to inform them that if they did he Should know how to deal with them. There was a further conflict between the po.ice and the Socialists at the close of the inquiry, I and a remonstrance made by Mr. Morris brought about that gentleman's arrest on a charge of creating a disturbance and assaulting a con- stable. The charge was herrd shortly afterwards, and Mr. Morris was liberated, the magistrate remarking that there appeared to be a disposition to make too much of the matter.

div.p: thisis a matter we have thought about, and we re, glad to know that the Warrington British ?cbools, better known as the People's Col- Lege, are so well managed, have so com- Pletely won their way on the principle of supply and demand, that they pay their way and give a first-class education in the flxbar- ,airi• Let the Parish Church Schools do ,ewise, if they can; and if they cannot might not be so terrible, after all, if they It'ere to step aside and make way for a School „Gard. The good givers are getting just a tittle tired oF " appeals to their feelings," and are not responding as they did a while ago. Turning to the latest Blue Book on 9uucation, we find that in 1876 the annual come per scholar from voluntary contribu- -41,°0s was 8s 81/sd ; this year it is 6s 84d, Lnat is two shillings per head less, notwith- standing the steady increase in the cost of education, The fact is people who prefer aPPeals to their understanding are beginning t° recognise that it is the business Pf the nation rather than of the Mdividull to make provision for Na- tional Education. They find that im- perially, and in some cases locally, they are Deing more and more taxed for education, Alld they not unnaturally demur to being taxed again in the shape of a particular con- tribution to a particular school. Being lay- en only, and as such compelled in the way of ordinary business to make themselves ac- 'quainted with primary facts, they are either befouled norfrightened when a clergy- an informs them that a School Board l'ould add 2S 6d in the £ to their expenses. f such a tale were told them across the counter, they would characterise it by a very Short word. Two shillings and sixpence in pound!ie How absurd I. The enemies of r ,ational Education are for ever prating about !'lle great expense of the School Board system lu London—with its high salaries and costly Sites, and what does that amount to? It amounts for 1883-4. to 7.4 el in the £—that is less than sevenpence halfpenny in the Pound. In Manchester the rate is 32d; iu Liverpool 2.9c1, and in 'Wigan id in the Pound. The average for the whole of Eng- land, boroughs and parisheS, is less than 61/2cl in the pound. Where has the Rector got his half-crown in the ? Perhaps he will tell us, and perhaps he 'will apologise 10r painting the latest hobgoblin five times as black as it ought to be? Or shall we say fteen times ; for it is not at all unreasonable to suppose that, if a School Board was formed, a rate of 2d in the E—which would be over £l,OOO per year—would, along with existing schools, meet the needs of Warring- for some time to come. Two and six- pence in the pound! The Rector, if he has reckoned at all, must have put down each schoolmaster at a salary equal to his own. Hcw ridiculous

-- Mr. LAWRENCE IRWELL, the Liberal can- didate for the Eddisbury Division, had a good reception at Frodsham, on Monday evening. It augurs well for him that the Town Hall was crowded with an enthusiastic audience. Mr. HENRY TOLLEMAcHE, the Tory candi- date, no doubt regards this part of Cheshire as a sort of family preserve; but a change has come over the spirit of the dream since he was sent to Parliament. There has been an extension of the franchise ; and the peasants of Cheshire as well as the pheasants are now demanding to be represented. Mr. HENRY I'OLLEMACHE was not born for the senate, and he would seem to have discovered that this is so, for it wts made known at the Illeeting that he bad voted in 31 divisions OUly out of 266. It would be best, therefore, e relieve him of all further attendance at the qOuse of Commons. The new electors have much to require of Parliament, and they can c4IIIIY obtain what they want by returning men '.O St. Stephens who are not only pledged to their interests, but will give their time as fr,eely as they give their word. It is ob- l'lolls from Mr. IRWELL'S speech that he can be relied upon to follow Mr. GLiADS- nNE, and follow not as one generally in the 'ear, but as one always in the front rank, arid ever ready to go forward to "fresh ..Woods and pastures new." He does not ggard it as creditable to our boasted civilisa- " that an agricultural labourer has nothing better to look forward to than the prospect of getting from I2S. to is. per week from Flanhood to old age. The Tory policy is to let things alone, but Mr. IRwELL will seek to mend matters by giving local authorities Power to acquire land, at a fair value, with a view to letting it in allotments to agricultural labourers. In this way he would endeavour tO raise the lowly—encourage the worker to become thrifty and independent, and, by em- Ploying the peasantry where there is still Plenty of room for them, he would relieve the congestion in the labour market of our Cities and towns. Although not a tee- totaller, Mr. IRWELL perceives the neces- -BitY of amending the licensing laws, and , ;het with an enthusiastic response whenH Ile said that as the people were so directly aff*, ected by public-houses they ought to have tne right of saying whether they would have them or not. He expressed himself in fav- Our of local government reform in other directions, and as desirous of seeing a reform of the House of Lords. In conclusion, be advised electors to give their votes according to their convictions—advice which we would e,4lPhasise, for a man is a traitor to himself 7.11 d his kind who basely sells his birthright ilc)r a mess of pottage. Working-men need a•ve no fear, whatever Tory agents may say, that it will be known how they have voted. tkhey are absolutely safe in the secrecy of 'e ballot; and it is little to ask of them, tinder the circumstances, that they should Show the courage of their convictions.

• L.TRE Exhibition which is to be held in illiverpool next year of Navigation, Travell- t,,g2 Commerce, and Manufacture promises °e of a truly international character; for , be on a scale commensurate with the liaracter of Liverpool as the second seaport lea'r the world. Edge. lane Hall Estate has itleee chosen as the site • it is about 35 acres f extent and it is less than a couple of miles , .00 ert the Exchange. As the land is intended .or vbe,,tte: Public Park, it could not receive a consecration to the public than it •plu, have as the site of an International eeibition. The estate is adorned with some tine Old fir trees ; and there can be no ques- then as to their adding to the attractions of ille grounds, which are to be brilliantly otlreinated at night with 'electric light. 0113e11-air concerts, musical bands, and orna- toetn,tel fountains will also lend enchantment bi,„`ee scene. Those who go to the Exhibi- t% "on as the place to spend a happy clan" flitilos gut, will not be disappointed, nor will e Who attend for the more serious busi- bc24S of the Exhibition proper. There will be plodels of every kind relating to travelling tz2and or water—from the ancient canoe to znodern, war ship; from the slow coach

to the Flying Dutchman. The illustrations of construction will be extensive, so as to bring the latest and best information to students of every class. To this end there will be models of docks, harbours, light- houses, &c., and everything appertaining to the use of steam for transit purposes. The animal, vegetable, and mineral kingdoms will be ransacked in order to comp'etely stock the commercial and manufacturing sections— what people eat, dr'nk, and wear being amply illustrated. It is gratifying to learn that vailoug Continental Governments have already shown an interest in the undertaking, and there are numerous promises of valuable models and examples from foreign museums. Her Majesty the QUEEN. • has consented to become a patron of the Exhibition, and the PRINCE OF WALES—who may also be des- cribed as the Prince of Exhibitions—has consented to take the office of president. 'There is a guarantee fund of over £50,000, so that there is every prospect of the great pro- ject being carried out successfully. The undertaking had its origin. with Alderman DAVID RADCLIFFE, the present mayor of Liverpool, and, at his suggestion, it is pro- posed to apply the surplus funds of the Ex- hibition to founding a Technical School to bear the name of the late PRINCE LEOPOLD, who earnestly advocated technical training in his last public appearance in Liverpool. The , Exhibition, we venture to predict, will prove the pride of Liverpool and the delight of I Lancashire.

Mr. JOHN CROSS, who is putting himself forward as a labour candidate for St. Hel ens, does not by any means appear to be accept- able to the labouring population. They see that he has not the remotest chance of mak- ing even a decent show on the polling day, I and, further, that he is playing the game of ' the Tories. Hence the attendance at his meetings has become 'fine by degrees and ' beautifully less." So far from having any- thing like a responsible Committee behind him, as he ought to have to justify the course ' he has taken, he does not seem to have any- body, and is reduced to the ludicrous shift of being his own chairman, and of proposing himself as "a fit and proper person " to • re- present the constituency. Working-men have no faith in a self-elected champion of their interests who goes in for Protection, and would improve their position by adding to the cost of their food and clothing % We notice that, parrot-like, he repeated such Tory statements as that if COBDEN had been alive he would have been a Fair Trader. Such nonsense could not mislead anyone who is familiar with COBDEN'S life and work.; but there are ignorant people in the world who seek to trade on the ignorance of their fel- lows. Mr. LEES KNOWLES, the Conservative candidate for the Leigh Division, has been trying it on in the same way—a fact which a wide-awake elector has brought to the know- ) ledge of Mr. JOHN BRIGHT. Answering his ;correspondent, Mr. BRIGHT says :—" Ask ' your juvenile Tory candidate how it is that Mr. VILLIERS has not abandoned Free Trade, ' and why I have not accepted the childish notions held by the Fair Traders? We have lived up to this time, and remain unchanged on the great question and policy of forty years ago. The only fair trade is Free Trade." It is to be hoped that, after this, we shall have heard the last of this abuse of the memory of RICHARD COBDYN. If Mr. CROSS and Mr. KNOWLES are not ashamed of themselves, it is because there is no shame in them.

div.head: LOCAL NEWS.
div.p: LOCAL NEWS.

HARVEST THANKSGIVING AT Sr. AMBROSE, WIDNES.— The annual thanksgiving for the ingathering of the harvest took place at St. Ambrose Church, Widnes, on Friday even- ing, when the pulpit was occupied by the Rev. Archdeacon Bardsley. On Sunday two sermons were preached to good congregations by the Rev. C. Rurnfitt, of Widnes. The edifice bad been neatly decorated for the occasion. SUPPOSED EXTENSIVE POACHING NEAR RUNCORN.--AbOut half-past seven on Monday morning P.C. Egerton, of Run- corn, stopped a horse and cart which was being driven to- wards Warrington by James Rigby, of Overton. 7n the cart Egerton found three hampers covered with straw, and containing 108 recently killed rabbits. He seized the game, which was sold by the orders of Superintendent Leah, and Rigby- will be summoned before the Runcorn magistrates. The game is supposed to be the result of a poaching expe- dition.

A RUNCORN VOLUNTEER SHOT.—A very serious acci- dent occurred at the Runcorn common rifle range on Mon- day during the progress of the annual competition of the Runcorn volunteers for Christmas prizes given by the gen- try and tradesmen. About one o'clock a bullet fired from the 500 yards range forced its way between the joining of the wood and iron of the mantelet, and lodged itself in the fleshy part of the left arm of the marker, Peter Whitlow. Firing was instantly stopped, and Whitlow, who is em- ployed at Camden Soap works, and lives in York-street, was conveyed to hi. ho_le. He was attended by Drs. Robinson and MacDougall, who extracted the lead, which had inflicted a very ugly and painful wound. A few months ago Whit- low was struck on the shoulder by a bullet whilst in the mantelet, but on that occasion he only received a slight bruise. On Monday morning both he and his fellow- marker were frequently struck on the face by "splashes " of metal. WIDNES HARRIERS ATHLETIC SPORTS.—The second an- nual sports of the Widnes Harriers and Gymnasium Club took place on Saturday afternoon at the Millfield Recreation ground, Appleton. There was only a poor attendance of spectators. Messrs. T. . Gerrard and H. Cooper performed the ramdumteyw ofa composed. The one mile handicap was confined to members, and there were ten runners. Result, IJ. Kelly yards). The first prizes in each (100 yards), 2 H Broome (25 yards), 3 G. div.head: EXAMINER. SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 26, 1885.
div.p: THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 26, 1885.

WESLEYAN BLUE RIBBON ARMY, WIDNES.--Under the auspices of this society a lecture was delivered in Oakland- street schoolroom on Monday evening by Mr. Lamb, a blind gentleman from Liverpool. There was a large attend- ance, and Mr. J. R. Hudson presided. The title of the lec- ture was " a dangerous corner." HARVEST FESTIVAL AT HALTON.—The harvest thanks- giving services were centinned at Halton Parish Church on Sunday. The Rev. J. Wright-Williams, vicar, occupied the pulpit morning and evening. Collections were made in aid of the Chester and Warrington Infirmaries, and the fruit was distributed amongst the sick poor of the parish on Mon- day. HARVEST FESTIVAL AT MALIN'S TEMPERANCE HALL, VrIDNES.—The juvenile good templarp of Widnes on Sunday celebrated the ingatherieg of the harvest by special services at Mali's Temperance Hall. In the afternoon Mr. T. Orm- royde delivered an address, and in the evening a service was held. On Monday evening a "harvest supper" was given I and subsequently an entertainment was held under the pre- sidency of Mr. Robert Balmer, of Oswestry. Recitations, songs, dm., were given. Collections were made in aid of the building fund. KINGSLEY PARISH Ciannca.—On Thursday evening week a special thanksgiving service for the safe ingathering of the harvest was held in the above church, the interior of which was decorated with a choice selection of fruit, dowers, dm. The lessons were read by the vicar, the Rev. A. Griers, the words of the anthem—" Fear not, 0 land," being taken from Joel, 2nd chapel.. 21st 23rd, 24th verses. The organist and choirmaster, was Mr. F. Cocker. An appro- priate sermon was delivered by the Rev. H. Achison, M.A., vicar of St. Peter's, Chester. The offertory was made on behalf of the Chester Infirmary and church expenses. SUDDEN DEATH AT RUNCORN.—Richard Orme, 56years of age, who resided at 44, Wellington-street, died very sud- denly on Thursday morning. About two o'clock be arose from bed in order to ascertain the time, and on returning his wife discovered that he could not speak. A lodger named Robert Yates ran for Dr. Robinson, but death had occurred before that gentleman's arrival. The doctor having certified that death waa the result of an apopletic fit, the coroner deems it unnecessary to bold an inquest. The de- ceased bad been employed at Messrs. Brundrit's shipbuild- ing yard for upwards of 20 years, and was highly respected for his upright character. THE SONS OF TEMPERANCE ON THE ELECTION.—The quarterly meeting of the Runcorn Sons of Temperance was held on Saturday last, at which there was a good atten- dance of members. There was a long discussion on the importance of united action at the forthcoming election. It was felt that the time had arrived for temperance refor- mers to make their power felt at the polling booths, and the following resolution was carried unanimously That this division of the Sons of Temperance is of opinion that no measure of temperance reform will be satisfactory which does not include the direct popular veto on the issue and the renewal of licenses; and this meeting pledges itself to use every legitimate means to secure the return of the can- didate most favourable to temperance legislation." A com- mittee of 14 members was formed to canvass all the mem- bers. This society is one of the strongest in the town, numbering 250 adult memleers. FATAL IMMERSION AT RUNCORN.—Mr. J. E. Worsley, the deputy-coroner, on Tuesday held an inquest at the Egerton Arms Hotel, Bridge-street, touching the death of Thomas Ellis, 13 years of age, son of Samuel Ellis, flatman, in the employ of the Bridgewater Navigation Co., who lives in Heath-road. On 14riday the boy was helping his father to paint his flat, which was lying at Howley Quay, Warring- ton. In walking over the wet deck he slipped into the canal, but being a good swimmer he was quickly taken on board and was put to bed. At night and on Saturday he appeared as usual, but on Sunday he was dangerously ill and Dr. Robinson was sent for. When the doctor arrived at the house the boy's features were swollen and livid, and the lungs were in a state of congestion. He prescribed for the boy, who died abont ten o'clock on the same night.— The Doctor deposed that the immediate cause of death was congestion of the lungs and brain, consequent on the immer- sion in the water, the boy at the time suffering from kidney disease.—The jury returned a verdict in accordance with the medical testimony. SAMARITAN LODGE 1.0.G.T., WIDNES.— On Monday evening about 30 brethren and sisters of this lodge paid a fraternal visit to the Woolton Perseverance Lodge. They journeyed to that interesting village in waggonettes supplied by Mr. Lea, of Victoria-road, and en their arrival had a hearty reception from the Wootton brethren, who had pro- vided ample refreshments for the party. The officers of the Samaritan Lodge took the official positions, Brother Machin, W.C.T., presiding. The visitors 'gave an entertainment of choice readings, recitations, songs, and solos, the pro- ceedings being taken part in by Brothers Fairhurst, J. Jones, G. Widders, Barker. Clark, Smith, Pheasby (Everton), Wright, and Machin ; Sisters Buckley, Jones (Crewe). A very enjoyable evening was spent, and the party arrived at Widnes about 11 o'clock. On Tuesday evening the usual weekly meeting was held at the lodge-room, Victoria-road. Brother Machin, W.C.T., occupied the chair, and after the routine business had been transacted, an eatertainment was given by the following :—Brothers Barker, Coombs, Toro• linson, Jones, Machin, Wright. and Bullivant, and Sisters Lamb and Buckley. On Monday next the Sisters will en- tertain the Brethren. SALVATION ARMY FUNERAL AT WIDNRS. —On Wednes day afternoon the funeral of Mr. William Pye, of 55, Kent- street, Widnes, took place at Farnworth Parish Church, in the presence of upwards of 1,000 persons. The deceased, who was 66 years of age, died very suddenly on Saturday morning when he was about to commence his usual duties at the gas works of the Local Board. He was a man of a very pious turn of mind, and for several years had occupied the position of colour-sergeant to the local detachment of the Salvation Army, by whom and by his fri n Is and neigh- bours he was held in the highest regard. His body was followed to the grave by about seventy nt de and female members of the order, walking two and two, and wearing white bands upon their arms as a token of mourning. In front of the procession marched the band playing a slow march. Upon the coffin was placed part of the deceased's nreform, and the well-worn flag he had /carried aloft on many occasions, besides numerous beautifn wreaths. Spec- tators thronged the rents of the cortege, and the blinds of the houses were drawn. The burial service was performed in church and at the grave side by the Rev. J. Jones, curate of Farnworth, and at the conclusion several hymns were sung by members of the army, and the atils delivered addresses. The proceedings, which were of a reverent and Impressive character, were under the control of Captain Wood, of Widnes, assisted by Captains Sharp (Sandbach). Hargreaves (Manchester). and Tyler, Runcorn. TEE Irma NATIONALISTS OF WIDNES.—About 60 persona gathered in the League Hall, Widnes-road, on Sunday after- noon, to hear a lecture on the subject of the "Industrial resources of Ireland," by Mr Lalor, of Liverpool. Dr. O'Keeffe presided. The lecturer said the chief wealth of Ireland lay in agricelture, but there were also seven great coal fields, amongst the most important in Europe, and there were copper, silver, and lead mines; which were highly valuable, and would yield immense results. Gold even ex- isted in some parte. He argued that Ireland, if properly governed, could support a population three times as large as it did at present. England had, however, prevented the development of the industries of the country by the tyranny of, her taws. It was the woollen industry which caused the accursed and iniquitous union that had laid Ireland so low, was carried. That union was the most disastrous thing that ever happened to England. Ireland was now al- most independent, and whenever she got her legislative in- dependence England would unfortunately have to suffer. In conclusion he urged those present to purchase Irish manufactured goods only, if possible.—Mr. Ford moved, and Mr. T. Williamson (Runcorn) seconded a vote of thanks to the lecturer; and the motion was carried.—Mr. F. Lough- lin (Warrington) moved:—" That we Irishmen of Widnes look upon the manifesto of Mr. Parnell as embodying the legitimate demands of Ireland; and we look with contempt on the proposals with regard to Ireland of the Radical party, as expressed in Mr. C amberlain's speech at War- rington."—Mr. Hill (Runcorn) seconded the motion, which was carried unanimously.—ln replying to a vote of thanks, Dr. O'Keeff said there were no orders from the "Captain" 'yet as to the general election; but he honed they would all be ready "at the rising of the moon." He also hoped there would be such an amount of unanimity as would make tyrants tremble. (Applause.) Mr. Chamberlain at War- rington forgot the Irish people of that town, and also that at Widnes there were sufficient Iriehmen to dictate terms. (Applause.)—The meeting then concluded. WIDNES GOOD TEMELARS AND THE POOLE PERJURY CASE.—Under the auspices of the United Good Templar Lodges of Widnes a public meeting to consider the" Poole perjury case " wds held on Saturday on the ground near St. Paul's Church, Anderson's Corner. About 100 persons assembled round the platform which bad been erected, and the Rev. G. Wright Williams occupied the chair Mr. T. Reay (hon. sec.) read several letters of apology for non- attendance. Mr. J. Brock, JP., regretted that he could

not attend ;so far as he could judge from the printed re- port, the whole matter required to be fully reconsidered. —Mr. T. Snape was satisfied that the offence Of per- jury was not proved against Detective Williams, and that, even if proved, the sentence was out of all propor- tion to the offence, and was unjustly severe. He was, ae vs e .R—. Hughesr E . Ca( rce ovn gd reecgl iantei odntaol satt)t ewn therefore, willing to sign a petition in favour of his re- G. ad s e"Xer r ee lt mein ego. r ry he could not attend. Baron Huddleston, he wrote, Was car- ried away by his personal feelings, and there was no reason- able evidence against Williams.—After a few remarks from the Chairman, Mr. T. Reay moved that this meeting pled- ges itself to petition Parliament and to memorialise the Home Secretary, calling for an impartial inquiry into the case which he described.—The Rev. R. Yeatman (Baptist) seconded. He believed Williams was wrongly sentenced, and that the judge dealt unfairly with the case. He ap- peared to have been committed for seven years' penal servi- tude because be was a private inquiry agent, and not be- cause he was guilty of perjury.—The Rev. B. Burdon (superintendent Wesleyan circuit) moved that the chair- man of the meeting be empowered to sign a petition and memorial OD behalf of the meeting. His firm opinion was that Henry Williams bad been subjected to all this injus- tice because he in carrying out his legal occupation hap- pened to damage the reputation of men who were engaged in a traffic that was cursing the country. (Hear, hear.) He criticised the action of the judge.—Mr. W. Williams (Penketh) seconded the resolution.—The Chairman, be- fore potting the resolutions to the meeting, observed that Williams's offence appeared to be exaggeration rather than , perjury, and he felt that seven years' penal servitude to a man whose life had been fairly upright before was unjustly severe.—The resolutions were then carried unanimously, and the Chairman signed the petition and memorial, whiCla asked for a full and impartial inquiry into the facts.

div.head: ' RINCORN SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: ' RINCORN SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was bald yesterday. Present the Rey. Father Fennelly, Messrs. T. Norman (in the chair), G. S. Hazlehurst„ and F. Rigby (clerk). The clerk read the report of the Her Majesty's inspector on Mill Brow Board School. It appeared that the amount of the grant was £B3 13s 3d, which was £7 131 91 less than last "year.—Mr. Hazlehurst said that the fact that' they were without an Assistant teacher three Months out of the twelve would ac- count for this.—The Clerk reported that the Greenwalr• road Board School was progressing satisfactorily. Mrs. Elizabeth Betley was appointed caretaker of the new build• logs at a salary to be fixed hereafter. A precept for £350 was signed, to be forwarded to the overseers. There was no other business.

div.head: UNITED METEIODIST FREE CHURCH,
div.p: UNITED METEIODIST FREE CHURCH,
WIDNES.

Thanksgiving services in celebration of the ingathering of the harvest took place in this church on Sunday. The interior -if the edifice had been very artisticalls and taste- fully decimated for the occasion with a profusion of fruit, cereals, vegetables, and plants. Mottoes wo, tied innbite letters vu a scarlet ground, and fringed with tote, adorned the walls of the building, and the general effect PM very pretty. The members of the congregetion are to be con- i gratulated on the skill and taste displayed. On Sunday morning the pulpit was occupied by the -Rev. J. D. Thomas, congregational pastor. Runcorn, whit preached an admirable sermon, and in the evening the Rev.. W. Vause, superinten- dent of the circuit, officiated. In the afternoon a imrvice of song entitled " Harvest Thanksjeing,' was given by the choir, who were assisted by a bend of instrumentalists. Mr. John Betoey conducted and Mr. a. Ogden accompanied on the harmonium. The narrative was read by the Rev. W. Vause. All the services were well attend° I, and the collec- tions amilunted to £7 12s. The proceedings were brought to a close on Monday evening when a fruit banquet was held. ;The edifice was well filled. In the absence of Mr. Barnett, Dutton, the char was occupied by Mr. Robert I Wrieht. Brief addresses were delivered by the chairman, the Rev. W. Vause, and Mr. Walter Bray. The choir ren- dered the following anthems in their usual efficient man- ner, Mr. Betrey again conductiog :—" The earth is the Lord's." "He that goeth forth and weepeth," and "0 praise the Lord' On the motion of Mr, P. Ireland, seconded by Mr. Wilson, a cordial vote of thanks was accorded to all those who had in any way contributed to the success of the services either by gifts of money or fruit, to those who had decorated the church, and to the children who had been en- gaged in collecting. The fruit, flowers, vegetables, and corn was contributed by the following :—Mrs. Naylor, Hale; Mrs. ilitchmougb, Halebank ; Mrs. Mellor, Widnes ; Mrs. Norcott, Widoes ; Mrs. T. Atherton, Mrs. George Tar. ton, Mrs. Vause,Runcorn ; Me.srs. James Dickson and Sons, Chester; Mr. Joseph Longton, Ditton ; Mr. George Yates, Hale; Mr. William Turton, Hale; Mr. Sutton, Halebank ; Mr. William Callhed, Ditton ; Mr. R. Leadbetter, Ditton ; Mr. Pownall, Halewood; Mr. Richard Mercer, Halton-view; Mr. Savage, Sankey Bridges: Mr. J. Hulse, Winsford ; Mr. Thomas, Widnes; Mr.' Hall, Mr. Crampton. Mr. Jones, Mr. Forrest. all of Widnes; and Mr. Thompson, of Liverpool. The object of the festival was to augment the fund for erec- ting a new school, and it was announced :that a number of the scholars had succeeded in collecting during the past few weeks upwards of £ll. The fruit, ric., was sold on Monday evening towards the same object.

div.head: DANGERS OF RUNCORN BRIDGE.-BRUTAL
div.p: THE DANGERS OF RUNCORN BRIDGE.-BRUTAL
ASSAULT ON A WOMAN.

At Widnes Petty Sessions on Wednesday, before Mr. H. Gaskell, junior, John Rigby, of Simms Cross, and John Trainor, of Be:lnquiet-street, were hl-ought up on remand charged with having, at half an hour past midnight on Sat• day, committed a rape upon Ellen Hulse, on Rencorn Bridge, and also stolen from her person the sum of is 7el. Mr. J. W. Knowles appeared for the prisoners.—Evidence was given by the prosecutrix ; Joseph Fox, 31, Waterloo- road. Runcorn, manager for Unsworth Brothers, batters, Widnes; William Stanley, furnaceman at Messrs. Golding, Davies, and Co., who lives at 36, Gerrard•street ; James Lambert, 44, Portland-street, Runcorn, ticket collector at the Bridee ; and P.C. Townley. It appeared that Hulse lived at 24, Pear-street, Widnes, and had led an immoral life; but for the past 18 months she had cohabited with a loan named Wilfrid Jennion. About nine o'clock this couple crossed to the Runcorn side of the river, where they called at two beerhouses. About ten o'clock they had "some words" and parted, the woman starting across the bridge about mideight. She staggered as she went up the "slope," and appeared to Lambert to be drunk. Near the centre of the bridge she was met by two men, wh were identified by Stanley as the prisoners. They threw her to the floor, and each committed the assault com- plained of, besides taking her purse and money from her pocket. At this point Fox, who had heard screaming, walked past, but the woman made no complaint to him, and when he had walked about fifty yards the screams again I commenced. He was afraid to return, and told Stanley what he had seen and heard. Stanley escorted the woman across the bridge, after speaking with the prisoners. The woman's screams had been heard by P.C's. Townley and Thompson who were on duty at the promenade. The con- stables went upon the bridge and met the prisoners whose names and addresses they took. They subsequently met the ; woman, who was in an exhausted condition, with Stanley. The prisoners were committe.. to the assizes for trial, bail being ref used.

WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD. The monthly meeting was held on Tnurselay. Mr. T. S. Timmis. J.P., presided, and there were present the Revs. Fathers Clarke and Finegan, Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. J. Brock, J.P., W. Bradshaw, Deacon, lmison, Glover, Davies, and O. B. Danby (clerk). DISTRICT EDTJCATION.—INTERESTING REPORT. The District Education Committee reported that during August 4 weeks' fees were recommended to be paid in 110 cAses, and 244 persons were summoned before the committee for contravention of the Education Act, and 47 were Prose- cuted and convicted before the magistrates, and one boy was seat to an industrial school. A tabulated report of the com- mittee's work for the year ended the 31st August last Was presented. There were 4,051 cases summoned before the committee, against 3,035 in 1884. There were 1,417 appli- cations for school fees, and they were recommended to be paid in 1,306 instances, an increase of 379 on the previous year. Of the 559 persons prosecuted before the magistrates 537 were fined Sc, and 6' boys were committed te an indus- trial school. There were now 32 boys in the industrial schools as compared with 40 last year. The average num- ber on the rolls was 5,737 7, against 5,4543. and the average attendance 47529, against 4,332 9 in 1884.—1 n moving the adoption of this report, Mr. Deacon said the increase in the applications for fees was a bad sign, because it meant that there bad been a great many men discharged from the various works in Widnes, and that there were more men out of employment now than last year. He Was much disappointed with the enormous number of prosecu- tions before the magistrates. He hoped last year they had reached the maximum, but apparently they had not. He did not think the committee could be accused of harshness. Many of these persons were fined ever and over again. There was one man who told the committee he was per- fectly willing to pay 5s every fortnight, and he was fined that amount every fortnight. He had only one child, it did not work, and he gave no explanation of his conduct. This was an exceptional case, and there were cases that were not absolutely so bad, which were, however, quite hopeless. He regretted to state that the Truant Echool had not been a success so far as the Board were concerned, and the com- mittee had therefore not sent any children tlsere. The cheering feature of the report was the increase in the average attendance, partly due, no doubt, to the work of the Board and its officers and to the Council of Education. —The Chairman observed that it must be a satisfaction to the committee that they had pot failed in any prosecution, and it Was most str;king evidence of the care the committee had used. He moved the adoption of the report, and that the thanks of the Board be rendered to the committee.-Father Finegan seconded the motion, which was carried. AN APPOINTMFNT. On the recommendation of the School Management Com- mittee tbe resignation of Mr. Thomas Roughley, assistant master, Warrington-road schools, was accepted, and Mr. Robert Devonald was appointed in his place at a salary of £BO per annum. MUSIC IN SCHOOLS.—IMPORTANT DISCOSSION. The School Management Committee also recommended they be authorised to purchase not more than nine musical instruments for use in the Board Schools, at a cost not ex- ceeding for pianos £2O, and harmonium £l2. Mr. Davies moved the adoption of this proposal, and argued that the committee were merely about to complete the furnishing of the schools, b.eause they must admit that the schools were not completely furnished until supplied with musical instru- ments. Then the matter had been urged upon the commit- tee by the action of the Board, and of H.M. Inspector, and also by the action of the teachers themselves. In three cases ihe teachers had considered it so necessary to have musical instruments that they had themselves supplied them in order to enable them to earn the excellent merit grant, and under these circumstances he thought it was un- necessary for him to say anything further. At present the committee only intended to purchase three instruments for the infant departments, and if the result was successful, they wobld provide instruments for the other departments,—The motion was seconded.--The Rev. Father Finigan objected to the discussion at the Board two months ago in his ab- sence being made an argument for providing these instru- ments, because that discussion was informal and illegal. If the object was to complete the furnishing of the schools as stated by Mr. Davies, then they must carry out such a statement to its logical conclusion, and furnish every de- partment of the Board with a musical instrument. Mr. Davies told them that the inspector had encouraged and almost forced the Board to this action. Hbhad no doubt such was the case, but at the same time such expressions of the Inspector had not been brought before the Board officially, and if he had said an be ought to report it, Another explanation had previously been given of the ' reason why the teacher took the piano to school. Far be it from him to depreciate the value. of musical instruction in schools, but if they adopted this plan be should call it the luxury of education at the expense of the ratepayers. (Hear, hear,) He argued that the instruments were more ' necessary for girls finishing their education than for chil- dren just commencing their education, and that nowhere were instruments more liable to abase that in the Infant Department. In twelve months, he predicted., there would be 15 or 16 instruments, they would have a contractor for repairing them, and they would have a tuner for tuning them, and all at an expense which the district was not able to bear. The number of persons applying for school fees was only a slight indication of the poverty of the district. The present rate pressed heavily upon those in poor cir-
rate-

cumstances, and was it not an inconsistency to as the .. payers to buy pianos or harmo ms niu out of the same rate that the poor were supplied. The rate already was 2s in the A 7d of which was used for schuol purposes in Widnes, and at the rate they were going it would have risen to 8d or 9d next year. He had no hesitation in saying it was unjust to the ratepayers, and especially to denomi- national schools that were engaged in the work of education n the district. They would put denominational schools in each a condition that they could not exist, and he was sure that such was not the wish of the Board; but if they pushed Ii on this system as they were doing, the result would be regretted by the Board and the ratepayers.-111r. Glover said if the Clerk wield be good enough to get the report of the Inspector for last year, they would find a written recommen- dation that instruments should be suppliedie all departments and he was surprised Father Finegan had not seen it. Father Clarke : He has exceeded his duty if be did so. The Clerk produced the report, which contained the recom- meedation stated.—Father Clark,: He has no right to make such a report. It is simply official officiousness.—afr. Glover : At any rate, there it is, and the knowledge that there was such a recommendation had a good deal to do with the unanimous nroposal of the committee. The par- ticular reason why the infant schools were selected first was that they were obliged to teach the Kindergarten eystern„ and he contended thcycould not do so thoroughly without the aid of the pianos. He did not think the Board ought to be reminded particularly that denominational schools might not be able to do all mess things. If musical instruments were necessary for the proper development of education, it was the duty of the Board to provide them. If his senses had not deceived him, Ile fancied he had heard the sound of a piano accomponving the chi:dren at St. Bede's school when he Lad passed on some occasions. (Laughter.)— Father Finigan : Evidently his senses have deceived him, and if there is a piano there it was not paid for by the ratepayers money, that is certain.—Mr. Glover contended that the increased grant that would lie obtained would pay for the purchase of the instruments as an investment. The re trd Schools were the schools of the ratepayers, and the rate- payers looked for the best that the Board could give them. He hoped the Board would support the recommendation. —Father Clarke stated that the full grant for singing could be obtained without musical instruments at all, and he therefore said they were unnecessary.—Mr. Deacon upheld the Inspector in making the recommendation. , It would be no use having an inspector if he did not point out the faults or defects in the thing inspected. In three years the capital expended on the instruments would be repaid.—Dr. O'Keeffe said if they would also provide pianos for St. Bede, nt. Patiicks, St. Mary's, and St. Luke's he would vote for the proposition.—The Chairman admitted that the discussion referred to by Father Finegan was informal and irregular, but they had been such a harmonious Board that the rules and regulation that'were only made for offepders bad almost become obsolete. No discourtesy was meant to Father Finegan as Chairman of the cernmittee. HIS (Father Finegan'e) services to that Beard had been very valuable indeed, as an educationalist; arid they knew that he had very eucctssfully conducted his own schools, and r had given a gre...t deal of time and attention to the Board, and he (the chairman) expressed his extreme regret that he should have had cause to complain. The Chair- man added that by this recommendation there was no in- tention mid no deeireo place the denominational schools at a disadvantage. Since its inception the Board had always endeavoured to trtat the denominational schools with per- fect fairness and justice.—Father Clarke said be did not think there would be any disadvantage.—The Chairman said the Board would be acting wisely if they passed the recommendation.—Dr. O'Keeffe asked who would use the instruments.—Mr. Davies said in every case the teachers could do so.—For the motion there voted :—Chairman, Messrs. Brock, Davies., Deacon, Glover, and Unison. Against: Fathers Clarke and Finegan, Dr. O'Keeffe, and Mr. Brad- , shaw.—The motion was declared carried.

div.head: MESSRS. CASSELL AND CO.'S PUBLICATIONS.
div.p: MESSRS. CASSELL AND CO.'S PUBLICATIONS.

"Greater London" is being published by Messrs. Cassell, in monthly parts at 7d. each. With the first issue there is a splendid large coloured map .showing the roads, railways, and chief features of interest. "Greater London" has many meanings, but in this case the title is fully justified, as the area covered embraces about 15 miles on an average from Charing Cross. The text, which is by Mr. Edward Walford, is to be embellished by about 400 illustrations. "Familiar Trees" is the title of another new work. The first part (price fid.) deals with the oak. It is charmingly illustrated, and it is sufficient of the work to say that it promises to be equal to "Familiar Wild Flowers" and "Familiar Garden Flowers." The book should have a ready sale, as, though all lovers of country walks like trees, there are few who know all they would like to know about them.
wor.

The "Miniature Library of the Poets" is a new venture on the part of this enterprising firm which is likely to prove most acceptable. It makes a good start with Wordsworth, the first volume of whose poems is just out. The work is neatly bound, readable as to type, and very handy for the pocket. It is prefaced with an interesting sketch of the life of Wordsworth. The series may be had in cloth with naarbled sides and cut edgesor in a special binding, vegetable parchment with uncut edges. It is so convenient for carrying about that it is sure to become popular; it is a triumph of the printer's art. "Gleanings from Popular Authors" (part 1„ price 7d) is a promise of good things. With it is presen- ted a large engraving of Joan of Arc, from a draw_ ing by Sir John Gilbert, R.A. It is a striking pic- ture—very suitable for framing. The frontispiece of the Gleanings is adorned with portraits of Lamb, Thackeray, Dickens, Burns, Kingsley, and Washing- ton Irving ; but the selections will not, of course, be confined to these authors, for. their name is legion. The first part is excellently illustrated, and it will be contrary to Messrs. Cassell's custom if there is any falling off in this respect. The book will be one that can be taken up by any person at any hour with the assurance that he will find something to his taste. It will be astorehouse of good things and will be invaluable to those who are in the habit of giving popular readings. "The Magazine of Art " for the current month leaves nothing to be desired; it is .alike varied in topic and illustration, and there 18 a display of abundance of skill in execution. Justice is done to Arnold Bocklin as a German painter. The, engrav- ings of his pictures show him to be apowerful and original painter. " Chloris," from the picture by . Raphael Sorbi, "beautiful exceedingly ;"- quite the reverse—to be candid—of the " Juliet "by C. Van Haanen. The latter, is, nevertheless, vigorous as a piece of work; but we cannot conceive of such a Juliet gushing with love. The pretty poem. "Reconciliation," by Mr. J. Arthur Blaskie, is cleverly illustrated by Mr. Walter Crane.. "The Quiver" for September has a capital fron- tispiece illustrating the heroin of the fireman; and there is a striking illustration of the "Song of a lily.- Amongst the more noteworthy papers are "Northern Methodism," by a North-Ceruntry Non- conformist ; "With the Hop Pickers," by F. M. Holmes; and "What is the drift of. Evolution." new volume of" The Quiver will commence with the November part, which will be issued on o.ct. 26th. Amongst the important features may be mentioned "What. Shall We Do in Heaven ?" loy the Rev. J. Hiles Hitchens, D.D. ; "Famous Pictures, and the Lessons they Teach Us," by the Rev. R. Maguire. D.D. ; "Mistakes about Prayer," by the Rev. George Everard, M.A. ; "Between You and Me : Plain Speaking on Plain Subjects,"• by the Rev. R. 11. Lovell; "Some, Unfamiliar Bible Stories," by the Rev. T. M. Morris; "The Ignorant and Vicious : Work amongst the Highways and Hedges;' by a late East End Curate; " Joshua Padgetts : His Recol- lections ~ Troubles, and Delights," by the Rev. J. T. Burton Wollaston; "Eye and her Daughters Chapters on the Women of Sacred Story," by the Rev. Gordon Calthrop, M.A. ; We have also to hand the current parts of Messrs. Casseit's "Popular Gardening," " The,. Book of Health," "The Encyclopmdic Dictionary, "Recent British Battles on Sea and Land," and the fine art, edition of the works of Longfellow.

BOYCOTTING.—At a meeting of the Irish National League in Dublin on Tuesday, Mr. Harrington, M.P., announced promises of pecuniary support from America.—Mr. John O'Connor, M.P., condemned the irregularities of local branches in imposing penalties, bat he regarded the boycott- ing of landlords as entirely justified.—Mr. Healey, m.p., aim, spoke. BrrrnoG SILFORD.—Tbe bearing of the cases arising out of the recent betting raids in ealford was resumed on Thursday before the Stinemliary Magistrate of the borough. A bookmaker named Daniel Hall was fined £lOO and costa for using the Rob Roy beerhouse, in Broughton-road, for the purpose of betting. Hall' was among those whn were convicted in Manchester in June last, when he suffered a penalty of £75 and the costs. Another case was that of Mark Addy, of the Boathouse Inn, Everard•street, Ordeal. lane, who was charged with using and permitting others to use his licensed premises for the purpose of betting. The prosecution were unable to prove to the satisfaction of the Bench that the defendant knew his premises were being used unlawfully, and the charge was therefore dismissed ; bat Addy's son and a man named Carter were fined, the former £lO and costs, and the latter £3O and costs, for using the house and a place adjoining for betting purposes. Several other persons were fined for offences of a similar character.
