It is definitely arranged that Sir Richard Cross ahalt open a new Conservative Club at Barnsley, on Thursday,. Oct. 6th. Beacstroot Devitnote.—At a meeting of the Liberal Ex- ecutive, on Saturday, Mr. Jerningham was present, end for- mally accepted the invitation to contest the division in the Liberal interest. He will commence an active campaign throughout the division in due time. The Right Hon. J. Chamberlain, M.P., Sir Lyon Play. fair, M.P.' Mr. W. E. Briggs. M.P., the Hon. E. Lyulph Stanley, M.P., Mr. W. Summers, M.P., and Mr. J. P. Thomasson, M.P., have promised to attend the annual meeting of the National Liberal Federation to be held at Bradford on Oct. let. The Daily News says :—The report to which we called at- tention en Friday, that Lord Salisbury intends to postpone the general election until the close of the present or the be• ginning of next year, continues to gain ground. It is confi- dently believed by well-informed persons in the inner circles of both political parties. CONSERVATIVE DIERESIS& AT BIRKENREAD.—Some doubt exists as to the eligibility of Mr. A. Allan, of the firm of Allan Bros., ship owners, Liverpool, whom the Birkenhead Conservatives had selected an their candidate for the bor- ough, to accept Parliamentary honours, owing to his firm having a Government contract for the conveyance of the Canadian mails. The matter has been referred to a law officer of the town. Tem CONSERVATIVE SPLIT AT GREENWICIL—Mr. J. W. Boord, M.P., has replied to the resolution recently adopted at a meeting of Baron H. de Worm's supporters at Green- wich that he "respectfully, yet firmly, declines to accept the suggestion of retirement conveyed by the resolution."— At a meeting of the Greenwich Conservative Association on Monday, it was resolved to sign a document to be presented to Mr. Boord, showing him that the members would not sup- port him. ME. LOWTHER IN A FOO.—Mr. James Lowther, M.P., speaking on Tuesday at Saltfleet-by-Louth, said very clear and distinct issues would be placed before the electors when next they had to record their votes, but the Conservatives experienced great difficulty in arriving at any satisfactory conclusion as to the policy with which they had to con- tend. He had read and re-read Mr. Gladstone's no-called manifesto, and the doubts he had previously experienced had been aggravated tenfold, instead of I.eing dispelled. ORMSEIRIC DIVISION.—Mr. A. B. Forwood's address to the electors of the Ormskirk Parliamentary Division is to be followed by the address of Professor Sheldon, in tee Liberal interest. The professor has promised to address meetings at Ormskirk, Present, Skelmersdale, and Seaforth, and the contest promises to be of an exciting nature. Both parties are determined to work with vigour, and to do their utmost to return their candidate. It is the endeavour of the Liberal party to get the Marquis of Hartiogton to address a meeting at Ormskirk. LORD SALISBURY AND MR. PARNELL.—A VAGUE REPLY. —A gentleman in Newry, having written to Lord Salisbury, asking if it was true that the Government had entered into a treaty with Mr. Parnell and his party, yesterday received the following reply :—" Foreign Office, September 22nd, 1885. Sir,—ln reply to your letter of the 16th inst., lam instrectxl by Lord Salisbury to call your attention to a speech recently delivered by the Chancellor of the Ex- chequer, and in which, his Lordship trusts, you will find a satisfactory answer to the statements to which you allude relative to Mr. Parnell.—Your obedient servant, C. A. Hop. WOOD, private secretary." OUTRAGES IN IRELAND:A Dublin correspondent states that the number of outrages in the south and west of Ire- land is increasing, and if they continue to multiply at the rate they have done recently the state of the country a month or two hence will be nearly as bad as it was three years ago. It in stated that a deputation is being projected frem the landlords of Ireland to the Prime Minister respect- . .

ing the difficulty of collecting rent in Ireland, and the necessity of enforcing the rights of landowners by the agency of the law. Memorials and statements have been received by the Government from individual members of the landlord body, and last week a dignitary of the Irish Church wrote inviting Lord Salisbury's earnest attention to the development of the National League organisation and the consequences likely to ensue. . . . .

MR. GLADSTONE.—Mr. Gladstone's voice has become much stronger since his return to Hawarden • the affection of the throat has seen gradually thrown off, and he hopes to be able to take an active part in the coming political campaign. In case the general election is not postponed, Mr. Gladstone will leave Hawarden about the middle of October. An Edinburgh correspondent says that the date of Mr. Gladstone's visit to Midlothian is not yet fixed, but it is expected that the meetings with the electors will take place in November. The party associations in the county are busily engaged in connection with the completion of the electoral roll. During his visit Mr. Gladstone will be the guest of Lord Rosebury, at Dalmeny. The banquet to be given to Lord Rosebury by the Scottish Liberal Club will take place on the 15th of November, when there will be

a large and representative gathering. Twis mesa NATIONALISTS.—SeveraI meetings were held on Sunday' at which followers of Mr. Parnell delivered addresses. The references to Mr. Gladstoee's manifesto were hostile in tenour, and Mr. T. D. Sullivan, M.P., de- clared—" The Irish question will never be settled by the concession of county hoards. We stand here te-day to carry on the battle of Irish Nationality, and we are not going to lower that flag. We cannot give away our country. We see nail after nail and plank after plank of that old system of ascendency, oppression, and tyranny torn asunder and swept away—(cheers)—and our claim for Ireland is that she shall be made what she was before—a free and self-govern- ing nation." That is my answer to Mr. Gladstone. (Cheers.)—A. meeting of the National League was held I on Sunday at Ballyfin, Queen's County. Mr. Lalor, M.P., denounced landlordism and land grabbing. At present the big graziers were losing ten shillings a bead on their cattle, and he did not think that the landlords would profit by the land grabbers. He advised the people to be careful to select proper representatives. When he last addressed them they were slaves. They had now their freedom in their own hands. MR CHAMBERLAIN ON LOCAL GOTERNMENT.—Oa Satur- day Mr. Chamberlain was presented with the freedom of the Burgh of Inverness. In reply, he said he believed that our local government ministered more directly, and in a greater degree, to the happiness and comfort of the people than even our Administration'and Imperial Government. It was in closer and in more direct connection with the people, and had a closer acquaintance with their wants and neces- sities. While he was afraid of anything in the nature of centralisation and State interference, he had no jealousy at the growth and spread of those municipal institutions which are the great honour and glory of this country, and which are in close touch with the people, and directly subject to their control and supervision. It had been well said that the present was the age of municipal enterprise. We no longer built palaces for our princes, bet we built schools for the children of our poor. (Cheers.) There were two great benefits of local institutions. In the first place, they afforded an opportunity to the natural ambition of every patriotic citizen to be of some service to those aur,rigst whom he lived. The second point to which he would refer was the contribution which this great system of local go- vernment made to the political education of the people., (Cheers.) Cheers for the 'youngest burgess of Inverness were afterwards givers with great cordiality.—At Perth as the train moved away hearty cheers were raised. A similar compliment was ntid to the Duke of Edinburgh, who travel- led by the same train, and both his Royal Highness and Mr. Chamberlain bowed their acknowledgments. Ma, Cwaltnurthatx IN SOUTH LONDON.—Mr. Chamber- lain addressed a great meeting held in South London on Thursday evening in connection with the London and Home Countiea Liberal Union. The right hon gentleman, speaking of dissensions within the party in London, urged that where two professing Liheials were standing for tilos same seat the friends of each should insist npon the candi- dates submitting their claims to an impartial tribunal, as has been suggested. Speaking of the present Government, he said they were placed in office by a combination which was shrouded in impenetrable mystery. It was not a bargain with the Irish members; it was a fortuitous coincidence that just on the eve of a general election the whole Tory party became converted to a policy of conciliation from that of repression which they had so long followed. Their submission to Mr. Parnell was not, however, more remarkable than their surrender to English Radicals on many previous occasions. In foreign affairs they had in most cases followed the policy of the late Government. Was it not the:very irony of fate that the crowning achieve- ment of the late Government, that " peace with honour" which was obtained at the risk of a European conflict, had now ignominiously collapsed, and under Lord Salisbury's Government? Re did not believe the Government would postpone the general election, for a postponement of the dissolution would be an outrage on the constituencies, and they dared not attempt it. Mr. Chamberlain said be was willing to subordinate himself to the wishes of the party, but he felt free to press forward those questions on which he felt so strongly, and concluded by expressing his faith in the new democracy.

LOUD IDDESLEI-GEt T ABERDREN.—The Earl of Icldes- leigh visited Aberdeen on Tuesday. In the afternoon he was entertained at luncheon by the local Conservative As- sociation. In responding to a toast, he said he thought that if it had not been for the stand of the House of Lords and for the campaign which followed, though they might have had a large extension of the franchise, they would not have got that redistribution ef seats which was necessary to complete the transaction, and which above all was neces- sary for Scotland in order to give it a fair share of represen- tation. He did not know what might be the verdict of the country in the course of two or three months, but the Government would lordly accept it, and whatever it might be they would never cease to look with satisfaction and pride on the steps they took when their adversaries threw up the game. Referring to Mr. Gladstone's manifesto,. his Lordship complained of its being too general in its terms. and also difficult to be understood. The less that was said , about it from the point of view of the statesman the better. Whatever else Mr. Gladstone was, he was the most consnm- r mate tactician this age had produced. A public meeting was held in the evening, at which Lord Iddesleigh made another speech, in which he credited Mr. Chamberlain with having sympathy with the principles of Jack Cade, and de- cribed Mr. Gladstone as the most d mgerous statesman be knew. He again took up Mr. Gladstone's address to his constituents. As to the land question, he said the Conserva- tives were as desirous as the Liberals of amending the law of land transfer; but according to Mr. Chamberlain the land question was one which would lead to an entire revo- lution in the system of property in this country. But they might depend upon it, it was not a question of landed pro- perty alone; it was a question of all property.

ITRH TEmmtmawcs PARTY—On Saturday afternoon a' temperance banquet was held in the Technical College, ' Bradford, when the reticence observed by Parliamentary candidates with reference to Local Option was strongity an- imadverted on. A special session of the Grand Lodge of England of Good Templaru was subsiquently held, and a resolution p.issed declaring that Good Tempters would ac- cept nothing short of Local Option in the form of a popular veto power over drink licenses.—At a meeting to celebrate the 17th anniversary of the establishment of Good Tem- piers in England, at Sunderland, on Monday night, presided over by the Mayor, and addressed by Mr. Malins, the Grand Worthy Chief Templar, a resolution was adopted expressing regret that Mr. Gladstone's manifesto gave no assurance of the drink question being dealt with in the spirit indicated by previous promises of the Gladstone Government.—At the Executive meeting of the Manchester, Salford, and District Temperance Union, held on Monday night, the following resolution was unanimously passed :—"Resolved that the Executive Committee of the Manchester, Salford, and Dis- trict Temperance Union desire to express their deep disap- pointment that the Right Hon. W. R. Gladstone in his Manifesto has not given to temperance legislation the pro- minence it demands, and which the people of this country had a right to expect, especially having regard to the fol- lowing statement made by the right hon. gentleman in the House of Commons on March 5, 1580:—' It has been said that greater calamities are inflicted on mankind by intemperance than by the three great historical scourges —war, pestilence, and famine. That is true for us . . . . and it is.ahe measore of our discredit and die- grace.'"—The Rev. C. Garrett, ex-president of the Wes- leyan Conference, has issued an address to the Methodist body, in which be urges, them to make the temperance questiot the foremost at the approaching general election. The reverend gentlemen advises his friends to "let party landmarks go, and vote straight for a sober country."

FATAL RAILWAY ACCIDENT. VERDICT OF MANSLAUGHTER. Mr. S. Brighouse, county coroner, on Monday afternoon resumed an inquiry, at the Bowling Green Inn, Bank Quay, Warrington, into the circum- stances of the death of James Knight (44), a brakes- man, forinerly in the employ of the London and North-Western Railway Company, which occurred on the 12th inst. It will be remembered that early on the morning of the 3rd of April deceased was in a brake van attached to a fast goods train of about 40 waggons,'which was at a standstill in a siding at Edge Hill Station, Liverpool, when a light engine in charge of a driver and a fireman, smashed into it, deceased sustaining injuries which, according to the medical evidence, had hastened his death. Mr. Ferrand, from the solicitors department, Liverpool, watched the case on behalf of the London and North-Western Railway Company, and Inspector Berry was present on behalf of the police. Addi- tional evidence, as given below, was taken. Thomas Kirby, signalman at the Huyton Junction signal box, said that the next box to his in the night time, on the down line, was the Roby box. He produced the traia book of his cabin, and in it was sho*n that on the 2nd of April he accepted a fast goods train from Prescot at 11-45 p.m. That train arrived at 11-54 p.m, and at 11-58 it arrived at 'Roby, and he received "line clear" from that station at 12-7 a.m.- At 12-5 a.m. on the 3rd April he received "be ready for light engine from Huyton. That engine entered his section at 12-6, the Roby signalman accepted at 12-7, the engine passed him at 12-10, and the Roby signal box gave "line clear" at 12-15, meaning' that the light en- gine had passed, his box. There should be an entry to that effect in the Roby signalman's box. John Richard Green, Edge-lane, Liverpool; said that on the 2nd April he was fireman of the engine of which Thomas Hume was driver, and which started from Manchester for Liverpool at about 11-15 p.m. Witness recolleoted passing Huyton Junction and Roby signal boxes, but could not shy whether the home and distance signals were on or off. When they reached Picho-lane signal box, the distance signal was on. Witness had been since discharged from the, company. He recollected the engine running into a goods train. When within 20 or 30 yards of the luggage, Hume, the driver, said "Oh God, Jack, here's a break with a green tail lamp and red side lamps;, hold fast, Jack." Hume was sober. The distance signal at Picho-lane was a red one, and was against them. James Starkey, recalled, produced the train regis- ter book of Pomfret, the Roby signalman, The fast goods train marked as "cleared the line" at 12-7 in the Huyton junction train book did not appear to be entered in this book at all. The light engine marked as "clear of the line' at 12-13 in the Huy- ton junction train book was not marked in that book.. The book was kept by Peter Pomfret, the night signalman. Although there was a curve Hume, the driver of the light engine, should be able to see the goods train 100 yards in front of him. John Munday, recalled, said he produced the train book for Picho-lane signal box. He accepted "be ready" signal for a fast goods train at 12-5, and the next train offered him after that was a slow goods at 1-40 from Roby. A light engine was not offered to him. Henry Valentine, Sankey, formerly a platelayer in the company's employ, said that at about eight o'clock on the night of the 2nd April he went into the Roby signal box. He took Peter Pomfret three pennyworth of whiskey in a bottle. He went in again a little after twelve o'clock, and remained there until Mr. Starkey came. As far as witness could see, Pomfret was sober. He had no right to be in the cabin, his work being on the ground. The Coroner, in summing up, said that a great deal of time had been taken up by the inquiry, but he did not think it had been wasted, because, although there had only been one death to inquire into, the circumstances were such tinst it was a miracle thre were not a great mo;,ay others. It showed such an amount of carelessness on some- one's part that the miracle was that there was Only the death, of Knight to inquire into. The first questio-.4 they would have to be satisfied upon was whet;ner death resulted from the injuries Knight reroeived on the 3rd April, and on that point they liad the evidence of Dr. Fox, who said that he was of opinion that deceased died from consumption, but that death was hastened by his injuries. They must also bear in mind that deceased never suffi- ciently recovered to resume work under his em- ployers. If they were not satisfied that death was so hastened or accelerated, there was no necessity to consider the circumstances of the col- lison. If they thought death had been so hastened they had next to . consider whether deceased came by his injuries accidentally, or in consequence of the neglect of someone. There were certain facts that could not be denied. They were that on Good Friday morning a goods train having passed Huyton Junction signal box, and Roby !signal box, passed a danger signal at Picho-lane Junction, and stood between Picho-lane Junction and the home signal. While that train was so standing a tight engine came into it and Knight was injured. The Huyton Junction signal man said that he received the goods train from Huy- ton, and that he received line clear from Roby, meaning that Pomfret passed the train into the Picho-lane section and then sent "line clear" to Huyton. That goods train went on to Picho- lane, and there could be no doubt that Pomfret not only accepted it from the Iluyton man, but that he passed it to Picho-lane. They ought, therefore, in his book to find entries corresponding with the others, but this train did not appear to be entered' in his book in any shape or form. Until the lug- gage train passed out of Picho-lane section the man at Picho-lane had no right to say that the line was clear, and he in evidence said that he was never asked to accept the light engine. Did they think on that evidence that Pomfret had received the light engine from Huyton, that he had allowed it to pass him, and sent it to Picho-lane without making any inquiry. According to the evidence Pomfret never communicated with Picho-lane, and allowed the engine to pass him without notice, not inquir- ing whether anything was standing between him- self and Pieho-lane. Hume was driver of the light engine, and another question was, did the jury think that he carried out the duties imposed upon him properly or not? Did they think, having re- gard to the circninstances and presuming every- thing in his favour, that he had his engine under, such control as to be able to stop at an obstruction, according to the rules. If they considered that there had been negligence on the part of anyone, then they must say whether it was culpable, or such as only called for censure. The jury then consulted ,in private. Afterwards they brought in a verdict that deceased died from the effects of the accident; they also found that there had been negligence on the part of both Hume and Pomfret, and that in the case of Pont- fret that negligence was culpable. The Coroner, at the request of the jury, then' censured Hume, who, he said, should feel that he was fortunate in not having been dealt With in the same manner as Pomfret. There was a great deal of responsibility resting upon railway servants, and they should carefully consider that the lives and !safety of many of their fellow-beings were in their hands. Hume might now go, but Pomfret would be committed to the next Liverpool Assizes on a charge of manslaughter.
THE EXAMINER, L§ATURDAY. SEPTEMBER 24, 1885

div.head: WARRINGTON REVISION COURT.
div.p: WARRINGTON REVISION COURT.

MONDAY. A court for the revision of the lists of persons qualified to vote in the Parliamentary and borough elections of War. Hilton was epened in the Assembly-room at the Lien Hotel, Warrington. on Monday, by Mr. Millis Coventry, barrister. The Liberals were represented by Mr. H. Roberts (Liberal agent), and the Conservatives by Mr. Nicholson, solicitor, Mr. Longton (solicitor), and Mr. Hammon (Con- servative agent).

• TBCHNICUL onamorrow. • One of the first claims to be considered was that of Ser- geant-Major William Byrne, of Orford Barracks, who was objected to by the Liberals. Mr. Nicholson said he had a point to urge which would effect this and a good many other objections. It was that the form of objection which had been served by the Liberals was insufficient under the Act as it did not specify the list upon which the name of the person objected to appeared. There were several fran- chise lists whieh the overseers were orde,red to prepare for Parliamentary purposes, and the notice bf objection did not state as to which franchise list it was laid, and that made it entirely bad. He maintained that it was absolutely es- sential that the objection should state the franchise list, and in the form of objection there WAS actually a blank left in front of the word " list" in which the particular franchise was to be stated.—Mr. Roberta said he under- stood Mr. Nicholson's contention was that the notice was calculated to mislead.—Mr. Nicholson : I say nothing about that. —Mr. Roberts contended that the notice was perfectly sufficient, and,that it complied with the require- ments of the Act in Avery particular. In the first place the man's number on the list was given, and in the second place to distinguish the particular list the township of Warring- ion was inserted, and then the polling district in which the voter resided, and, then the words "division 2, Parliamen- tary' In Warrington the list divisions were 1,2, and 3, and the old lodgers' list. That "division 2, Parliamen- tary " could not possibly refer to any other list than the list noon which the objected person's name appeared.— The Revising Barrister said the only question in his mind was whether that division' 2 Was sufficient.—Mr. Roberts hold that the revising' barrister had the power to amend the mistake "if there was one.—Mr. Nicholson said the re- ;rising barrister had no power to amend, as it was not simply an error but ,an omission.—The Revising Barrister: Is this the form which you used last year P—Mr. Roberts : Yee; it has been heed in this court for five or six years.— Mr. Nichol Sen Mid' that Mr. Roberts had continued to use old forms which Were now of no use.—The Revising Bar- riser: Are all your notices in this form.—Mr. Roberts: Yes, sir, all of them.—The Revising Barrister: I must take time to consider this•, I cannot on the spur of the moment invalidate' the whole of the objections on one side. —The Barrister then stated that he would give his decision the next morning.—At the close of the silting on Monday, Mr. Nicholson rebewed his argument, and held that the Re- vising Barrister could not amend the notices of objection, and he added that if be could he ought not to do so, as it would be putting a premium on careleseness.—On Tuesday morning after some further arguments by Mr. Nicholson, Mr. Roberts was about to reply to the objection when the Revising Barrister said he did not think it necessary for Mr. Roberts to reply. Me had considered the matter and had come to the conclusion, that the notices would do. The question arose in this way. The form of notice of ob- jection given by the last Act, and which they must take to be the Statutory form, and, the matters mentioned in it as being practically specified in the Act of Parliament, is this: "I hereby give you notice that I object to the name of— being retained on the -- list of Parliamentary voters," and so on; and then underneath is thim note: "The notice of objection irr each of the above two cases should specity the i list to which the objection refers." That, as Mr. Nicholson had very well said, had received the interpretation of the superior court; and the interpretation is that this list, which must be specified in the body of the notice, is the franchise list; that is, it must specify whether it is the list of occu- piers or of lodgers or to, which list the noticcof objection related, and therefore the only,,question they isad to decide was whether the notice of objection before theas sufficiently specified the list. At first he had some doubts, because the note said that where there is a list it must be specified, but there the list was hot named, and if it was specified at all it was only specified by the words Division I. or 11. in the notice. Was that stifficient ? They look at the lists in that township. They had four, to which it could refer. The list of claims they must put out of the question, because the notice of objection did not refer to those, so that they got to four—the list of occupiers in Latchford, the list of lodgers in Latchford, the list of oc- cupiers in Wsurington and the list of lodgers in Warrington. The Latchford list could be put out of the question. because 'the notice was headed " township of Warrington," so that they were reduced to the lists for the townshipof Warrington ; and as everyone knew the occupiers list was divided into three divisions, and Division 11., must refer to, the oecapiers' list, because there was no division in the lodgers' list. That to his mind was sufficient, and he thought he might say that there was authority for it in a Me which had just been quoted by Mr. Nicholson. He thought they might fairly interpret that naming the divi- sion was really naming the list. His Honour, therefore, overruled Mr. Nicholson's objection, and Mr. Nicholson gave notice of appeal.

div.head: AN ALDERMAN DISERANCHISED.
div.p: AN ALDERMAN DISERANCHISED.

Alderman Pickmere claimed in respect of the joint occu- pation of an Office at 45, Bridge-street. In answer to Mr. Roberts, the assistant overseer (Mr. Tanstall) said that the premises 45, Bridge-street were rated to William Travis Pickmere.—Alderman Pickmere said the premises were ' owned by him, but in the occupation of his son, to whom, however, he allowed £lO a year out of the rent for the joint use of the office in question. He was agent for a life and fire office, and be used the office for the transaction of the business connected with that agency. There was a separate entrance to the office, and he had a desk of his owe in the office. The office was also used by his sod for the purposes of his own business.—ln answer to Mr. Roberts, Alderman Pickmers said that he thought anyone would be glad to My £2O or £25 a year for the office in respect of which the elaim was made.—The Revising Barrister said that it seemed to him that Mr. Pickinere paid £lO a year for the right to transact his business in the office, and for that pur- pose be had a desk. He (the Revising Banister) however did not think that was a sufficient qualificatiow.—The claim was disallowed.

A. LUCKY VOTER. • William E. Atkins claimed as a ledger in a house in Grappenhall-road. Mr. Roberts, who objected to the claim, pointed out that the present claimant appeared before the revising barrister of the Knutsford division of Cheshire on the Friday previous and sustained a lodger claim in respect of the very same rooms for the township of Grappenhall, which was one of the townships in the Knutsford 1 —The Revising Barrister: Is the house in the borough of Warrington P—Mr. Roberts said that was what they had to decide; he believed that the boundary line ran through the house. (Laughter.)—Mr. Nicholson : Through the garden lam told.—Mr. Hawkins (assistant overseer of Latchford township) said that the house was in the township of Latch- ford, and the whole of the house was on the Latchford rate book.—The claim was allowed—Mr. Nicholson : This man is in the unique position of having two rotes in respect of the same place.

SIR A. B. WALKER'S CLAIM TO VOTE. Robert Rose claimed in respect of the occupation of the Woolpaok public-house at the corner of Bold-street and Bankey-street.—ln answer to Mr. Roberts, Mr. Rose said that Sir A. B. Walker, who was one of his employers. had a dining ands bedroom reserved for him in the house, and these rooms had been furnished by Mr. Walker. Mr. Walker had the right to occupy those rooms at any time but he bad not slept there daring the Past-12 months. Mr. Roberts pointed out that Sir Andrew B. Walker claimed in respect'of a brewery in Gol borne-street, and Mr. P. C. Walker also claimed in the South-west ward and in order to con- form to the statute pat down their residence as being in Bold-street. It was quite clear that if they had any such residence there and if , Mr. Rose's vote was allowed the other two would fie disqualified. The claims of Sir A. B. Walker and Mr. P. C. Walker were then considered, and in answer to questions Mr. Rose said that Sir A. B. Walker had not slept in the Bold-street premises for six or seven year.—The Revising Barrister: lam afraid that is not an occupation.—With regard to Mr. P. C. Walker, Mr. Rose could not say that he had slept in the Woolpack during the past 12 months —The claims of Sir A. B. Walker and Mr. P. C. Walker were disallowed, and that of Mr. Rose was allowed,

div.head: COLLEGIAN'S CLAIM.
div.p: A COLLEGIAN'S CLAIM.

Frederick R. Roberts claimed as being a lodger with his father at his house in Bewsey.—The claim was opposed by the Conservatives.—ln answer to Mr. Nicholson, the claimant said that be had been away at Owen's College and was still there, but while be was away from borne his rooms were not occupied by any 1)04 else. He occupied these premises during the vacations, and last June be paid £3O for their use during the previous 12 mouths. There bad been no express arrangement to pay for the use of these rooms, but it was understood that he should paw as soon as be was in a position to do so.—Mr. Nicholson contended that there had been no definite arrangement sufficient to substantiate a lodger claim.—The claim was, however, allowed.

div.head: TUESDAY.
div.p: TUESDAY.
The court 4a5 resumed on Tuesday betare Mr. Coventry, barrister. The two parties were represented as on the pre- vious day.

CAN SOLDIERS VOTE? The claim of Sergeant-Major William Byrne, of Orford Barracks, tbe consideration of which had been adjourned on the previous day, was next taken. The claim was objected to by the Liberals. In answer to Mr. Roberts Sergt.-Major Byrne said the barracks were surrounded by a brick wall, and there were three entrances, the front one of which was only used regularly. At the front gate there was a sentry day and night. He was subject to the usual military disci- pline in the barracks, but during the last three weeks he had lived out of the barracks. The commanding officer was Colonel Tnackwell, who lived at Bewsey Hall. He had never known the officer came into his quarters without having previously sent notice of the visit. He could not say what was the power of the commanding officer in that res- pect, but he believed that by virtue of his power he might come into his (the claimant's) residence.—Mr. Roberts con- tended that the claimant was not a tenant as he only occu- pied quarters from Whichhe could be removed at any time. Ho thought the power of inspection which military law conferred upon the officers deprived the claimant of any right 'which onikht be conferred by section 3 of the Repre- sentation of the People Act, 1884.—After some further con- sideration, the Revising Barrister said that on the

whole he should decide that the claimant was entitled to vote, but of course Mr. Roberts could have a case for appeal. —Mr. Roberta then said that he would state a case for ap- peal, and the rest of the claims for officers and non-com- miesioned officers at Orford Barracks, 39 in nramber, were passed, subject to the appeal by the Liberals. - '

aiwiturrir's mutt. -- James Townend Moore, solicitor, claimed in respect of offices in Bank-street. The Liberals objected to the claim. —Mt Moore stated that he was made banknipt on the 15th July this year, and the official receiver took possession of his office on that day.—Mr. Nicholson: Ile had occupied for the qualifying period when the official receiver took pos- -1 session.—The claim was allowed.

A succissaux. cnivermit. - Joseph James Joseph. surgeon's assistant, Bold-street, claimed to have his name Inserted on the lodgers list. The claim was opposed by the Liberals.—ln answer to questions the claimant stated that he had been away ' from Warring- ton for six months owing to a disagreement with his brother, who is a Surgeon practising in the town. When heleft Warrington he practically gave up his residence in the town.—By Mr. Nicholson: My lodgings were reserved for me, as I had the privilege of coming back at any time.— The claim was not allowed.

A PECULIAR MARRIAGE. The Conservatives objected to the claim of a married woman who lives apart from her husband in Priestley- street, on the ground that she had contracted an illegal marriage.—The applicant when cress-examined stated that she had married her mother's sister's husband.— The Revising Barrister having referred to the Prayer Book, decided that the marriage was legal, and the claim was allowed.

WEDNESDAY. LODGERS' CLAIMS. Thomas Greenell Litton claimed as a lodger with his father, who lives in Liverpool-road. The Liberals objected to the claim, and in answer to Mr. Roberts, the claimant said that he was 21 last January. He was sure that he was more than 18 years of age, and had been engaged at Parr's Bank two years. Mr. Roberts said he had information that the claimant was not 21 years of age, but as the datter swore positively that he was 21 last January the claim was allowed.—Mr. Litton also appeared on behalf of Arthur John Robinson, Bridge-street, who also claimed as a lodger with his parents. Mr. Roberts, who objected to the claim, said that he desired the presence of the claimant in order that he might ask him certain questions. There ought,Mr. Roberts said, to be no difficulty Is producing either the claimant himself or some other member of his family, as they lived only about three minutes' walk from the court. The vote was disallowed. Later in the day Mr. Robinson personally attended the court, but the Revising Barrister declined to re-open the case.

THE MANAGER OF THE THEATRE'S YOTE. Richard Stringer, out-door manager of the Theatre Royal, Scotland-road, claimed to be put on the lodger list. He said he lodged with Mr. Sheridan, the proprietor of the theatre, to whom he paid 16s for hoard and lodgings. The claim was allowed. TFIB REV. R. meiEn's VOTE. The Rev. R. Pilcher, 8.A., was objected to by the Con- servatives, but the objection fell through on Mr. filcher stating that he had occupied his lodgings in Wilson- Patten-street continuous.ly for the past fifteen months.

A FINE ARGUMENT. Alfred Dowd, 117, Bridge-street, claimed to have his name placed on the lodgers' list. Mr. Longton, on behalf of the Conservatives, objected on the ground that the claimant was too young at the time ha signed the claim. Claimant stated that he was 21 last month.—Mr. Roberti contended that there was nothing to prevent the claimant from quali- fying providing he was of full age when he came to sub- stantiate his claim—After some argument the Revising Bar- rister took this view, and the claim WIS allowed.

div.head: Burnes STORY.
div.p: A Burnes STORY.

A young man named Grounds, the son of a farmer at Orford, claimed to be put on the lodgers' lint. The claim was objected to by the Liberals.—ln answer to Mr. Roberts, the claimant said he worked for his father, but it was not absolutely necessary that he should live in his father's house in order to perform his work. He could do the same work if he lived a mile away. He was pAid £6O a year. and out of this he paid £l5 a year fer his rooms and £26 for his maintenance. Last Christmas his father paid him 1.60 in gold, and he (the claimant) repaid him the two sums referred to.—The Revising Barrister did not think that would do ; it was absolutely incredible that the father should pay his son £6O, and that the latter should then re- turn what he owed for his lodgings and maintenance.—The claim was not allowed.—Grounds also appeared on behalf of his brother Thomas, who, he said, was engaged on ex- sactly the same terms as himself, His brother was paid at the same time as himself, and he saw the former hanel back £l5 for his lodgings. He was quite clear as to the ar- rangement betreen his father and his brother, which had existed for the past two years.—The Revising Barrister said his judgment was that the story was absolutely in- credible. He could not believe that any farmer who had two sons working for him, making any such arrangement as the one that had been sworn to, that he should pay them £6O a year, and that they should pay him back so much. Why should not the father pay the balance, and that was what really would happen.—Mr. Longton : Your Honour will not forget the declaration.-1 he Revising Barrister: Yes.—The claim was disallowed.

div.head: CLAIM IT A CIINTENARIAL
div.p: CLAIM IT A CIINTENARIAL

r The claim to have his name put on the lodgers' list made by James Kean, 39, Factory-lane, was objected to by the Liberals. The claimant was represented by his grand- son, who said that Mr. Kean was 102 years of age and lodged with his daughter. He Lad an income of between 17s 6d and 20s a week, which was paid him by his two sons, one of whom was Alderman Kean.—The vote was not allowed.
THURSDAY. DRAWING ON THE BLN/C.

Benjamin Balsbaw claimed as being ; lodger with his mother at the White Bull Inn, Horsemarket-street. In answer to Mr. Roberts, who objected to the claim, Bal- shaw said he lived with his mother, who was manager of the White &Una. He worked at the cotton mill, but had been out of employment over twelve months. During that time he bad sot been performing the duties of assistant manager and waiter. He had not served customers regu- larly in the White Ball since his father died. He had had nothing to do during the past twelve months but to walk about, and he only helped in the bouee when he thought fit. He bad kept himself, having paid his mother 15s every week during the past 16 months —Mr. Iteberts asked that the claim should be rejected, as the evidence was utterly incred- ible.—The Revising Barrister (to claimant) : Where did you get your 15s a week from ?—Claimant : It came out of my own pocket. —The Revising Barrister : How did it get into your pocket ?—Claimant : I drew it out of the bank.—Revising Barrister : How did it get into the bank? —Claimant : I worked for it ; it is my savings.—Revis- leg Barrister : Did you earn it by walking about the streets ?—The Claimant said that when he was working at Cockhedge Cotton Mill he earned from £2 21 to £2 5s per week, and sometimes a little bit more. It was then that he saved money, which he bad lived on since.—The claim was not allowed.

div.head: BROKEN OCCUPATION.
div.p: A BROKEN OCCUPATION.

I Thomas Woodsy, a young man, living in Hoyle-street, was objected to by the Conservatives on the ground of his not having continuously occupied the premises claimed for during the whole of the qualifying year. In answer to Mr. Nicholson, the claimant said he had been three months in Americt, and his wife during that time lived in Stafford- shire, but the house was rented in his name, and it was his 1 furniture that was in it, though his father lived in the I house. His father lodged with him before he went to America, and had done so since he came back.—The Re- vising Barrister considered that the occupation had been broken, and the vote was accordingly not allowed.

div.head: ALLEGED DOUBLE CLAIM.
div.p: ALLEGED DOUBLE CLAIM.

Henry Turner, a young man, claimed as an eccupier of a house in S tekey-street. The Liberals objected to the claim. Two uotice of claims were produced by the assistant over- seer, both of which were signed Henry Turner. The claim- ant said that he had signed one of the papers, bat not the other, and Mr. Roberts stated that he had information that the two notices referred to the present claimant —Mr. Hampson said the claims were signed by different persons altogether, and he could produce the other Henry Turner,— In answer to Mr. Roberts, the claimant said he would swear that he had been married over twelve months, and if any- one said be had been married this year he would say that statement was false.—Mr. Roberts said be did not believe a word that was said.—Mr. Nicholson thought that was a very improper remark ; the Revising Barrister had been very severe upon him for what he had said, but he never said anything li4e that —The claim was allowed. "TOO CLEVER."

John Slade Calvert, a young man. claimed to be put on the lodgers' list in respect of rooms in his father's house, Friars' Green. He was objected to by the Liberals, and in answer to Mr. Roberts said that he paid 7s 64 a week to his father for board, and is 6d for his rooms. He was sure he only paid,7s 64 for his board. He got most of Lis meals at home, but, being a joiner, he was obliged on account of his work sometimes to be away, from home, and he did not take his fond with him:—Mr. Roberts: You are too clever for me. (Laugb ter.)—The claim was allowed. " A RASH OBJECTION.-11E&VY COSTS.

An objection was toads by the Conservatives to the vote of Edward Abel, leather merchant, 67, Bridge-street, on the ground tint he resided at St. Helens, more than seven miles from Warrington.—Mr. Roberts said that the claim had been previously proved several years ago, and it was putting them to considerable experFe to have to prove it again.—Mr. Pickavance (who represented Mr. Abel) said the vote had not been objected to for the last five years. Mr. Abel lived in Hardshaw-street, near to the Town Hall, Ss. Helens.—Mr. Roberts said be would produce professoinal evidence to prove that Mr. Abel resided within severs miles of Warrington.—Mr. Perry, architect and surveyor, produced an ordnance map, and said that the distance from the boun- dary of the borou7h of Warrington to the Town Hall, St. Helens was 6 miles 203 yards.—Mr. Pickavance said he bad, independent of the present witness, had the distance mea- sured, and he was informed that it was 6 miles 3 furlongs 36 yards—Mr. Nicholson said St. Helens was generally thought to be about 12 miles from Warrington, and if it was less than seven miles it was certainly contrary to the general impression of the people in this town. He said this to show that the objection was not a frivolous one.— mr. Perry said the distance was what he had stated. asithe crow flies.—The Revising Barrister : I think the ordnance map is the criterion in these cases.—Mr. Nicholson : I don't think the Act bays so.—The Revising Barrister: It has been taken in a good many cases that the ordnance map is correct.—Mr. Roberts : It is specially provided, sir.—The Revising Barrister said the vote must stand.—Mr. Perry

asked for his expenses.—Mr. Nicholson argued against this application on the ground that Mr. Perry's evidence had been voluntary.—The Revising Barrister asked who was responsible for Mr. Perry itt coming there.—Mr. Roberts raid he was responsible; it the' had net produced profes- Biwa' evidence the chances were that they would not have been able to sustain the vote.—Mr. Nicholson then pointed out that Mr. Abel was described as having a residence at 67, Bridge-street, while it had been stated that he resided at St. Helens.—Mr. Roberts said that was not the objection. and he could have proved that Mr. Abel had a residence in Bridge-street as well. There was not the slightest ground for this objection.—The Revising Barrieter said he would make an order for £2 COSI& DRAPERS' ASSISTANTS. Oliver Abbott, assistant to Messrs. Dutton, drapes, San- key-street, claimed as a lodger, and was objocted to by the Conservatives. In reply to 'Mr. Nicholson, the claimant said he lived along with other assistants in a house provided by Messrs. Dutton. lie valued his room at 6a per week, but there had been 'nothing said about the amount to be de- ducted from his wages on account of living in these pre- mises. He was not compelled to reside where he did.—The Revising Barrister did not think the claimant occupied the position of a lodger, and the claim was disallowed. AN ARBITIOCS "ERRAND BOY." William Brown, 14, Napier-street, a young man of rather juvenile appearance, claimed a vote as being a lodger with' his father. The Liberals objected to the claim, and in answer to Mr. Roberts he said he was 21 years of age last birthday.—Mr. Roberts : Why, you were the errand boy only the other day in the office next to mine. (Laughter.) —Claimant could net remember the year he was born, but be was quite sure he was 21 last January. He paid 16s for board and lodgings. There were two bedrooms in the house. His father and mother, grandmother and sister, slept in one room, and his brother, 16 years of age, slept with him. The sitting room was used by the whole family. He would not give 2s for the bedroom if unfurnished.—The vote was not allowed.

"HR COMBS AND GOES." WM. Ireland, who was represented by his wife, a good- looking young woman, claimed in respect of the occupation of a house in School-street, Latchford.—Mr. Roberts who objected to the claim, asked if her husband had not left her. —Mrs. Ireland : Yea, he has left me for nine sears, but he keeps coming and going. (Laughter.)—The Revising Bar- rister: Why does he leave you P—Mrs. Ireland: Ile leaves me when we fall out. (Laughter.) She admitted having put her name in the rent book in place of that of her hus- band, in order to frighten him.—The Revising Barrister: Did heleave because he was frightened.—Mrs. Ireland: No, sir, he's frightened of nothing. (Laughter.)—Mr. Roberts: Did von go and live with your husband's mother 2--Pdrs. Ireland : Me ?—(laughter)—no, it's nine years since I I.ved with her, and I will never live with her again. (Loud laughter.)—Mr. Reberts: You are a sensible woman. (Laughter.)--The claim was allowed. AN INCIDENT. On a lodger claim made by a man named Jolley, in the Conservative interest, Mr. Roberts was cross-examining when he was somewhat abruptly interrupted by Mr. Nicholson. The Revising Barrister said Mr. Nicholson must not interfere in such a way. He hoped Mr. Nichol- son would allow him to know his own duties and leave him to conduct the court himself.—Mr. Nicholson did not reply.
FRIDAY. The court was resumed on Friday morning, and the re- maining cases. none of which were of public interest, were disposed of, and the lists read over and signed oy the Revis- ing Barrister.
WARRINGTON CRICKET CLUB. DENTON'S BENEFIT MATCH.-MR. S. M. CEOS- FIE LD'S V. WARRINGTON WITH BEAUMONT AND SMITH.

.......---. This match took place on Saturday, in Arpley, before a large number of spectators, and resulted in a draw. The visiting team, although strong, was not as strong as the captain expected. Crosfield won the toss, and went in part- nered by C. L. Jones to Beaumont and Smith bowling. Runs came slowly, and the first wicket fell at 16. Cham- pion and Jones left at 23, and Kevan came in. Now came the sensational cricket of the afternoon. Kevan hit every- thing, and several high hits almost came to hand. But luck was all with him, and when he was joined by Evans, runs were put on at a rapid pace. Kevan at last was bowled, having been in while 160 runs were put on. His 94 was not without blemishes, but was a good example of free hit- ting. Evans continued to bat steadily, and Woodhead ably seconded him. The last wicket put oe 34 runs, and the in- nings closed for 234 runs. Beaumont, Smith, and J. C. Lawton all bowled successfully. With only 45 minutes to play, the brothers i awton went to the wickets, and so well did they defend their posts that 70 runs were put on with only one wicket down. Four bowlers were tried, but runs were rapidly hit up, C. G. Lawton scoring much faster than his brother. A young widow, named Sarah Brown and her mother are in custody at Stockport, the former o a charge of kil- ling her illegitimate child by wilfully starving it, and the latter on a charge of aiding and abetting At Southport, on Thursday, two colliers, named Acifers and Shepherd, residing near Wigan, were charged with shooting at Thomas Cox with intent to injure him. The prisoners were committed for trial at the assizes. Mies Catherine Scott, who was some time aeo returned as a member of the Holborn Board of Guardians, has been declared by the Local Government Board not to have been duly elected. Her rating qualification had been called in question.

Twe platelay ers were killed on Thursday morning near Selburst station en the London, Brighton, and South Coast Railway. They stepped aside to allow a train to pass, hut were knocked down and killed by a train coming in the op• posite direction.

SANITARY CONORESS.—The annual congress of the Sani- tary Institute of Great Britain was opened-on Tuesday at Leicester. The president, Professor De Chaumont, in his address, said most sanitarians believed the death-rate could be reduced to 15 per 1,000, and the large infant mortality was a blot on our social system. FALL OF A HousE.—At Annagb, near Ballyhaunis, on Saturday, a house occupied by Mr. Tyrrell, whilst under- going repair, suddenly fell in, burying a labourer named Waldron, who, on being extricated from the debris, Was found to be Quite dead. Several other persons. 'including Miss Tyrrell, were injured, and Mr. Tyrrell himself had a miraculous escape. Wolters! RIGHTS —The Clerkenwell police magistrate on Thursday, granted a summons agaiast a woman whose husband is chargeable to the parish, calling upon her to show cause why the ',should not contribute to the man's maintenance. The proceedings are taken under the Mar- ried Women's Property Act, which seems to operate pretty frequently to the discomfort of married women. THE DISASTROUS COLLISION IN THE CHANNEL.—A search was being made by divers in the Downs on Thursoay for the bodies of the missing persons who were drowned in the collision between the Dolphin and Brenda, and who are , thought to be still in the vessel's cabin. Several of the re- latives of Mr. Leach are staying at Weimer to ascertain what are the results of the divers' search. A COLLIERY MANAGER HEAVILY FINED —John Lix- smith, a certificated colliery manager, of the Soydale Hall Colliery, Westhoughton, near -Bolton, who pleaded guilty. was Stied 13Y the county justice, on Thursday, .£2O and costs for breaches of -the colliery rules. Mr. Turton, assis- tant inspectoiretated that the state of the ventilation of the colliery through neglect was such as to cause surprise ihar there had not been an explosion. SUSPECTED MURDER OF A SWEETHEART. On Thurs- day, Alexander Cooper, who was apprehended yesterday on suspicion of having caused the death of his sweetbeart, Margaret Cunningham, was brought up at the Edinburgh Police Court on a charge of murder, by throwing a girl over a cliff at Salisbury Crags. Cooper, who appeared to fell his position very keenly, is about 27 years of age, arid deceased was till recently a fellow servant of bis at the University Club. Nothing further has transpired to tilt° t, light on the case.

110YAL GEORGE HOTEL, LararacE, To Messrs. FRANCIS & CO. Eagle Telegraph Werke, Hatton Garden, London. July 2ocl, 1885. Gentlemen,—' am p.eased to say that, by the plain and complete instructions you sent me with the goods, I have suc- ceeded in fitting your Electric Bells and Indicators throughout the whole of the new wing at this Hotel, and without pro- fessional aid all was in working order within the time it generally takes an ordinary bell-hanger to clear away carpets and flooring. Mr, A. Allan, of the Allan Line of steamships, has with- drawn his candidature for Birkenhead, in consequence of his firm holding Government contracts. It is stated that a scheme is on foot for the construction of a low water dock at Cardiff, designed for the Atlantis trade, at an estimated cost of £1,500,000. THE Theolc END OF JUMBO—Further and detailed de- spatches from St. Thomas would seem to show that Jumbo lost his life in endeavouring to save that of a small per- forming elephant which was named Tom Thumb. The latter b,came bewildered by the shouts of his attendants and the whistle and roar of the approaching locomotive, and kept on the track. Jumbo, who was leading, is said to have deliberately stopped, turned, and pushed Tom Thumb off the track, and was himself about to follow, when the locomotive was upon him. The flesh of the huge corpse has been cremated. The skeleton will be presented to the Smithsonian Institute, and the hide will be stuffed and added to Mr. Barnum's Museum. Scott, the English keeper of the defunct animal, will be pensioned by Mr. Barnum.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.

LONDON, THURSDAY. It is by an odd irony of fate that Lord Salisburyl finds himself in office just now. A little more than seven years ago he Was at Berlin in company with Lord Beaconsfield settling the affairs of Europe after the great conflict between Russia and Turkey. It was settled that Bulgaria. still stiff with the wounds it had received from the brutal and mur- derous emissaries of the Porte, should become prac- tically independent. On the other side of the Balkans was Eastern Roumelia, Bulgarian in all but name. It was proposed that the two provinces, united in race in religion, in social customs, and in habits of thought, should be made one. Then Lord Beaconsfield, supported by Lord Salisbury, protested against this arrangement and declared that Eastern Itonmelia should remain in the clutches of the Porte. All the other Powers, save Austria, were op- posed to this scheme. But Lord Beaconsfield blus- tered, even threatened war, and the other Powers not caring for the little Balkan province quite to that extent gave way, and hapless Eastern Roumelia was relegated to the tender mercies of the Pashas. Now Eastern Roumelia has sprung up, rushed into the arms of Bulgaria and received a warm and brotherly welcome. The news came with a great shock. Few were thinking of the Eastern Ques- tion at the moment, and still fewer had their eyes upon Eastern Roumelia. It is true that seven years ago, when the details of the Berlin Treaty were under discussion, Mr. Gladstone had prophesied that the arrangement made at the instance of Lord Beaconsfield was unnatural and could not last. But that warnisg word had been forgotten, and news of the revolution came like a thunderbolt out of a blue sky. The importance of the movement, local though it be and immediately concerning a small province, was testified to by the commotion it crea- ted in the capitals of Europe. What will be the end of it no one can say. Turkey has formally in- timated to the Powers that she intends to avail herself of the rights conferred upon her by the Treaty of Berlin, and will put dewn the revolt by force of arms. All the efforts of the Powers will be directed to preventing this consummation. A con. flict between the Roumelian people and the Turkish troops would light a candle in Europe whose flame would speedily- grow to the proportions of a con- flagration. It is to be hoped, and I think may be believed, that this calamity will be averted. But what a commentarythisis upon the boasted subtlety and success of Conservative foreign policy ! If Lord Beaconsfield had not happened to have been in attendance at the Conference on the day when the question of Roumelia came up, Europe would not to-day be standing on the verge of a possible continental war. Mr. Stanhope has characterised Mr. Gladstone's manifesto as " weak and worthless twaddle." Lord Iddesleigh recognises in it the work of a consum- mate tactician, though he somewhat obscurely says "regarding it from a statesman's point of view," it had been to him disappointing reading. There is no doubt upon this latter point. Up to the last the I Conservatives hoped that Mr. Gladstone would find himself unequal to the task of leading the Liberal hosts in the coming battle. The issue of his address to the electors of Midlothian dispelled this fond hope. So Conservatives of the calibre of Mr. Stan- hope violently abuse the manifesto, whilst odiers like Lord Iddesleigh minimise the admiration ex- torted from them by praising its tactical *skill. Amongst Liberals the manifesto is regarded with increased satisfaction the more thoroughly it is studied. Its very length and its calm judicial tone at first repelled the more ardent politicians. But as they find time to master its contents they find in it a comprehensive and convincing profession of Liberal faith, not of the rest-and-be-thankful order, but pressing forward and making of past re- forms stepping stones to fresh ones. There has been a rumour of intention on the ar3,rt of the Government to postpone the general election.i Ido not believe there is any foundation for this.l Except another quartef s salary, a consideration too paltry to have any weight, there is no advantage to I be gained by the Government in playing such a trick upon the people. On the contrary, the earlier the ' issu,e is braved the better are the Conservative chances, because the less opportunity will there be for making mistakes. What has happened in the South-East of Europe is a warning of what might any time happen as a consequence of delay. Sup- posing the general election could have taken place last week, the Conservatives would not have been at the disadvantage of having this inconvenient re- minder of the mischief their leaders are capable of doing in foreign politics. I believe we shall find the general election all over before the sth of December. An event took place at Liverpool the other day which has excited the keenest interest throughout a large community. Mr. Thomas Ismay and Mr., Imrie, managing directors of the White Star Line, were entertained at dinner by the shareholders of the company, and had presented to them tokens of esteem upon which a sum of .£lO,OOO had been spent. This interesting event grew out of a pro- posal made a short time ago by the shareholders that in recognition of their services the managing directors should receive increased remuneration. This they declined, and as the accumulated profits had to be disposed of sothe way, the articles of association were altered so as to allow of a larger dividend being paid than was contemplated when they were first framed. The shareholders were, however, not to be baulked in their desire to ex- press their gratitude, and they accordingly voted a sum of .£lO,OOO, which as invested in plate and pictures for presentation to the tWo directors. This reads more like an idyll than an item of news of the day. It would be remarkable in any commercial enterprise. In a steamship company at the present epoch it is almost incredible. The P. and 0. Company still pay a dividend, and one or two other of the large steamship companies • nohnage to pay a reduced dividend. But the Cunard Line, a competitor of the White Star, has not paid a dividend for two years. So recently as three years ago, and for some time earlier, steamship shares were one of the most popular and apparently most remunerative investments. A favourite form of in- vesting 'money was to form a small Limited Lia- bility Company, buy a steamer, place it in the hands of a manager, who for some time managed to pay ten per cent. I suppose there are few moderately well-to-do people on the North-east Coast who have not /got shares in such companies. Two years ago the bubble burst. There was 110 work for the steamers to do. They were laid up in hundreds, and thou- sands of families found their income greviously reduced. I have personal acquaintance with at least half a dozen people who were accustomed to draw their ten per cent, from their steamship shares, and now do not get a penny. And here is the White Star Line getting bigger dividends than . ever, and pressing a present of .£lO,OOO upon their bashful directors! This is marvellous manage- ment. It is the general impression, which I confess I shared, that when Lord Sherbrooke, throwing off the weeds of his widowerhood, took to himself a wife, the lady in question had subdued him by her youth and beauty. I happened to meet Lord Sherbrooke lately in company with the bride, and had the impression corrected. Lady Sherbrooke is most estimable, but facts forbid the theory that she is young, and fiction could not rise to the height of calling her beautiful. She is tall and spare, not to say angular, and is not ashamed of the many silver threads in her hair. She dresses very quaintly, and is not likely to set the fashion in whatever circle she may move. The other bride who has lately, and somewhat surprisingly, been raised to the peerage, is definitely said to be young and pretty. But Lady Coleridge has not yet returned to town from her honeymoon trip, and we must Wait to see. Lord Randolph Churchill is still staying with his brother-in-lawlin Ross-shire, fishing in tne smooth • waters of its loch. Sir Frederick Roberts, the newly- appointed commander of military forces in India, has set out for Lord Wimborne's place in order to confer with the Secretary of State before leaving for his new command. This is a little circumstance Which brings strongly before the mind the marvel of the fact that the destinies of India should be even temporarily committed to the charge of a political madcap and swashbuckler. I suppose Lord Ran- dolph will gravely advise the veteran general as to military affairs generally in India, and Sir Frederick Roberts would doubtless receive the advice with respect. No bulletins respecting the health of Lord Randolph have been issued, but it is definitely set- tled that he will not be better before the 6th of October, Freemasons will read with amazement and amuse- ment Mr. Healy's disquisition on Freemasonry, de- livered the other day at the meeting of the National League. It appears that Lord Carnarvon, as Deputy- Grand Master Freemason, has been obliged by the principles of his order to appoint a Freemason to the vacant office of Inspector-General of Constabu- lary. The Bank of Ireland is also a Freemason un- dertaking. Farquharson, the absconding manager of the Munster Bank, through Freemasonry signs corn- lounicated secretly to the Bank of IM,and, and so

brought down the fall of the Munster Bank. This and much else be told his gaping countrymen with that gravity he knows so well how• to preserve. 13[is hearers were not a bit astonished, being pre- pared to believe anything about the Saxon. But Freemasons, I fancy, will be a little surprised to hear of these machinations of the craft. 1 There comes strange news across the Atlantic, strange at least in its probable European results. Some years ago a law was passed by .which the Government of the United States bound itself to coin a certain amount of silver every year. The law was called the Bland Bill, and the greatest advantages were expected from its operation. Its results were most disastrous. All sorts of interests were harassed, and its repeal is now considered as certain. At first sight there seems no connection between this bit of American finance and the com- fort of the British tourist in foreign parts. And yet I believe it will affect him very considerably. What is called the Latin Monetary Union expires this year. By its regulations France, Belgium, Greece, and Italy have had practically the same coinage. Whatever head was on the coin, whatever legend was printed on its rim, the values of similar coins were the same. Italian silver was current in Paris, and the big 5 franc pieces coined in Athens, and bearing an inscription in Greek characters, circulated without, question in the shops of Brussels. The comfort to the Englishman was great. Worried by the irreconcileable qualities of Dutch, German, and Austrian silver pieces, it was all smooth water and fair sailing once he passed into a Latin country. And now all this peace is likely to be broken up, and that unlucky Bland Bill is the cause of it all. Its repeal will liberate quan- tities of silver now stored in the Government cel- lars at Washington for • coinage. The metal will find its way over here; the market will be flooded, and all sorts of complications brought about Euro- pean Governments do not quite see their way, and are slow to enter into contracts the precise bearings of which it is hard to appreciate. In the meantime the Union lapses by efflux of time, the different Governments take over their own coins at their nominal value; that is unless something can be done about the Union before the year ends. At the present moment the only silver coins depreciated on the Continent are the late Pope's lire or francs, and that I fancy chiefly for political reasons. They cirL, culate freely in Paris, and I have seen them ex- hibited at premium here at a money changes near Leicester-square.

WARRINGTON FARMERS' CLUB A meeting of the committee of this club was held at the White Bull Inn, Horsemarket-street, on Wed- nesday evening, when Mr. W. Whitlow (Preston Brook) was erected to preside, in the absence of Mr. Marsh, the chairman. There. was not a large attendance.—The first business was in reference to the agricultural programme sent to various Parlia- mentary candidates by the club, asking their opinions on questions of interest to*farmers, andthe ' SECRETARY (Mr. Stelfox) stated that one or two ! more letters had been received. Mr. J. T. Brunner, Liberal candidate for the Northwich Division, had ; written congratulating the club upon its formation. He (Mr. Brunner) proceeded to say that he hoped . that the members of the club would proceed to en- large its operations, and to maintain it as a bond of I real and effective union among the farmers, the cir- cumstances of whose life and occupation kept them, as a rule, too far asunder, and rendered united ac- tion on their part precarious and difficult. He was more and more convinced that farmers could not secure rightful treatment from landlords, railway companies, and rating authorities, except/ by com- binations. The skilled artizans of Great Britain had, by intelligent and firm union, secured a basis for equitable treatment at the hand of their employers, and had made their power felt in Parliament. The results obtained by their action were the envy of their fellow-workmen on the Continent. By clubs such as theirs alone could farmers cope with land- lords, who, by their position and by their gigantic trades union, the House of Lords, were at present, and had always hitherto been, masters of the situa- tion. With regard to the proposals that the club put forth he readily accepted them as an instal- ment of necessary reforms, which, however, in order to be effective, must include the entire abolition of the law of distress, the prohibition of entail and long settlements, and the abolition of the so-called law of primogeniture. Such reforms would enorm- ously benefit farmers, as well as all other classes of the community, although they were far from repre- senting a thorough reform of the landed system, which must speedily be undertaken. He wished the club increasing success. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Brookes, Conservative candidate for Altrincham Division, wrote in reference to railway charges and agricul- tural produce, asking for further information, and expressing a hope to assist the cause of the farmers if placed in a position to do so. The sec- retary also read a further letter from Mr. I. S. Leadam. Liberal candidate for Altrincham Division, who has before dealt with and expressed approval of the farmers' programme, and one from Mr. Ver- din, Conservative candidate for Northwich Division, who desired to be verbally asked the questions. On the suggestion of the Secretary, a deputation was appointed to attend one of Mr. Verdin's meetings, and put the questions to him.—Mr. War. DARBY- SHIRE asked if there was any information to hand from the Bridgewater Navigation Company in re- spect to the works at Latchford Weir, and the SEC- RETARY said he had received a letter saying that it was hoped that the works would not injure any one; and a second one saying that what was being done at Howley had for its object the passing of flood water.—Mr. DARBYSHIRE said that no doubt that was so, but it must not be forgot that many farmers suffered from the company building the water so high in the river that the drainage hi the land was prevented. The farmers complained of the underground drainage being prevented from flowing into the river, making the land to become a marsh.—Further consideration of the matter was ad- journed.--The SECRETARY said that he had, as in- structed, written to Mr. Whitley, of Stretton, asking for the name of the tenant farmer, a member of the club, who said that he had farmed in worse times than these, saying that as soon as he got the sanction of the member he would write again. The letter of the club was dated on the 14th August, and the reply the 22nd September.—A letter was read from Lord Iddesleigh, acknowledging the receipt of copy of a 'resolution adopted by the club, and saying that the question of railway charges would not be lost sight of by the Royal Commission on Depression of Trade. Other members of the com- mission wrote that the matter should have their consideration. The Secretary was instructed to communicate further on the subject, to ascertain if there was any likelihood of the club having an opportunity of giving evidence before the'committee, and reiterating the main causes of depression in their trade, and the unequal charges made with regard to railway rates and taxes, &c.—The London and North-Western Railway Company wrote, in answer to a memorial from the club, that they could quote stated modified charges for carriage. The Secretary remarked that he answered this communication in rather a sharp tone, as•the so- called modifications, and also a clause that made them apply to traffic to, and not from Liverpool, was so unsatisfactory. The quotations he wrote in reply were not of the slightest use to most of the farmers of the' district, and, in his opinion, the letter had been written with a view to showing a a semblance of concession, when in reality there was none. (Hear, hear.) The Cheshire Lines Com- mittee had also replied, but their letter was not considered satisfactory. After some discussion, it was resolved that the Secretary write further, men- tioning the stations used by the club members, and asking for a certain reduction on all articles to anywhere they desired to send them,—Mr. Percival mentioned a plan which he thought calculated to do away with middlemen and many inconveni- ences. It was to start landlords' and farmers' co- operative supply stores on a system that he explained, carriage being by traction engines. Several members thought that if combined action could be brought to bear on the subject the plan was a feasible one, and the hope was expressed that it might form the subject of discussion at a general meeting.—The committee then adjourned.

I Two m^n were killed on Thursday' night at Maindly Colliery, Rhondda Valley, by a heavy fall of rubbish. A second fall made rescue after the first fall impossible. A RECKLESS MINER.—The Barnsley magistrates had be- fore them on Wednesday a youth named Hirst, who whilst at work in the Strafford Colliery wilfully broke a safety lamp belonging to another collier. The mine was a " fiery " one, and when Hirst thus recklessly exposed the naked flame of the lamp there were over three hundred men in the workings. He was summarily committed to prison for two months. .

SOLDIERS' VOTES.-Mr. Christopher Rawlinson, the re- vising barrister at Portsmouth, on Wednesday heard 62 applications from officers, non-commissioned officers, and men of the Royal Marine Artillery at Eastney Barracks for votes. He allowed 53 of them, remarking that, in his Opinion, notwithstanding the opposite decision of barristers in different parts of the country, the applicants were en- titled to the votes.
THE EXAMINEE, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 26: 1886.
