-,...------ MANCHESTER SHIP C&NAL. Sir,—l observe by your papers the great interest taken by the working classes in this project, which indeed might be expected, considering the enormous advantage it will be to Warrington when completed. Surely the great and power- ful mercantile and manufacturing industries connected with your ancient borough, could, with the aid of Manchester, easily accomplish it. But, if you will permit me, I would suggest a mode by which every inhabitant might be enabled to take at least one ten pound proprietary share in this undertaking, viz., by forming a syndicate company, limited, registered under the Company's Act, limited by a guarantee, with an indefinite number of shareholders. Oa this plan numbers of markets and town halls have been built, paying from five to ten per cent. interest. Such a company could advance four-fifths on the amount paid up on the shares, holding them as security. This syndicate, it appears to me, should be formed for the purpose of financing or float- ing the shares and bonds of the Manchester Ship Canal Company, and perhaps be under their sanction and direc- tion. It is well known that many canal shares of far less im- portance and prospects than this have paid, in many cases, from fifty to seventy per cent interest on their paid up capi- tal, and from the high character of the directors, combined with the soundness of the undertaking, I see no reason why , this one should not do the same.—l am, sir, Yours drc., A. B. C.
NB—lt such a syndicate were formed in each of the towns adjacent to the canal, they would partake of the same advantages.
THE ANTI-VACCINATORS' FIASCO.

_ Sir,—My previous epistle under this heading appears to have raised the ire of the local anti-vaccinators and well, indeed, it might. The exposure of any class or society which falsely boasts of its strength and following, and the recital of a miserable failure of anything under its auspices is sure to bring down upon those who possess enough moral courage to love truth better than falsehood, and facts better than fiction, the denunciations of those who prefer darkness to light, and disorder to peace and quietness. More es- pecially is this the case in relation to the anti-vaccination controversy, and a striking example is afforded by the last phase of Earlestown anti-vaccination. Some scribe under the signature "A Bona Fide Anti-Vaccinator" favoured (?) another newspaper with what was supposed to be a reply to my previous letter to you. Unless one class of readers are favoured with both sides of a question it is positively use- less, and it would be a nuisance to them to give them only one side of the controversy. Therefore I distinctly decline to enter into a ent-sided war with " Bona Fide, Am," who in his contemptible action has just adopted the principles of the majority of his fellow fanatics, and that is express their bigoted opinions at " hole and corner meetings," or through channels where they know or fancy their opponents will not venture to fellow or attack them. If the anti-vac- cinators of Earleetown cannot turn out a better defender than " A Bona Fide Anti-Vaccinator" I pity them. His communication is no credit to the cause he advocates, and his false assertions are a blot upon the principles of which he would have us believe he is a 'Bone Fide" sup- porter. I have now briefly to allude to the letter signed "Anti-Vac." which appeared in the Examiner last week. In doing so I most of necessity knock from under " Anti-Vaccinator " and "A bona fide anti-vaccinator" al- most the sole foundation and ground upon -which they stand. "Anti-Vac." accuses me of being a wolf in sheep's clothing, while the verbose "Bona fide" and the rest of his name describes me in language conspicuous for its coarse and brutal character. A printer's error has given rise to this. I signed my first letter "An Anti-Anti-Vacci- nator," as a strong opponent of the anti-vaccinators, but by some means it was printed "An Anti-Vaccinator "—just the opposite what I intended it to be. Therefore, I would ask my opponents what becomes of the rigmarole about a wolf in sheep's clothing, &c.? My written opinions were signed by a truthful and legitimate signature, and for any error not committed by myself lam not responsible. "Anti- Van's " excuses for the miserable affair are only ghat they are worth. They do not alter my statement of the fact that the "demonstration" was a failure in more ways than one. To go through " Anti-Vac's " assertions would simply, mean a reiteration of my previous statements for the truthfulness of which lam prepared to vouch. I must, however, give a word of thanks to " Anti-Vac.." for his courteous reply to my letter. There is great contrast between that letter and tbe one signed a"A bona fide, .kc.," but probably the difference is one due to education and truthfulness neither of which "Bona•fide" appears to possess.—Yours AN ANTI-ANTI-VACCINAI OR. Eariestown, September 22, 1885. WALKING DAY IN WARRINGTON. Slr,—With regard to the Mayor's meeting on Mon- day evening, I had up to noon of the same day in- tended to move a resolution " That the term Walk- ing Day be substituted by Sunday Schools Treat, and that each denomination select the day and month they think best for their own treat." But on looking over some figures that had been got together by us during the week ending Monday morning last, I abandoned the idea. Instead of finding, as we thought, our rollers and other con- tractors were employing about 100 boys who attended the last Walking Day treat, we found that they were employing over 300. It was evident that one-third or one-fourth of this number being absent at one time would either stop the works entirely or cause serious loss of wages to the men, and add to the loss, or diminish the profit, of the com- pany. Taking the heads of families employed by the company in Warrington into account, over 77 per cent. were in favour of the aid day—Race Friday, and so long as there was a Newton Race Friday, and that Friday had happened as it did formerly, on the second, third, or fourth week in June (the latter week rarely,l believe)it wasundoubtedly a time oZ the year when far more favourable weather might be expec- ted than the very uncertain Friday (Whit-Friday) that has been selected, which sometimes falls in May. The Mayor hoped each succeeding Mayor would ratify the day that was agreed upon, and so far as we are concerned, from in- quiries that have been made since Monday evening, it will suit us fairly well. Still, I very much question whether the few cold wet days that often come in May will net deter parents from sending their children to the treat; whether the day school teachers will not object, because it will ire- terfere, from what I hear, with school attendance and the breaking-no period; and whether the first Monday in Au- gust, which is Bank Holiday, and on which day a Tem- perance, or Band of Hope, festival has been held for some years, growing more popular every year, will not become such an attraction to the young people as may cause them to neglect their duties and be a source of annoyance ard loss, making it, se far as the employers of labour are con- cerned, a second Walking Day in the year. However, these things have ts be experienced before we can have full knowledge. I endless the abstract of figures quoted from. If you t think they are sufficiently interesting to your readers, you may insert them with these few remarks. As one who has the welfare of Warrington and its people at heart, I remain, yours truly, THOS. MORRIS. Warrington, September 24th, /835.

Right Hon. Joseph Chamberlain, M.P. The reply is as folfows:— • Highbury, Moor Green, Birmingham, Sept. 21, 1885. Sir.—Mr. Chamberlain has received your letter of the 15th inst. on his return from Scotland. In reply, I am instructed to say that your statement of the reforms desired by the Radical party in con- nection with the land is perfectly accurate, except that the paragraph numbered 4 in your last should read "restitution of common land, or other public rights which have been illegally appropriated." Yours truly, aVar. WOODINGS. Mr. B. Kniveton.

"ODDS AND ENDS."

Sir,-1 suppose it is quite within the province of anyone to draw attention to matters that affect the earnings of workmen. There are so many questions now before the pub- lic that it is no wonder some, and those not the least impor- tant, Should be overlooked. When I speak of matters affec- ting the earnings of workmen, I, of course, aro now referring to what indirectly adds to the cost of living, as, no doubt, We are as much interested by what goes out as expense, as by what comes in as wages. I have, with a few friends. been interested just recently in looking through "The Borough Treasurer's Report of Receipts and Expenditure for the Borough of Warrington," and we were quite agreed that some of the items were, to put it mild, curious. Person- ally I have not the least objection to all being made as de- cent as possible that pertains to the comfort and well-being of our corporate officials, but it seems strange that £2 should be given for a coal box, while £1 lOs was sufficient for a fire grate. Perhaps the latter was only intended for the comfort of a clerk, while the former had to add to tke dignity and respectability of the private office. In looking through this report one is struck with the fre- quency of the mention of Thomas Longdin. I see," Thomas Longdin, travelling expenses, re purchase of gravel, 155," and I am constrained to ask are the business connections of our officials of so antiquated a nature that they cannot buy £2l worth of gravel without an expenditure of 15s in tra- velling expenses? On the next page, again, Thos. Long- din, expenaes of himself and deputation to various towns. re enlargement of the baths. This is remarkably cheap, Mr. Longdin and deputation could not visit many towns .at a much lees cost, but why in the name of common sense should a borough surveyor "and deputation" be required to hunt over the kingdom for plans for enlarging the baths?

div.head: CLIFFORD DIX.
div.p: CLIFFORD DIX.

A POLITICAL HUMBUG; OR HALF AN HOUR WITH LORD RANDOLPH CHURCHILL. Sir,—A pamphlet bearing the above title was ;lent to me by a friend a few days ago. The writer has collected speci- I mans of Lord Random's abuse of a number of the leading statesmen of the day. It should be read by every elector who values uprightness and consistency in our public men. The following passages in which Mr. Gladstone is aspersed and malignantly held up to public odium are taken from Lord R. Churchill's speeches :—On one occasion Mr. Glad- stone is described as" An unkenneled fox ;" on another as " A purblind and sanctimonious Pharisee ;" on another as " A poltroon and a traitor in the garb of a Minister of the Crown ;" on another as " That evil and moon- struck Minister." Then we read that "Mr. Gladstone's hands are literally dripping and reeking with blood," The venerable and venerated John Bright does not escape his low and vulgar vituperation. "Mr. Jahn Bright and his dear friend Mr. Cobden were nothing more than two plun- dering cuckoos who shamefully ejected Mr. Charles Villiers from the nest which he had constructed, and who reared therein their own chattering and silly brood." . . . "Mr. John Bright swallowed two bloody wars with the calcu- lating meekness of the sect to which he belonged, lie has fabricated doctrines of the straitest of the Radical Pharisee. . . . The robe of righteousness with which he has clothed his squalid and corrupted form shall be torn asunder." Earl Granville, Lord Harlington, General Gordoni Mr. Childers, Mr. Forster have all been assailed with brutal discourtesy. It is unnecessary to speak at length of Lord R. Churchill's accusations against Mr. Chamber- lain. In the presence of the House of Commons and the country, the member for Birmingham smashed and pul- verised his puny libeller, and held him up to the contempt of all thinking men. The working classes have also come in for a share of Lord R. Churchill's polite attentior. The peonle have been referred to as "the scum " and "the dregs." Speaking at Edinburgh in December, 1883, his lordship said, " The assimilation of the franchise in town and country is uncalled for, premature, inexpedient, un- natural, and therefore highly dangerous." " The la- bourers," he goes on to say, " are uneducated men, and of feeble political intelligence." But the vital point is this After writing and speaking in this fashion as to the unfit- ness of working-men for the franchise, Lord Randolph, as soon as the Act is fairly passed, claims for himself some of the merit of passing it. As a sample of political humbug, we are asked to com- pare the noble lord's views of the caucus. Speaking in Londoa in April 1884, he said "The caucus is undeniably the only form of political organisation which can collect, guide, and Control for common objects large masses of elec- tors, and there is nothing in this particular form of political combination which is the least repugnant to the working classes in this country." Now observe the change. Speaking at Woodstock a little later on in the same year, be says—" The caucus is rothing more nor less than an immense maehind for political corruption. The persons who have art interest in hunting up the records of the caucus are the law officers of the Crown and the ser- geants of police." So that in one place he blesses the cau- cne, and in another curses it altogether. I would Commend to the Irish electors the following re- marks taken from various epeeches of this great statesman : —"Mr. Gladstone has a weakness for effecting his objects by Acts of Parliament; the Irish a preference for the more rapid and startling dynamite." (Blackpool, 1884.) " Mr. Gladstone and his colleagues to destroy Lord Beaconefield did not scruple to appeal to the most desperate inetincts of the human race; and now, to control and crush down these rebel Irish, this legion of foul fiends, the resources of civili- zation are almost exhausted." "The destiny of the coun- try is in the hands ef a gang of political desperadoes, and it is through them that the Government of Mr. Gladstone is enabled to remain in office." On the 20th of December, 1883, Lord Randolph Churchill spoke as follows—"I be- lieve the Tory party is not prepared ts give way an inch to the Irish party in this matter [of further concessions] ; it is I resolved to stand firm, and I tell you truly and sincerely that on this question the Tory party is entitled to your sup- port. It is time, and high time, to pall rip. Concede no- thing more to Mr. Farrell, either on the land or the fran- chise, or on local self-government." Lord R. Churchill and his party shrieked and howled for coercion in Ireland, they denounced Mr. Forster, and jabbered about what they called the Rd mainham Treaty, and now they have allied themselves with the "desperadoes " "the legion of foul fiends " they so violently denounced. For the present Lord Salisbury and Lord Randolph Churchill are the very humble, obedient servants of those Irish members who were at that time the subject of their hysterical harangues. The above passages from his lordship's speeches, taken at random, will serve to show what manner of man he is. Every workicx-man, and the new electors especially, should read it. With the great majority of the community the great test of integrity in public men is consistency. Taking this as a criterion, Lord B. Churchill will 'be found utterly wanting. We in this country honour and love men whose hairs have grown grey in the service of their Queen and who have laboured for the interests of humanity. I believe the result of the coming general election will prove that this great country has faith in the principles advocated by the Grand Old Man, and declines to hand over the reins of government to political mountebanks of the Churchill type.—Yours, dec., FELIX BOLT. September 18th, 1885.

17xariareemantat Yotrras.—Before Mr. P. Stubs, at the Occasional Court House, Warrington, on Tuesday, Chas. Day and Wm. Day, aged respectively 16 and 13 years, were charged with sleeping in a waggon in the cart shed of Mr. James Fairclough, Fairclough•street, Earlestown, at half- Past eleven on the previous night. P.S. Commins found the prisoners and locked them up.—Tbe elder boy ((Marks) admitted that he had been sleeping out in yards and closets for the last six weeks ; sad the younger lad said he had been similarly sleeping for about a week. The stepmother Of the two prisoners said they were completely unmanage- able. They lad a good home to go to if they liked. The elder boy had been employed at the bottle works of Mr. Hor- ror, but be had left on several occasions, and his younger brother had been ' employed by Mr. Walton, paraffin oil dealer, and also by Mr. Hunt, farmer, but he ran away from his work—The maaistrate asked the lads if they would look for work and be better in future, and when they promised to do this they were discharged. If they came bsfore him again they would be sent to prison.

PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHAPEL SERSIONS.—The an- nual sermons in aid of the trust fund were Preached in the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Legh-street. Barlestown, on Sanday, by the Rev. Robert Hind, of Durham. In the morning there was a fair congregation, and the preacher based his remarks on the words "Go tell his disciples and Peter," urging on his hearers that while the Divine Father cared for the whole community, he did not overlook in- dividuals. There was a large congregation in the evening. when Mr. Hind preached an exeellent and impressive ser- mon on the crucifixion of Christ, and His Divine character and influence. A special service was held in the afternoon, and was conducted by the Rev. F. N. Shimmin, resident minister. The principle feature was an instructive address by the Rev. R. Hind. At each of the services the choir, under the leadet -thip of Mr. W. Banton, sang a sett ction of hymns, and Mr. W. Austin accompanied on the harmonium. The collections, which were in aid of the trust fund and to defray the expenses of beautifying tho chapel, amounted to £Blss.

div.head: LATEST NEWs.
div.p: LATEST NEWs.

Summonses have been issued for a Cabinet Council to be held to-day (Saturday). The Central News learns that the Admiralty have deci- ded to discharge all the hired transports as they arrive from Egypt.__•
IVI. Waddington, the French Ambassador, arrived at Gharing Cross Station by the Faris express at six o'clock last evening.

lutelligence has reached Dundee of the total loss of the whaler Cornwallis. She was crushed in ice on the 21st of August. The crew has been saved. Great activity is displayed throughout the United States in raising funds to defray the expenses of Irish 'candidates at the approaching election. At the Cambridge Registration Court, on Friday, the arguments respecting the University votes were concluded. The Barrister said he would take time to consider his de- cision.

The National Society for ' Women's Su rage, ffrage having failed to obtain their demands from Parliament, has now issued an appeal to the electors " to put an end to the tin- jut exclusion of women from representation!' Lord Shaftesbury passed a restless night, and was very weak on Friday. It is feared that the veteran philanthro- pist is sinking. The bulletin issued at half-past six this evening stated that there was no perceptible change in his Lordship's condition. Most of the members of the family I are now at Folkestone.

MINERS' WAGES.-At the National Miners' Conference at Nottingham, on Friday, it was stated that although trade had greatly improved, wages continued to be most inade- quate. After some discussion, it was resolved that the dis- tricts represented at the Conference should forthwith demand an increase of 15 per cent. THIE BIGAMY Casa—The extraordinary bixamy case, in ' which James Malcolm was charged with feloniously marry- ing a young lady at Brighton during the life of his wife, concluded at the Central Criminal Court on Friday evening. Although Mr. Justice Hawkins summed up against the prisoner, the jury were unable to agree, and were dis- charged._

Awn-VAccrwAnotr.—Seventeen persons were summoned at Leicester on Friday for refusing to comply with the Compulsory Vaccination Acts. The defendants urged con- scientious objections and declined te carry out the opera- tion. The magistrates made orders and inflicted fines in each case. The latest returns for the twelve months, just issued, show that out of 4,800 children born, only 1,200 were vaccinated, and it is becoming more and more difficult to deal with the cases.

_ THE LONDON SOCIALISTS.—Mr. William Thompson, bar- rister, attended before Mr. Lushington, at the Thames Police Court, on Friday, with Miss Annie Besant and Mr. H. Hyndman, and offered the two last-named as sureties in the case of Lewis Lyons, sentenced to imprisonment for an alleged assault at Sunday's Socialist meeting at Li ME house. After some formal questions their surety was accented, and Lyons ordered to be released. It is stated that this is the first case where the bail of a married woman has been ac- cepted. The Socialists are organising a demonstration for Sunday. JUMBO'S RamenTs.—i New. York correspondent tele- graphs that the taxidermist who has had charge of the work upon Jumbo's body states that the elephant's stomach contains many English coins—gold as well as silver and bronze. Ills tusks had by the collision with the train been driven neatly through the skid!. According to late accounts as to the accident, Jumbo at the last moment faced and charged the locomotive. The elephant's skin was found to be an inch and a half thick, and it weighed 1,5371b5. The skeleton weighs 2,4001b5., and the total weight of the body was over six tons. The cost of stuffing the elephant will be 2,000 dollars, besides the wages for three months of those engaged in the work.

div.head: SWISS VILLAGE BURNED DOWN.
div.p: A SWISS VILLAGE BURNED DOWN.

_ GENEVA, FRIDAY.—The village of Fettan, in the Canton of Grisons, has been totally destroyed by fire. Sixty houses were burned down. A REBEL FORT CAPTURED IN THE SOUDAN. Canto, FRIDAY.—The friendlies under Sheikh Salela of the Kabbabish tribe have captured the fort at Debbeh, whereby the rebels communication has been out off.

div.head: GERMANY AND SPAIN.
div.p: GERMANY AND SPAIN.

MADRID, FRIDAY.—The German Government have pro- posed the mediation of the Pope, instead of arbitration, for the settlement of the differences between Spain and Germany, it has been accepted by the Spanish Govern- ment.

div.head: TERRIBLE CYCLONE IN INDIA.
div.p: TERRIBLE CYCLONE IN INDIA.

.... Information received in Liverpool on Friday morning re- ports a terrible cyclone off Calcutta. The Liverpool ship Viscount is reported lost. Nothing is known of the crew, about 30 in number. The British India Company's steamer Boaldana is ashore' and the British ship Brittannia is par- tially dismasted. Other vessels are badly damaged. ST. LOUIS MURDER.—IDENTIFICATION OF

div.head: PHOTOGRAPHS.
div.p: PHOTOGRAPHS.

Captain Lingard, s-uiTe;iii-eTici;;;-f-r;olice at Hyde, has in his possession seven portraits received from Ashley C. Clover, circuit attorney, St. Louis. They are copies of photographs found in Maxwell's trunk. Four of them are easily recognisable. One is that of Hugh Mottram Brooks. late of Hyde. Though the lower part of the features is hidden by a beard and moustache, his mother and sister and another relative have identified the portrait. Two girls and a young man cannot be identified. Dr. NEW TURKISH MINISTRY. C.;:k ,TANTINOIMR, FRIDAY, 11-30 A.M.—The Ministry has been dismissed rid replaced by a new Cabinet, which is composed as follows :—Kiamil Pack', Grand Vizier; Said Pacha (at present Turkish Ambassador in Berlin), Minister for Foreign Affairs; Munir Pacha, Minister of the Interior; Server ream, Minister of Justice; Aarifa Pacha, President of the Council of State ; Artin Effendi, Mustecbar at the Ministry for Foreign Affairs; Syreya Bey, First Secretary to the Sultan. Edbam Pacha has been appeinted Ambassador to France, Essad Pacha (at present Ambassador in the French capital) being transferred to Berlin. INVASION OF ROUMELIA BY THE TURKS.
Secretary

PARIS, FRIDAY.—A telegram from Constantinople to-day states that the Turks have occupied a Roumelian village near the frontier for the purpose of asserting their rights, but they would not advance until an agreement had been arived at with the Powers.
ST. PEITHRSBIIRG, FRIDAY.—The Novoe Vreinge of to- day hints at the possibility of Bulgaria being occupied by Russian troops. _
CONFERENCE OF EUROPEAN POWERS.

VIENNA, FRIDAY Montana —lt is reported here on good authority that Count Kalnoky will propose a Conference of the European Powers to discuss the East Roumelian difficulty. All indications go to show that such a Confer- ence would be accepted. The recent rumours of fighting between the Turkish troops and the gonmelian Militia are untrue. No collision has as yeti taken place. No credence is given here to the ransours of an intended Rassian invasion of Roumelia. ,No Turkish troops are available, except the garrison at Constantinople, and these troops the Sultan refuses to put in the field, fearing A revolution in their absence,

div.p: MOVEMENT OF TROOPS.
BBLGRADIA, FRIDAY.—Twelve battalions of troops have gone south. Goods traffic on the railways is stopped to facilitate the movements of troops

div.head: CONSERVATIVE AIEETIN AT
div.p: CONSERVATIVE AIEETIN AT
RUNCORN.

Last night Mr. W. H. Verdin, the Conservative can- didate for Northwich division, addressed a meeting in Holy Trinity Girls' School, Runcorn, There was a good audience, amongst whom were many Liberals. Dr. Steele presided.—Mr. Verdin mentioned that he had been a rate- payer in Runcorn for the last 14 years, and the firm of which he was a member had been ratepayers for a much longer time, and had shipped salt from the port of Runcorn for 40 years. His interests were theirs, and as a fellow - ratepayer ha should have pleasure in assisting them in every way he possibly could in order that the rates might be kept down in the town. (Applause.) His opponent had said "Fancy an Egerton being succeeded by a Verdin." It was his (the speaker's) proud boast that he was the son of an Englishman and a Cheshire man ; he came there as such to uphold the principles of Conservatism ; and one of the most prominent principles of Conservatism was that the son of an Englishman should represent an English consti- tuency. (Applause). Mr. Chamberlain was making the cry of free education a bait to the working classes. He seemed to be of opinion that the working classes desired to have their children educated at the public expense entirely. There was a honest pride amongst the working classes which he (Mr. Verdin) was sure would not permit them to have free education forced upon them as political food. (Ap- plause.) Free education would be a blow to Church Schools, Wesleyan Schools, and Catholic Schools; and an enormous expense would be thrown upon the country. At I present Board schools cost as much again as the voluntary schools. The Radicals told them they wished to benefit the working classes by free education. But what did he find ? the Radical candidate for Northwich Division even proposing that those who needed relief should not have it given to them outside the Work- house, but must go to the Workhouse for it. He believed the working classes of Ruocorn would say they would not tolerate such a want of sympathy with the poor, and they would return the Conservative candidate to represent them in the House of Commons in order that he might resist any attempt to trample upon the feelings, the rights, and privileges of the poor. (Applause.)—On the motion of the Rev. W. Preston, seconded by Mr. J. W. Shores, a vote of confidence and support was passed.

THE EARLEsTows LIBERAL CLUB.—A. special mew', ing of the members of the Earlestown and District Liberal Club, called by requisition, was held in the billiard-room on Tuesday evening. There was a large attendance, and Mr. W. Urquhart, who presided, was supported by Mesere. John Clarke, John Ball, 51.Birkhead, T. Howard (secretary), and others. The Secretary read the requisition, signed by 20 members, which stated that the business was "to take into consideration the question of providing refreshments for the members of the club." Au animated dis- cussion took place in which Messrs. Kelly, McEvoy. Hollvocke, Hall, and others took part, and it was ultimateiy resolved, on the motion of Mr. G. Green, seconded by Mr. Ball, that it was desirable refreshments such as ginger beer, lemonade, bottled beer, and stout, tea, coffee, meat pies, cakes, kc., shou:d be kept in the club, and sold at a fixed scale. This was the only business.

eontracto. _ RUNCORN-UNION.:-CONTRACTS for PROVISIONS and SUPPLIES for the half-year ending 31st March, 1886.—The GUARDIANS of the 'eon of the RuNcoux Minns are desirous of receiving TENDERS from parties willing to CONTRACT for the supply of Flour and Oatmeal, Gro- ceries, Peas, Cheese, Salt Butter; Cod Liver and Paraffin Oil; Quinine; good Beef, to consist of vein and brisket pieces, the price to include about 301bs. per week of the best butcher's meat for the officers, and sides of Mutton; • Best Brand lots American or English Bacon; Potatoes ; Wheat Straw ; Drapery and Clothing ; Men's, Women's, Boys' and Girls' Shoes, of various sizes, as per samples, to be seen at the Workhouse, Button; House Coal (colliery to be named); good Deal Coffins, specifying size, and including plate with name, age and date of death, to be delivered in the Union when and where required; Carting at per mile, and Funerals at per funeral. Parties tendering for the supply of the above-mentioned goods will be required to deliver the same at the Workhouse, free of cost to the Guardians. how and when required. Tenders to be accompanied with samples (except drapery goods) as far as practicable. The Guardians do not bind themselves to ac- cept the lowest or any tender. Persons desirous of tendering must apply by letter to my office, in Frodshsun, for a printed Form of Tender (and none other can be entertained), where a schedule of the various articles required and further particulars may be obtained. Sealed Tenders, addressed to the Guardians, to be forwatded to the Clerk's office. Frodsham. on or before Monday, the 28th day of Sept,.mber. 1885, endorsed " Tender for ." The tenders will be opened and considered at a meeting of the Guardians to be held in the Board Room, Dutton, on the 29th September, 1885, at Two p.m. Parties whose tenders are accepted must eater into a written contract, and be prepared to enter into a bond with two sureties, if re- quired by the Guardians. By order of the Board, H. LINAK ER. Frodsham, 11th September. 1885, Clerk to the Guardians.

He got into a third-class carriage in Which Were already five men, and, as he entered, seeing a pascal of thin papers on the floor under the seat, picked them up. Looking at them and then at his com- panions,he asked if any gentleman had lost a bundle of papers. Each man replied in the negative, and the hunts- man called the Stationmaster, and as the train was mov- ing off, handed the bundle to him saying, "As they ap- pear to be banknotes, I had better leave them with you." The men in the carriage agreed that he had done right; but after a time one of them began to feel in his pockets, and with many imprecations on his own stupidity, an- nounced that he had lost a bundle of notes which he had received that day at the market. A discussion ensued as to what was best to be done, and it was agreed that the best thing was for the owner of the notes to get out at the next station, take a fly, and go back as hard as he could to claim his notes. This was done, and as the vic- tim hurried off, the huntsman laughed a quiet laugh, and said, "I thought there would be one rogue out of six men. It was a bundle of playbills !" RUNCORN V. TOTTIEGTON.—The Runcorn Football Club opened the season on Saturday by playing a match with Tottington, a club by which they were defeated last year. Great interest was taken in the match, and between one and two thousand persons passed through the gates. The members of the „home team appeared in the new myrtle green jersey, which has just been supplied by Messrs. Uneworth Bros. The jersey is tastefully made, and with a good appearance combines durability. The ball was set in motion by Lewis for the home team, and it made good pro- gress against the strong wind that was blowing. It was, however, well charged down by the visitors, and driven into touch. On being thrown into the field, Coop for Totting- ten secured the right of a free kick from a drive by Broady. The ball was well returned by the home forwards, and soon fell into a scrimmage in which the visitors made slight headway. After some loose play, in which no point of im- portance was made, the Runcorn forwards seriously menaced the visitors' quarters, but their charge was diver- ted by Hammett and Fogg, the latter of whom passed to Green, who succeeded in placing the ball. Coop kicked for the goal, but the ball fell .vide of the mark. On the ball being kicked into play byaWright, the visitors were not long before Barlow had registered another try to their credit. At this time the Runcorn men roused themselves and displayed a little ef their old energy. By strong ex- ertions, Barnes, Hoffland, and Gatley rushed up to the line , of the visitors, but their point of advantaae was cut short by Woods touching down for the Tottington team. Still undaunted, the ball was no sooner in play than the home team made a gallant rush, but unluckily the ball was kicked dead. The play in the second half was a little faster, and Andrews obtained a good try for his team. The main defect in the play of the home team was the absence of passing tactics, which was a ,noteworthy feature of several of last year's matches. Apart from this, the game was I marked by great good humour, and a combination of unity and dash that won the home team much praise. The mem- bers will soon find themselves in form. Many had not donned the jersey since last season, and Saturday must have found them somewhat out of practice. They have, several first-class teams to meet during the year, and quite understand what is required of them. Hamnett. ' Mr. W. Ireland, of Widnes, was the referee. NOTES BY THE WAY. The decision of ttfe Scotch Football Association Commit- tee to prevent professionalism gaining a foothold over the border,' has caused great commotion on both sides of the Tweed. From the state the question was left in at the close Of last season, it was evident that something must be done. That something has been done, aid the committee have landed the association into a similar position to the one in which the English Association found itself at the beginning of last season, and we venture to prophesy that sooner or later the same goal—professionalism—will be reached in Scotland as in England. The case so far is on all-fours with that of England. Judging from two or three notes to be found in some of the leading Scotch athletic papers professionalism has by this time gained an entrance into Scotch clubs. As a proof of this, one needs only to bear in mind that last year two of the men belonging to the Heart of Midlothian were dis- qualified for accepting payment; that in the tie in the Scottish Cup competition played between the Glasgow Rangers and 3rd L.R.V., Thomson, a professional in the North End, was fetched from Preston, and that threats of exposure were made by each club, but afterwards hushed up. In the Scottish Athletic Journal of last week appeared the following :—" I have it on very good authority that the canvassing-for-players epidemic has broken out in a promi- nent Dundee club, who have for some time been pestering Easton, of the Strathmore, to join their ranks. I only wish some of our Northern clubs could see the sad effects wrought upon several of our Southern teams by this detestable sys- tem of poaching, and I am certain they would shut their doors against it for ever. I have for a long time looked upon the Dundee district as the only spot in Scotland which had not been contaminated by this vile system of football plagiarism, but I find to my sorrow that I have been mis- taken."
